bills.title: Laken Riley Act
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Secretary of Homeland Security to take into custody aliens who have been charged in the United States with theft, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Laken Riley Act requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain any non-citizen who entered the country unlawfully or without required documents and who has been charged with, arrested for, or convicted of burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or any crime causing death or serious bodily injury. It also gives state attorneys general the right to sue the federal government in federal court over immigration enforcement decisions they believe harm their states.
bills.brief: Requires DHS to detain unlawfully present non-citizens charged with theft, burglary, or violent crimes, and allows state attorneys general to sue the federal government for immigration enforcement failures.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Detention Trigger
subs: DHS must detain unlawfully present non-citizens charged with burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, or assault of a law enforcement officer
Detention also required for any charge resulting in death or serious bodily injury to another person
DHS must issue a detainer and take custody if the person is not already held by federal, state, or local officials

top_lines.headline: State Enforcement Rights
subs: State attorneys general may sue DHS or the Attorney General for injunctive relief over immigration enforcement failures
States are considered harmed if residents suffer any harm, including financial harm exceeding $100
Covers five categories: release decisions, border inspection failures, visa penalty violations, parole restrictions, and removal-period detention failures

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on January 29, 2025, as Public Law 119-1. The bill passed the Senate 64-35 and the House 263-156 with bipartisan support.

sections.label: Section 2 — Detention of Certain Aliens Who Commit Theft

items.main: Amends the Immigration and Nationality Act to require mandatory detention of unlawfully present non-citizens who have been charged with, arrested for, or convicted of specified offenses.
items.detail: The specified offenses are burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, and any crime resulting in death or serious bodily injury. The trigger applies to non-citizens who are inadmissible because they entered without inspection, used fraud or misrepresentation, or lacked required documents. DHS must issue a detainer and take custody of the individual if they are not already held by other authorities.

sections.label: Section 3 — Enforcement by Attorney General of a State

items.main: Grants state attorneys general standing to sue DHS or the U.S. Attorney General in federal district court for injunctive relief over five categories of immigration enforcement failures.
items.detail: The five enforceable categories are: failure to detain during border inspection, failure to fulfill removal requirements, failure to stop issuing visas to nationals of countries that refuse to accept deportees, unauthorized parole grants not made on a case-by-case basis for urgent humanitarian reasons, and failure to detain during the removal period. A state or its residents are deemed harmed if they suffer any harm including financial harm of more than $100. Courts must advance and expedite these cases.

items.main: Removes the limit on injunctive relief that previously barred courts from enjoining the federal government's class-wide immigration enforcement decisions.
items.detail: Section 242(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act previously prohibited injunctions that operated on a class-wide basis against immigration enforcement. The bill adds a carve-out exempting state AG lawsuits filed under the new state enforcement provisions from that prohibition.

underreported.summary: Amends Section 242(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to exempt state attorney general lawsuits from the existing prohibition on class-wide injunctions against immigration enforcement. Courts may now issue injunctions that apply broadly, not just to individual plaintiffs, in state AG cases.
underreported.why_unreported: The section title refers to limiting injunctive relief, but its operative effect is the opposite for state AG cases — it removes an existing limit on the scope of relief that courts may grant, potentially enabling nationwide or statewide injunctions against federal immigration enforcement. This effect is not described in the bill's short title or stated purpose.

gaps: The bill requires DHS to issue a detainer for qualifying individuals but does not set a deadline or enforcement mechanism for how quickly DHS must take physical custody after the detainer is issued.

The bill defines the covered offenses by reference to the jurisdiction in which they occurred, but does not specify how DHS is to verify a charge when formal records from local jurisdictions are unavailable or contested.

The bill grants state standing to sue over five specific categories of immigration enforcement failure but does not address what remedies courts may order beyond injunctive relief, leaving open whether courts could compel specific federal detention actions.

Section 2 covers only the inadmissibility categories listed in INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), and (7), which excludes certain other categories of unlawfully present individuals not subject to those specific grounds.

added: Mandatory detention requirement for unlawfully present non-citizens charged with burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or crimes causing death or serious bodily injury
State attorney general standing to sue federal government for injunctive relief over five categories of immigration enforcement failures
Definition of covered offenses by reference to the jurisdiction where acts occurred
modified: INA Section 236(c)(1): expanded mandatory detention categories to include inadmissible non-citizens charged with theft and related crimes
INA Section 242(f): added carve-out exempting state AG enforcement lawsuits from the class-wide injunction prohibition

bills.title: Trafficking Survivors Relief Act
bills.official_title: An Act to provide for the vacating of certain convictions and expungement of certain arrests of victims of human trafficking.
bills.summary: The Trafficking Survivors Relief Act allows human trafficking victims to ask a federal court to vacate their convictions for non-violent federal offenses and expunge arrest records for both non-violent and violent offenses — if those offenses were a direct result of being trafficked. It also creates a new federal 'human trafficking defense,' allowing defendants in criminal cases to claim duress based on being a trafficking victim at the time of the offense.
bills.brief: Allows human trafficking victims to vacate non-violent federal convictions and expunge arrest records that were directly caused by their trafficking, and creates a duress defense based on trafficking victim status.

top_lines.headline: Motion to Vacate Convictions
subs: Trafficking victims may file a motion to vacate any non-violent federal conviction if the offense was a direct result of being trafficked — court reviews by preponderance of the evidence
If granted, the conviction is vacated, the verdict set aside, and all official records of the arrest and proceedings are expunged
The motion is retroactive — applies to convictions and arrests occurring before, on, or after the date of enactment

top_lines.headline: Arrest Record Expungement
subs: Trafficking victims may move to expunge arrest records for non-violent federal offenses if the conduct leading to arrest was directly related to being trafficked
Arrest records for violent federal offenses may be expunged if the charge was dismissed, not pursued, or reduced to a non-violent charge that was also dismissed or vacated
No filing fee may be charged; all motions and related documents are filed under seal and not available for public inspection

top_lines.headline: Human Trafficking Duress Defense
subs: In any federal prosecution, a defendant may establish duress by demonstrating they were a victim of trafficking at the time of the offense
Failure to raise this defense at trial does not prevent using trafficking victimization as a mitigating factor at sentencing or in post-conviction relief proceedings
A failure to assert the defense also may not be used to disqualify a convicted person from federal programs that aid trafficking victims

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on January 23, 2026, as Public Law 119-73. The bill passed the House on December 1, 2025, and the Senate on December 18, 2025.

sections.label: Section 2 — Federal Expungement for Victims of Trafficking

items.main: Creates 18 U.S.C. 3771A, establishing a federal court process for trafficking victims to vacate non-violent federal convictions and expunge arrest records for non-violent and certain violent federal offenses.
items.detail: For non-violent offenses, the court may grant vacatur or expungement on finding by a preponderance of the evidence that the offense was a direct result of the movant being a trafficking victim. An affidavit or sworn testimony from an anti-human trafficking service provider or clinician is sufficient evidence if the court finds it credible and no other evidence is readily available. The government has 30 days to file opposition, after which a hearing must be held within 15 days. If no opposition is filed, the court may hold a hearing within 45 days. All motions are filed under seal.

items.main: Courts may also reduce sentences for currently incarcerated persons who committed offenses as a direct result of being trafficked, upon motion by the prisoner or the court's own motion.
items.detail: The court must consider the sentencing factors under 18 U.S.C. 3553(a), including danger to the community and crime victims, before reducing a sentence. The government must conduct a particularized inquiry of the original sentencing facts and circumstances for any such motion.

sections.label: Sections 4 and 6 — Legal Representation and Duress Defense

items.main: Permits existing federal grants for legal representation — including Office of Justice Programs and Office on Violence Against Women grants — to be used for post-conviction relief proceedings by trafficking survivors.
items.detail: Section 6 creates a new federal duress defense at 18 U.S.C. 28, allowing defendants in criminal prosecutions to demonstrate duress by showing they were a trafficking victim at the time of the offense. Failure to raise the defense at trial does not preclude later use as a mitigating factor at sentencing or in post-conviction proceedings, and does not disqualify the person from federal trafficking victim assistance programs.

underreported.section: Section 2(b)(1)(C) — Expungement of Arrest Records for Violent Offenses
underreported.summary: Allows expungement of arrest records for violent federal offenses if the underlying conduct was related to trafficking victimization — but only if the charge was dismissed, not pursued, or reduced to a non-violent charge that was also dismissed or vacated. Does not allow expungement if the person was convicted of the violent offense.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and summary focus on non-violent conviction vacatur. This provision extends to arrest records for violent offenses under limited conditions, meaning trafficking victims who were arrested for violent crimes but not convicted may also benefit — a scope not apparent from the bill's headline.

gaps: The bill creates a federal vacatur process but does not create a parallel state-level process or require states to recognize federal vacatur orders — trafficking victims with state convictions arising from the same trafficking are not covered.

The bill requires GAO to report within 3 years on the number of survivors who file motions, but does not require any reporting on outcomes within the first year beyond the U.S. attorney district-level reports to the Attorney General.

The bill permits use of existing legal representation grants for post-conviction relief but does not authorize new funding for legal aid organizations to assist trafficking survivors with these motions.

added: 18 U.S.C. 3771A: federal court process for trafficking victims to vacate non-violent convictions and expunge arrest records
18 U.S.C. 28: federal human trafficking duress defense allowing defendants to establish duress by demonstrating trafficking victim status
Sentence reduction authority for currently incarcerated trafficking victims
No-fee filing requirement for all vacatur and expungement motions
Sealing requirement for all motions and related documents
modified: Existing federal legal representation grant programs: grantees may now use funds for post-conviction relief representation

bills.title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To require SelectUSA to coordinate with State-level economic development organizations to increase foreign direct investment in semiconductor-related manufacturing and production.
bills.summary: The Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act directs SelectUSA — Commerce's investment promotion program — to consult with state economic development agencies about how to attract more foreign direct investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing. SelectUSA must report back to Congress within two years. No new funds are authorized.
bills.brief: Directs SelectUSA to gather state agency input on attracting foreign investment in semiconductor manufacturing and report findings and strategies to Congress within two years.

top_lines.headline: State Input on Semiconductor Investment
subs: SelectUSA must solicit comments from state economic development organizations within 180 days on federal efforts to attract foreign direct investment in semiconductor fabrication, advanced packaging, and materials and equipment manufacturing

Comments must cover barriers to investment, public opportunities, and resource gaps; also recommendations on how SelectUSA can partner with states and protect U.S. efforts from benefiting foreign adversaries

top_lines.headline: Congressional Report Within Two Years
subs: SelectUSA must submit a report to Congress within 2 years covering: review of state comments, description of ongoing SelectUSA activities, and strategies for increasing semiconductor foreign direct investment
No additional funds are authorized for carrying out the Act

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House in April 2025 with bipartisan support and was received in the Senate. Semiconductor supply chain security has broad bipartisan appeal. However, the bill is a study and coordination measure with no new funding, which reduces urgency. The 60-vote Senate threshold and low cosponsor count (2) suggest limited political organizing behind this bill.

sections.label: Sections 4–5 — Coordination and Reporting

items.main: Directs the Executive Director of SelectUSA to solicit comments from state economic development organizations within 180 days on strategies to increase foreign direct investment in semiconductor fabrication, advanced packaging, and materials and equipment manufacturing.
items.detail: Comments must address barriers to investment, public opportunities states have identified, and resource gaps. State organizations must also provide recommendations on how SelectUSA can work independently or with state partners, and how to ensure foreign adversaries — as defined in the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 — do not benefit from U.S. efforts. SelectUSA must then report to Congress within 2 years with a review of comments, a description of current activities, and an assessment of implementation strategies. No new funds are authorized.

gaps: The bill requires SelectUSA to solicit state comments and report to Congress but does not require SelectUSA to implement any of the recommendations it receives or take any specific actions to increase semiconductor investment.

The bill restricts the scope to foreign direct investment but does not address domestic investment barriers in semiconductor manufacturing, which industry groups have identified as a parallel supply chain security concern.

added: Requirement for SelectUSA to solicit state economic development organization comments on semiconductor investment within 180 days
Congressional report due within 2 years on semiconductor investment strategies and state recommendations

bills.title: SPEED Act
bills.official_title: Streamlining Procurement for Effective Execution and Delivery and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
bills.summary: The SPEED Act is the House procurement reform title of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026. It rewrites the stated objective of the defense acquisition system to prioritize expeditious delivery of capabilities to the Armed Forces, creates two new DoD organizational bodies to integrate requirements and acquisition, raises most procurement dollar thresholds — some by 10x or more — to reduce paperwork on routine purchases, establishes a Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium, and requires GAO and DoD reviews of the acquisition workforce.
bills.brief: Rewrites acquisition system objectives, raises procurement thresholds, and creates new DoD integration bodies to accelerate capability delivery to warfighters.

top_lines.headline: Acquisition Thresholds Raised
subs: Simplified acquisition threshold raised to $10M — set directly in statute replacing prior cross-reference to civilian federal standard
Micro-purchase threshold raised from $10,000 to $100,000
Major defense acquisition program threshold raised from $300M (FY1990 dollars) to $1B (FY2024 dollars)
MDAP total-expenditure threshold raised from $1.8B (FY1990 dollars) to $5.5B (FY2024 dollars)

top_lines.headline: Noncompetitive and Pricing Thresholds Raised
subs: Justification threshold for noncompetitive contracts raised from $10M to $100M
Upper noncompetitive justification threshold raised from $75M to $500M
Cost or pricing data submission threshold raised from $2M to $10M
Simplified procedures for small purchases threshold raised from $5M to $50M

top_lines.headline: Acquisition System Objective Rewritten
subs: 10 U.S.C. 3102 rewritten: primary objective changed to expeditious delivery of capabilities to the Armed Forces
Secretary of Defense must revise DoD Directive 5000.01 within 30 days of enactment
Service acquisition executives required to use iterative development and terminate programs with cost growth, performance deficiencies, or schedule delays

top_lines.headline: New DoD Integration Bodies Created
subs: Requirements, Acquisition, and Programming Integration Directorate (RAPID) established to coordinate requirements, acquisition, and budget decisions
RAPID must provide recommendation to Deputy Secretary within 30 days of receiving a joint capability requirement from the Joint Requirements Council
Mission Engineering and Integration Activity (MEIA) established within 120 days to conduct cross-service technology integration

top_lines.headline: Industrial Base and Commercial Tech
subs: Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium established within 90 days to address industrial base challenges
Bridging Operational Objectives and Support for Transition (BOOST) program created under Defense Innovation Unit; sunsets December 31, 2030
DoD required to negotiate data-as-a-service access rights before entering weapon system procurement contracts

bills.likelihoodReason: The NDAA has passed every year since 1961, making enactment of some version highly probable. This House bill passed 231-196 on September 10, 2025. The Senate produces its own NDAA; the final enacted law emerges from House-Senate conference. The sharp threshold increases in Title III and the new organizational bodies in Title II are likely to face Senate scrutiny, and provisions in this House bill may be modified or dropped before final enactment.

sections.label: Title I — Aligning Acquisition to Warfighter Priorities

items.main: Rewrites 10 U.S.C. 3102 to make the primary objective of the defense acquisition system the expeditious provision of capabilities to the Armed Forces to address evolving threats in the most cost-effective manner practicable.
items.detail: The Secretary of Defense must revise DoD Directive 5000.01 within 30 days. Service acquisition executives must use data-driven trade-off analysis among life-cycle costs, delivery schedules, performance objectives, technical feasibility, and procurement quantity objectives, and must use iterative development cycles and discontinue or terminate programs that diverge from approved requirements or exceed approved cost thresholds or schedule baselines.

items.main: Establishes a new Program Executive Officer (PEO) role in statute (new 10 U.S.C. 1732) as the senior official responsible for oversight of plans, budgets, and execution of assigned programs, including life-cycle management.
items.detail: PEOs may adjust requirements — other than key performance parameters — to maximize agility and speed. PEOs may serve as milestone decision authority when directed by the service acquisition executive or designated by the Secretary of Defense.

items.main: Creates a new Product Support Manager role (new 10 U.S.C. 1733) responsible for managing support functions required to field and maintain readiness of covered systems throughout the life cycle.
items.detail: Product support managers of major defense acquisition programs must have at least 8 years of life-cycle logistics experience, at least 2 of which were performed in a systems program office. Product support managers of significant nonmajor programs must have at least 6 years of experience. Each covered system must have an approved life-cycle sustainment plan.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of Defense to submit a plan within 1 year for reorganizing program executive office portfolios around Major Capability Activity Areas (MCAAs), and to designate at least 2 Pathfinder MCAAs within 90 days.
items.detail: Pathfinder program executive officers may transfer funds among programs within a Pathfinder, subject to a cap of 40 percent of the total amount authorized for that Pathfinder. Transfers may not be used to initiate a new start program or terminate an existing program. DoD must report to Congress on Pathfinder effectiveness within 540 days and annually thereafter through December 31, 2029.

items.main: Amends 10 U.S.C. 8669b to require the Navy Senior Technical Authority to report directly to the program executive officer and to determine that all vessel design requirements are directly related to a key performance parameter or key system attribute.
items.detail: Any requirements the Senior Technical Authority determines are unnecessary to meet a key performance parameter or key system attribute shall not be approved.

sections.label: Title II — Accelerating the Requirements Process

items.main: Renames the Joint Requirements Oversight Council to the Joint Requirements Council and expands its duties to include continuous evaluation of global trends and adversary capabilities, and providing recommendations to the new RAPID directorate.
items.detail: The Council must provide recommendations on quick action requirements within 30 days of receipt, and on other joint capability requirements within 60 days. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs must revise JCIDS policies within 30 days of enactment. Repeals prior JROC-related provisions from the FY2008, FY2001, and FY2009 defense authorization acts.

items.main: Establishes a Requirements, Acquisition, and Programming Integration Directorate (RAPID) within DoD, co-directed by the Chairman of the Joint Requirements Council and the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation.
items.detail: RAPID must provide a recommendation to the Deputy Secretary of Defense within 30 days of receiving a recommendation from the Joint Requirements Council, with one possible 30-day extension for non-quick-action requirements. The Deputy Secretary must approve, approve with modification, or reject the RAPID recommendation within 30 days. If the Deputy Secretary fails to act within 90 days of the Council's original recommendation, the Secretary of Defense must notify the congressional defense committees.

items.main: Establishes a Mission Engineering and Integration Activity (MEIA) within DoD within 120 days of enactment to lead cross-service activities developing integrated technology solutions for joint operational problems.
items.detail: MEIA must use existing authorities including 10 U.S.C. 4022 other transaction authority. The Secretary must submit an implementation plan to the congressional defense committees within 90 days of enactment. Within 5 years of MEIA's establishment, the Secretary must submit an assessment of whether MEIA should be modified, made permanent, or terminated.

sections.label: Title III — Striking the Balance Between Regulation and Efficiency

items.main: Requires the Secretary of Defense within 90 days to identify and reduce or eliminate cost accounting standards (CAS) compliance requirements where generally accepted accounting principles would achieve the same result or other existing requirements sufficiently protect DoD interests.
items.detail: A report with findings and recommendations for statutory changes must be submitted to the congressional defense committees within 180 days. A separate assessment of whether GAAP can replace CAS as the baseline for defense contract financial reporting must also be submitted within 180 days.

items.main: Raises procurement dollar thresholds across multiple statutes: simplified acquisition threshold to $10M; micro-purchase threshold from $10,000 to $100,000; major program thresholds from $115M/$540M (FY1990) to $275M/$1.3B (FY2024); MDAP thresholds from $300M/$1.8B (FY1990) to $1B/$5.5B (FY2024).
items.detail: Cost or pricing data submission thresholds raised from $2M to $10M. Multiyear contract threshold raised from $500M to $1B. The simplified acquisition threshold for contingency and peacekeeping operations is set at two times the standard threshold. Noncompetitive contracting justification thresholds raised from $10M/$75M to $100M/$500M.

items.main: Creates a new alternative capability-based pricing authority (new 10 U.S.C. 3906) allowing agency heads to determine whether commercial solution prices are fair and reasonable based on value to the Government rather than cost buildup.
items.detail: Value may be assessed on suitability, capability improvements, estimated total cost avoidance, or input from intended end users. Does not apply to subcontracts. Clarifies that payments for services acquired through commercially utilized acquisition strategies — including consumption-based and technology subscription models — are not advance payments under 10 U.S.C. 3801.

sections.label: Title IV — Strengthening the Defense Industrial Base and Leveraging Commercial Innovation

items.main: Establishes a Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium within 90 days of enactment, open to government, industry, and academia, focused on eliminating impediments to the industrial base, addressing supply chain fragility, expanding domestic manufacturing, and developing the advanced manufacturing workforce.
items.detail: The Consortium must support use of other transaction authorities under 10 U.S.C. 4021 and 4022. A working group within the Consortium must develop recommendations on qualification and acceptance of products manufactured using advanced manufacturing within 180 days, with a report to Congress within 1 year of enactment.

items.main: Requires DoD to negotiate data-as-a-service solutions before entering weapon system procurement contracts, to ensure access to technical data and computer software for depot maintenance and core logistics capability.
items.detail: For commercial products, the offeror must price and provide data access commensurate with commercial practices. DoD may not require different access from what the offeror customarily provides unless specifically negotiated. Guidance implementing this requirement is due within 180 days; applies to contracts entered into on or after enactment.

items.main: Rewrites 10 U.S.C. 4401 to strengthen requirements for modular open system approach and modifies 10 U.S.C. 3771 to extend government purpose rights in module interfaces and key interfaces in perpetuity.
items.detail: Sections 4402 and 4403 of title 10 are repealed. Guidance implementing the new requirements is due within 180 days. The government's ability to enforce rights against third parties that have not obtained a license is clarified.

items.main: Establishes the Bridging Operational Objectives and Support for Transition (BOOST) program under the Defense Innovation Unit to accelerate adoption of commercial technologies into programs of record.
items.detail: The Director of DIU must issue guidance within 90 days. The BOOST program sunsets December 31, 2030. A report on BOOST effectiveness is due to congressional defense committees within 2 years of enactment. Funding comes from amounts authorized for DIU research, development, test, and evaluation.

items.main: Requires the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Industrial Base Policy and the Director of Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy to jointly report to congressional defense committees by March 1, 2026 on regulations that discourage surge capacity investment.
items.detail: The report must address DOGE efforts coordinating with the Office of the Secretary of Defense on acquisition barriers, identify policies incentivizing reduction of surge capacity including FAR 31.205-17 on idle facility costs, and address steps taken under Executive Order 14265 (April 15, 2025) on modernizing defense acquisitions.

sections.label: Title V — Developing a Mission-Oriented Defense Acquisition Workforce

items.main: Requires a comprehensive assessment of the Defense Acquisition University (DAU), conducted through the Director of the Acquisition Innovation Research Center, with a report to congressional defense committees within 1 year of enactment.
items.detail: The assessment must evaluate DAU's mission alignment with 10 U.S.C. 3102 as amended, curriculum, staff composition, funding sufficiency, and use of external experts. The Director must provide recommendations to the Secretary of Defense to strengthen DAU's training of the acquisition workforce.

items.main: Requires the Comptroller General to review management, training, and development of the acquisition workforce and submit a report to congressional defense committees by April 1, 2026.
items.detail: The review must evaluate current organization and staffing including number of vacant positions, recruiting and retention authorities, hiring trends over the preceding 5 years, and impediments to training including lack of funding and excessive workload demands.

items.main: Requires the Comptroller General to review education, training, and career development programs for the acquisition workforce and assess career development policies under 10 U.S.C. 1734, with a report due July 1, 2026.
items.detail: The review must assess retention rates of personnel in critical acquisition positions compared to other DoD civilian and military workforce, competitive career progression, and benefits of minimum assignment periods of at least 4 years for critical acquisition positions.

underreported.summary: Raises the DoD micro-purchase threshold from $10,000 to $100,000, allowing individual contracting officers to make direct purchases without any competitive procurement process up to that amount.
underreported.why_unreported: Section title describes a threshold adjustment. The operative effect is a 10x increase in the ceiling at which a single contracting officer can purchase without competition across the full DoD acquisition workforce, substantially expanding the aggregate amount of defense spending that bypasses competition requirements.

underreported.summary: Requires a joint DoD report by March 1, 2026 on regulations discouraging surge capacity investment, specifically directing the report to address DOGE efforts coordinating with OSD and steps taken under Executive Order 14265 (April 15, 2025).
underreported.why_unreported: Section title describes a reporting requirement. The operative text directs the report to address whether FAR 31.205-17, which governs whether idle manufacturing capacity costs are allowable on cost-type contracts, should be modified. Changes to this regulation would affect contractor incentives to maintain excess capacity across the defense industrial base.

underreported.summary: Allows the Secretary of Defense to transfer funds among programs within a designated Pathfinder program executive office up to 40 percent of the total amount authorized for that Pathfinder, without returning to Congress for reprogramming approval.
underreported.why_unreported: Section title is labeled Major Capability Activity Areas and Pathfinder Programs. The operative text creates an administrative transfer authority for up to 40 percent of authorized Pathfinder program funds, bypassing normal reprogramming notification requirements, subject only to prohibitions on new starts and terminations.

gaps: The bill raises the cost or pricing data submission threshold from $2M to $10M but does not establish an alternative audit or transparency mechanism for contracts between $2M and $10M.

Title II establishes RAPID and MEIA as new coordination bodies but does not specify funding levels, staffing minimums, or resource requirements; implementation is left entirely to executive discretion.

The bill requires DoD to reduce or eliminate CAS compliance requirements within 90 days but does not specify minimum accounting standards that must remain in place, leaving the scope of reduction to executive branch discretion.

Section 403 requires DoD to negotiate data-as-a-service access before entering weapon system contracts but contains no remedy or enforcement mechanism if negotiations fail to produce data access terms.
Title V requires GAO reviews of the acquisition workforce but does not require DoD to respond to or implement GAO recommendations within any specified timeframe.

New 10 U.S.C. 1733: Product Support Manager role codified in statute with experience requirements (8 years for MDAP, 6 years for significant nonmajor)

Bridging Operational Objectives and Support for Transition (BOOST) program under Defense Innovation Unit (sunsets December 31, 2030)

bills.title: Deploying American Blockchains Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To direct the Secretary of Commerce to take actions necessary and appropriate to promote the competitiveness of the United States related to the deployment, use, application, and competitiveness of blockchain technology or other distributed ledger technology, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Deploying American Blockchains Act designates the Secretary of Commerce as the principal presidential advisor on blockchain technology policy and directs Commerce to create a Blockchain Deployment Program within the Department. The program will develop best practices, establish advisory committees including industry and government representatives, and report annually to Congress. The program terminates after seven years.
bills.brief: Creates a Blockchain Deployment Program at Commerce, designates Commerce as the President's principal blockchain technology advisor, and requires annual congressional reporting on U.S. blockchain competitiveness.

top_lines.headline: Commerce as Principal Blockchain Policy Advisor
subs: Secretary of Commerce designated as the principal advisor to the President on blockchain policy, including deployment, application, and competitiveness of blockchain technology, tokens, and tokenization
Commerce must develop policies on cybersecurity, decentralized identity, artificial intelligence, supply chain resiliency, e-commerce, healthcare applications, and fraud reduction using blockchain

top_lines.headline: Blockchain Deployment Program
subs: Commerce must establish a Blockchain Deployment Program within the Department; the program terminates 7 years after enactment, and advisory committees must be established within 180 days of enactment
Program must develop best practices for blockchain deployment, interoperability, cybersecurity risk reduction, and value quantification through comparative analysis with competing technologies

Advisory committees must include federal agency representatives, blockchain infrastructure operators, application developers, small and large businesses, academics, nonprofits, and artists and content creators

top_lines.headline: Annual Reporting to Congress
subs: Commerce must submit its first annual report to Congress 2 years after enactment and annually thereafter
Reports must describe program activities, legislative recommendations to strengthen U.S. blockchain competitiveness, and emerging risks and long-term trends

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate in June 2025, but has only 1 cosponsor and a narrow focus on blockchain promotion rather than regulation. The 60-vote threshold for Senate floor action, a crowded legislative calendar, and the relatively niche focus of the bill make Senate passage uncertain. Some senators may view a standalone blockchain promotion program as lower priority than broader crypto regulatory legislation.

sections.label: Section 3 — Department of Commerce Leadership on Blockchain

items.main: Designates the Secretary of Commerce as the President's principal policy advisor on blockchain technology, tokens, and tokenization, and directs the establishment of a Blockchain Deployment Program within the Department of Commerce.
items.detail: The program's activities include developing policies on blockchain-related cybersecurity and key storage security, supporting interoperability, promoting open-source blockchain infrastructure, examining how federal agencies can benefit from and adopt blockchain technology, and coordinating blockchain activities across federal agencies. Advisory committees must be established within 180 days, with seats for industry operators, developers, academic institutions, nonprofits, consumer groups, small businesses, rural stakeholders, and artists and content creators.

items.main: Best practices developed under the program must cover deployment, interoperability, cybersecurity risk reduction, and value quantification — including quantifying cost savings from blockchain adoption versus competing technologies.
items.detail: The bill includes rules of construction specifying that private entities are not required to share information with Commerce, request assistance, or implement any Commerce recommendations. The Blockchain Deployment Program terminates seven years after enactment.

sections.label: Section 4 — Annual Report to Congress

items.main: Commerce must publish its first annual report on the Blockchain Deployment Program two years after enactment and annually thereafter, covering program activities, legislative recommendations, and emerging blockchain risks and trends.
items.detail: Reports must be made public on the Commerce Department website and submitted to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

gaps: The bill creates a promotional and advisory program for blockchain technology but does not allocate any specific funding or staffing for the Blockchain Deployment Program, leaving implementation dependent on existing Commerce Department resources.
The bill directs Commerce to examine how federal agencies can benefit from blockchain adoption but does not require any agency to implement blockchain solutions or set any adoption targets.

added: Blockchain Deployment Program at the Department of Commerce with 7-year term
Designation of Commerce Secretary as principal presidential advisor on blockchain policy
Advisory committees for blockchain best practice development, including industry, government, and civil society members
Annual congressional reporting requirement starting two years after enactment

bills.title: Hotel Fees Transparency Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To prohibit unfair and deceptive advertising of prices for hotel rooms and other places of short-term lodging, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Hotel Fees Transparency Act requires hotels, short-term rentals, and booking platforms to show the total price — including all mandatory fees — whenever they display a price for lodging, from the first listing through to checkout. Taxes set by government entities and optional add-ons are not required to be bundled in but must be disclosed before the final purchase. Takes effect 450 days after enactment.
bills.brief: Requires hotels and lodging platforms to display the total price including all mandatory fees whenever any price is shown, from the first listing to checkout.

top_lines.headline: Total Price Required from First Listing
subs: Covered entities must show the total services price — base price plus all mandatory service fees — in any advertisement, marketing material, or price list whenever a price is displayed
Total price must appear from the moment lodging is first shown to a prospective buyer and at every step of the booking process
Individual fee components may be shown separately but must be less prominent than the total price

top_lines.headline: Government Taxes Disclosed Before Purchase
subs: Any tax, fee, or assessment imposed by a government entity, quasi-government entity, or government-created special district must be disclosed before the final purchase — but are not required to be included in the total services price
Optional products and services (such as parking, breakfast, or travel insurance) are also excluded from the required total price display

top_lines.headline: Enforcement and Preemption
subs: FTC enforces as an unfair or deceptive practice; state attorneys general may also sue on behalf of state residents
Third-party booking platforms have an affirmative defense if they relied in good faith on price data from hotels that turned out to be inaccurate and acted promptly to correct it
Federal law preempts stricter or different state fee disclosure rules, but states retain authority over fraud and contract law

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House with bipartisan support and has been placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar (Calendar No. 60), which reflects a lower hurdle than most bills. The hotel junk fees issue has bipartisan appeal and consumer groups support it. However, the hotel and short-term rental industry has historically lobbied against mandatory fee disclosure, and the 60-vote Senate threshold and crowded legislative calendar create obstacles. The bill's relatively small number of House cosponsors (6) suggests limited organizing capacity.

sections.label: Section 2 — Prohibition on Unfair and Deceptive Advertising of Hotel Prices

items.main: Requires all covered entities — hotels, short-term rentals, third-party booking platforms, and intermediaries — to prominently display the total services price, including all mandatory service fees, whenever any price is shown.
items.detail: The total services price includes the base price and all mandatory service fees but excludes government taxes and optional add-ons. Covered entities must disclose government taxes before the final purchase step. Takes effect 450 days after enactment and applies to advertisements, marketing, and offers made on or after that date.

items.main: Enforcement is split between the FTC and state attorneys general, with a good-faith affirmative defense for booking platforms that relied on inaccurate fee data from hotels.
items.detail: FTC may enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act. State attorneys general may bring civil actions as parens patriae in federal court, with notice to the FTC. The preemption clause bars states from maintaining different fee disclosure requirements — states may not require stricter or alternative disclosure formats — but preserves state fraud, contract, and data breach laws.

underreported.summary: Preempts any state law that affects the manner in which a covered entity may advertise or display lodging prices and requires fee disclosure, unless the state law requires the total services price in the same manner as this Act.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to require national all-in pricing. The preemption clause separately overrides state-level junk fee disclosure laws that may be stricter or structured differently, potentially weakening consumer protections in states that already require broader disclosure than the federal standard.

gaps: The bill covers hotels and short-term rentals but does not address fees imposed by vacation rental platforms, which in some markets charge platform service fees that are separate from both the host's base price and the platform's booking fee.

The bill requires disclosure of government taxes before final purchase but does not specify the format or prominence required for that disclosure, leaving enforcement of the tax disclosure requirement subject to FTC interpretation.

added: Federal requirement to display total services price including all mandatory fees from first listing through checkout
Requirement to disclose government taxes and quasi-government fees before final purchase
FTC and state AG enforcement authority for hotel price advertising violations
Affirmative defense for good-faith reliance on inaccurate price data by third-party booking platforms
removed: State laws requiring different fee disclosure formats for hotel and short-term rental advertising are preempted

bills.title: ROUTERS Act
bills.official_title: To direct the Secretary of Commerce, acting through the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to conduct a study of the national security risks posed by consumer routers, modems, and devices that combine a modem and router, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The ROUTERS Act directs the Department of Commerce to study the national security risks posed by consumer routers, modems, and combined modem-router devices that are designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by entities owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia. Commerce must report findings to Congress within one year.
bills.brief: Requires a Commerce Department national security study on consumer networking equipment made by entities linked to China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia, with a congressional report due within one year.

top_lines.headline: National Security Study on Foreign-Linked Routers
subs: Commerce must study national security risks from consumer routers, modems, and combined modem-router devices made by entities owned, controlled by, or subject to the influence of China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia
Report to Congress due within 1 year of enactment covering the study results

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate in April 2025. The national security framing around Chinese networking equipment has bipartisan support in both chambers. However, with only 1 cosponsor in the House and no visible Senate companion, floor time may be limited. The 60-vote threshold and the fact that this is a study bill rather than a direct regulatory requirement may reduce opposition but also reduce urgency.

sections.label: Section 2 — Study of National Security Risks Posed by Certain Routers and Modems

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Commerce, acting through the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to study national security risks from consumer routers, modems, and combined modem-router devices made by entities owned, controlled, or subject to the influence of a covered country.
items.detail: The covered countries are those specified in section 4872(d)(2) of title 10, United States Code. Commerce must submit a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee within one year of enactment. The bill does not prescribe the contents of the study, restrict the sale of covered devices, or authorize any regulatory action.

gaps: The bill directs a study but does not require Commerce to include any specific findings in the report, recommend any regulatory action, or propose a timeline for follow-on policy action based on the study results.

The bill covers consumer routers and modems but does not address enterprise or carrier-grade networking equipment from the same covered countries, which may present equal or greater national security risk.

added: Requirement for Commerce Department national security study on consumer routers, modems, and combined modem-router devices from entities linked to China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia
Congressional report due within one year of enactment

bills.title: Taiwan Assurance Implementation Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Taiwan Assurance Act of 2020 to require periodic reviews and updated reports relating to the Department of State's Taiwan Guidelines.
bills.summary: The Taiwan Assurance Implementation Act requires the State Department to review and update its internal guidance on relations with Taiwan at least once every five years and to report those updates to Congress within 90 days of completing each review. Under current law, the review was required only once; this bill makes it an ongoing obligation.
bills.brief: Converts the State Department's one-time review of its Taiwan guidelines into a recurring obligation — required at least once every five years — with a congressional report due 90 days after each review.

top_lines.headline: Recurring Taiwan Guidelines Review
subs: State Department must conduct a review of its Taiwan guidance — including the 'Guidelines on Relations with Taiwan' and any successor or related documents — at least once every five years
After each review, State must reissue the updated guidance to all executive branch departments and agencies
Congress must receive an updated report within 90 days of each completed review

top_lines.headline: Report Content Requirements
subs: Each updated report must include all information required under the original one-time reporting requirement
Must also describe how the updated guidance meets the goals and objectives described in subsection (b) of the amended Taiwan Assurance Act of 2020 provision

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on December 2, 2025, as Public Law 119-45. The bill passed the House on May 5, 2025, and the Senate on November 18, 2025.

sections.label: Section 2 — Increased Reporting Regarding Department of State Taiwan Guidelines

items.main: Amends the Taiwan Assurance Act of 2020 to require the Secretary of State to review and reissue the Department of State's Taiwan guidance at least once every five years and to report to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Foreign Affairs Committee within 90 days of each review.
items.detail: The amendment also expands the definition of the documents subject to review to include any successor document or related document containing guidance on relations with Taiwan, not just the original 'Guidelines on Relations with Taiwan' memorandum. The obligation continues for as long as the State Department maintains any guidance governing relations with Taiwan.

gaps: The bill requires the State Department to review and reissue its Taiwan guidance at least every five years but does not require the Secretary of State to take any specific action if the review identifies restrictions on U.S.-Taiwan relations that are not aligned with congressional findings.

The bill expands the scope of documents subject to review to 'related documents,' but does not define what constitutes a 'related document,' potentially leaving open which internal State Department policies are covered.

added: Recurring five-year review and reissuance requirement for State Department Taiwan guidance
Requirement to report updated Taiwan guidance to Congress within 90 days of each review
modified: Taiwan Assurance Act of 2020 Section 315: one-time review converted to recurring at least every five years; definition of covered documents expanded to include successor and related documents

bills.title: Kayla Hamilton Act
bills.official_title: To amend the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 to enhance efforts to combat the trafficking of children.
bills.summary: The Kayla Hamilton Act tightens the placement process for unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody. It requires the Department of Health and Human Services to place children 13 and older in a secure facility if they have gang-related tattoos, markings, or an arrest record linked to gang activity in their home country. It also prohibits placing any child with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the U.S., and requires DHS to receive detailed background information on all adult household members at any placement home.
bills.brief: Requires secure facility placement for unaccompanied migrant children 13 and older with gang-related indicators, bans placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present, and mandates sharing of household adult background information with DHS.

top_lines.headline: Secure Facility for Gang-Affiliated Minors
subs: Before placing an unaccompanied child 13 or older, HHS must contact the child's home country consulate or embassy to request the child's criminal record
HHS must also examine the child for gang-related tattoos and markings
If the child has a gang-related tattoo, marking, or a gang-related arrest record or criminal conviction from their home country, HHS must place them in a secure facility

top_lines.headline: Sponsor Vetting Requirements
subs: No child may be placed with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the United States

Before placement, HHS must share with DHS: names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, immigration status, contact information, and background check results for all adult residents of the placement household
Required background checks include a sex offender registry check, a public records check, and an FBI fingerprint-based criminal history check for every adult in the household

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate in December 2025, but has only 2 cosponsors and no Senate companion bill visible. Democrats have broadly opposed bills that restrict HHS placement flexibility for unaccompanied migrant children, and the 60-vote threshold for Senate floor consideration makes bipartisan support essential. No Senate committee action has been reported.

sections.label: Section 2 — Additional Safeguards for Placement of Unaccompanied Children

items.main: For unaccompanied migrant children aged 13 and older, requires HHS to request a criminal record from the child's home country consulate or embassy and conduct a gang marking examination before making any placement.
items.detail: If the child has a gang-related tattoo, any other gang-related marking, or a home-country arrest record, pending charge, or conviction related to gang affiliation, HHS must place the child in a secure facility. The bill exempts children aged 12 or younger from the gang-screening requirement. The Secretary is not required to review placement in a secure facility under this provision.

items.main: Prohibits placement of any unaccompanied child with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the United States, and requires HHS to transmit detailed household information to DHS before completing any placement.
items.detail: Required information includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, immigration status, contact information, and background check results for all adult residents of the proposed placement household. Background checks must include a Department of Justice National Sex Offender public website check, a public records background check, and an FBI National Criminal History fingerprint-based check. The amendment also changes 'may consider' to 'shall consider' in making placement determinations, converting a discretionary consideration into a mandatory one.

underreported.section: Section 2 — Change from 'May Consider' to 'Shall Consider'
underreported.summary: Changes the HHS placement standard from permitting consideration of placement-determination factors to requiring that consideration, by striking 'may consider' and inserting 'shall consider'. This makes the assessment a mandatory step in placement determinations, rather than a discretionary one.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose focuses on gang screening and sponsor vetting. This separate textual change — from 'may' to 'shall' — alters the baseline placement standard for all unaccompanied children regardless of gang affiliation, broadening the scope of the bill beyond its headline provisions.

gaps: The bill requires HHS to contact a child's home country consulate for a criminal record before placement, but does not establish a timeline for how long HHS may hold a child while awaiting a response, or what happens if the consulate does not respond.

The bill prohibits placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present but does not address what happens to a child if no lawful placement is available, potentially requiring indefinite secure facility detention.

added: Mandatory consulate/embassy criminal record request for unaccompanied children aged 13 and older before placement
Mandatory gang tattoo and marking examination before placement for children aged 13 and older
Mandatory secure facility placement for children aged 13 and older with gang-related indicators
Prohibition on placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present in the United States
Requirement to transmit household adult background check results to DHS before each placement
modified: 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(2): 'may consider' changed to 'shall consider' in making placement determinations

bills.title: Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Reserve Act to prohibit the Federal reserve banks from offering certain products or services directly to an individual, to prohibit the use of central bank digital currency for monetary policy, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act prohibits the Federal Reserve from creating, testing, or issuing any form of digital currency that would be a direct liability of the Fed and available to the general public. It also bans the Fed from using such a currency to conduct monetary policy. The ban covers both direct issuance and indirect issuance through banks or other intermediaries.
bills.brief: Permanently prohibits the Federal Reserve from issuing, testing, or using a central bank digital currency in any form, directly or through intermediaries.

top_lines.headline: Federal Reserve Banned from Issuing Digital Dollar
subs: Federal Reserve banks may not offer products or services directly to individuals, maintain individual accounts, or issue any central bank digital currency or substantially similar digital asset
Federal Reserve banks may not offer a central bank digital currency indirectly to individuals through financial institutions or other intermediaries
The Board of Governors may not test, study, develop, create, or implement a central bank digital currency

top_lines.headline: Monetary Policy Use Prohibited
subs: The Board of Governors and the Federal Open Market Committee may not use a central bank digital currency to implement monetary policy
Exception: open, permissionless, and private dollar-denominated digital currencies that fully preserve the privacy protections of physical cash are not prohibited

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House in July 2025 with strong Republican support and 135 cosponsors, all Republican. In the Senate, 60 votes are needed to break a filibuster and Democrats have shown little interest in restricting a financial technology that the Federal Reserve has not proposed deploying in a retail form. The Senate Banking Committee has not advanced the bill.

sections.label: Sections 2–4 — Prohibitions on Central Bank Digital Currency

items.main: Amends the Federal Reserve Act to prohibit Federal Reserve banks from offering any products or services directly to individuals, maintaining individual accounts, or issuing any central bank digital currency directly or indirectly through intermediaries.
items.detail: Section 4 additionally prohibits the Board of Governors and the Federal Open Market Committee from testing, studying, developing, creating, or implementing a central bank digital currency, and bars the use of any such currency to implement monetary policy. A central bank digital currency is defined as a digital form of money denominated in U.S. dollars that is a direct liability of the Federal Reserve and widely available to the general public.

items.main: Explicitly preserves the legality of open, permissionless, and private dollar-denominated digital currencies that fully preserve the privacy protections of U.S. coins and physical currency.
items.detail: This carve-out means that privately issued dollar-pegged stablecoins with open and permissionless blockchain infrastructure would not be affected by the prohibition. Section 5 expresses the sense of Congress that the Federal Reserve currently lacks the authority to issue a central bank digital currency without a new grant of authority from Congress under Article I, Section 8 powers.

underreported.summary: Separately prohibits the Federal Reserve from offering a central bank digital currency indirectly through financial institutions or other intermediaries, in addition to the direct issuance prohibition in Section 2.
underreported.why_unreported: A two-tier central bank digital currency model — where the Fed issues a digital currency to commercial banks that then distribute it to customers — has been proposed in academic and policy contexts as a privacy-preserving alternative to direct Fed retail accounts. Section 3's separate prohibition on indirect issuance forecloses that design without discussing it in the bill's title or stated purpose.

gaps: The bill prohibits the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency but does not address whether the Treasury Department's existing coin and currency issuance authority could be used as an alternative legal path to a government-issued digital currency.

The bill defines a central bank digital currency as one that is a direct liability of the Federal Reserve and widely available to the general public, but does not define 'widely available' — leaving open the question of whether a wholesale central bank digital currency used only by financial institutions would be prohibited.

added: Prohibition on Federal Reserve banks offering products or services directly to individuals
Prohibition on Federal Reserve banks maintaining individual accounts
Prohibition on Federal Reserve banks issuing a central bank digital currency directly or through intermediaries
Prohibition on the Board of Governors testing, studying, developing, or implementing a central bank digital currency
Prohibition on using a central bank digital currency for monetary policy
modified: Federal Reserve Act Section 16: two new paragraphs (18 and 19) added banning direct and indirect central bank digital currency issuance
Federal Reserve Act Section 10: new paragraph banning central bank digital currency testing, development, and monetary policy use

bills.title: Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To require the Secretary of the Treasury to pursue more equitable treatment of Taiwan at the international financial institutions, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act requires the U.S. representative at the International Monetary Fund to advocate for Taiwan's admission as a member of the IMF, its participation in IMF economic surveillance, employment opportunities for Taiwan nationals at the IMF, and Taiwan's access to IMF technical assistance and training. The requirement sunsets when Taiwan is admitted or after 10 years.
bills.brief: Directs the U.S. IMF representative to actively support Taiwan's IMF membership, surveillance participation, employment access, and technical assistance, with annual Treasury testimony required.

top_lines.headline: U.S. Must Advocate for Taiwan at IMF
subs: U.S. Governor of the IMF must use voice and vote to support Taiwan's admission as a member, if Taiwan seeks admission
Must also support Taiwan's participation in IMF surveillance activities, employment of Taiwan nationals, and Taiwan's access to technical assistance
Secretary of the Treasury may waive requirements for up to 1 year at a time if providing the waiver promotes Taiwan's meaningful participation at international financial institutions

top_lines.headline: Reporting and Sunset
subs: Secretary of the Treasury must include Taiwan participation efforts in the next 7 annual congressional testimonies
Section 4 requirements expire when Taiwan is admitted to the IMF or after 10 years, whichever is earlier

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and has been placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, suggesting some momentum. However, with only 3 cosponsors in the House, it has limited visible support. Taiwan's IMF membership is complicated by China's opposition, and some senators may be reluctant to direct Treasury votes at the IMF on such a sensitive diplomatic issue. A Senate floor vote has not been scheduled.

sections.label: Section 4 — Support for Taiwan Admission to the IMF

items.main: Requires the U.S. Governor of the IMF to use the U.S. voice and vote to support Taiwan's admission as a member, Taiwan's participation in Article IV surveillance consultations, employment of Taiwan nationals at the IMF without nationality-based restrictions, and Taiwan's access to IMF technical assistance.
items.detail: Taiwan held IMF membership until China was seated in 1980. The bill notes that Taiwan is the 21st largest economy in the world and the 10th largest U.S. goods trading partner, and cites IMF Articles allowing membership by 'countries' without requiring statehood as a condition. The Secretary of the Treasury may waive any requirement of this section for up to one year by reporting to Congress that the waiver will substantially promote the objective of securing Taiwan's meaningful participation at international financial institutions. The section expires when Taiwan is admitted or after 10 years.

gaps: The bill requires the U.S. IMF Governor to support Taiwan's admission but does not require the U.S. to vote against any IMF action that would further marginalize Taiwan, such as surveillance exclusions or staffing restrictions.

The bill is conditioned on Taiwan seeking admission; if Taiwan chooses not to formally apply, the core admission advocacy requirement in Section 4(a)(1) does not activate, even though the bill's findings indicate Taiwan announced it would seek membership in October 2024.

added: Statutory requirement for U.S. IMF Governor to advocate for Taiwan's IMF admission, surveillance participation, employment access, and technical assistance
Annual Treasury testimony requirement covering Taiwan participation efforts for the next 7 years
U.S. policy declaration not to discourage or deter Taiwan from seeking IMF membership

bills.title: GENIUS Act
bills.official_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of payment stablecoins, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The GENIUS Act creates the first U.S. federal law governing stablecoins — digital tokens designed to hold a fixed value, typically pegged to the dollar. Only licensed entities (banks, federally approved nonbank issuers, or state-licensed issuers with under $10B outstanding) may issue stablecoins for U.S. customers. Issuers must back every stablecoin dollar-for-dollar with U.S. cash or short-term Treasury securities and publicly disclose their reserves every month.
bills.brief: Creates a federal licensing and 1:1 reserve requirement for stablecoin issuers, bans unlicensed stablecoin issuance in the U.S., and classifies stablecoins as neither securities nor commodities.

top_lines.headline: Only Licensed Issuers May Issue Stablecoins
subs: Three years after enactment, it is unlawful for any unlicensed person to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States

Three permitted issuer categories: bank subsidiaries, federally approved nonbank issuers chartered by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and state-licensed issuers with $10B or less outstanding
Violations carry penalties of up to $1M per violation and/or up to 5 years in prison

top_lines.headline: 1-to-1 Reserve Requirement
subs: Permitted issuers must maintain reserves of at least 100% of outstanding stablecoins (an at-least 1-to-1 basis) at all times
Eligible reserves: U.S. currency, deposits at insured banks, Treasury bills with maturity of 93 days or less, overnight repo agreements backed by Treasuries, and government money market funds

Reserves may not be rehypothecated (pledged as collateral) except for margin obligations, standard custodial services, and limited liquidity needs — liquidity repos must be centrally cleared or have prior regulator approval

top_lines.headline: Monthly Disclosure and Certification
subs: Issuers must publicly publish monthly reserve composition — total outstanding stablecoins, amounts by reserve type, average maturity, and custody location
The CEO and CFO must certify the accuracy of each monthly report; false certifications subject to the same criminal penalties as federal securities fraud
A registered public accounting firm must examine each month-end reserve report

top_lines.headline: Stablecoins Not Securities or Commodities
subs: Payment stablecoins issued by permitted issuers are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'security' under the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and related laws
Payment stablecoins are also excluded from the definition of 'commodity' under the Commodity Exchange Act
Permitted issuers are excluded from the definition of 'investment company' under the Investment Company Act of 1940

top_lines.headline: Stablecoin Holders Prioritized in Bankruptcy
subs: In any insolvency proceeding, stablecoin holders have first priority claim on required reserve assets ahead of all other creditors
Required reserves are excluded from the bankruptcy estate and courts must begin ratable distributions to stablecoin holders within 14 days where reserves are available
Bankruptcy court automatic stay does not apply to redemptions from required reserves

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 18, 2025, as Public Law 119-27. The bill passed the Senate in June 2025 with bipartisan support and the House on July 17, 2025.

sections.label: Section 3 — Issuance and Treatment of Payment Stablecoins

items.main: Prohibits any entity other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from issuing a stablecoin in the United States, with the prohibition taking effect three years after enactment.
items.detail: The three-year grace period allows existing issuers time to obtain a license or wind down operations. Digital asset service providers may not offer or sell stablecoins from unlicensed issuers to U.S. customers after the effective date. The Secretary of the Treasury may grant limited safe harbors by regulation for de minimis transaction volumes or in unusual and exigent circumstances with prior congressional notification. Peer-to-peer transfers between individuals and self-custodied wallet transactions are explicitly exempt.

sections.label: Section 4 — Reserve and Disclosure Requirements

items.main: Requires all permitted issuers to maintain 1:1 reserves using only U.S. currency, demand deposits at insured banks, Treasury bills with maturities of 93 days or less, overnight repo agreements backed by Treasuries, or government money market funds.
items.detail: Reserves may not be pledged or rehypothecated except in limited circumstances: satisfying margin obligations in permitted repo investments, standard custodial arrangements, or creating liquidity for expected redemptions using cleared or pre-approved repurchase agreements. Issuers must publish the composition of their reserves monthly on their website, including total outstanding stablecoins, amounts by reserve type, average tenor, and geographic custody location. The CEO and CFO must certify accuracy of each monthly report; false certifications carry criminal penalties equivalent to those for false SEC certifications under 18 U.S.C. 1350.

items.main: State-qualified issuers may only operate under state supervision when their total outstanding stablecoins are $10B or less; growth above $10B requires federal approval.
items.detail: State payment stablecoin regulators have primary supervisory and examination authority over state-qualified issuers, but the Federal Reserve may intervene in unusual and exigent circumstances after 48 hours' notice to the state regulator. The Federal Reserve's intervention authority includes issuing cease and desist directives limiting redemptions and affiliate transactions; these directives automatically lapse if the Board does not affirm, modify, or rescind within 10 days of the issuer's response.

sections.label: Sections 11, 17–18 — Insolvency, Legal Classification, and Foreign Issuers

items.main: Grants stablecoin holders first-priority claims on required reserves in any insolvency proceeding, amending the Bankruptcy Code to exclude required reserves from the bankruptcy estate and lifting the automatic stay for redemptions from those reserves.
items.detail: Courts must use best efforts to begin ratable distributions to stablecoin holders within 14 days where reserves are available. Payment stablecoins are removed from the definitions of 'security' and 'commodity' under all major federal financial statutes, and permitted issuers are excluded from the Investment Company Act.

items.main: Foreign stablecoin issuers may offer their stablecoins to U.S. customers if the Treasury determines that their home country regulation is comparable to the GENIUS Act's requirements and the issuer holds sufficient U.S. reserves for U.S. customers.
items.detail: Foreign issuers must register with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and must not be domiciled in a country subject to comprehensive U.S. economic sanctions or in a jurisdiction the Treasury has determined to be of primary money laundering concern. The Treasury may make a comparability determination only upon a recommendation from the other members of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee — the Chairs of the Federal Reserve and the FDIC — and must decide a complete request within 210 days.

underreported.section: Section 19 — Disclosure Relating to Payment Stablecoins
underreported.summary: Amends federal financial disclosure law to require federal officials and employees to disclose payment stablecoin holdings only if the holdings aggregate more than $5,000, creating an exemption from the existing requirement to disclose deposits without a minimum threshold.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to regulate stablecoin issuance. This provision separately modifies federal ethics disclosure requirements for government officials holding stablecoins, creating a de minimis reporting exemption that does not apply to ordinary bank deposits. The provision is not referenced in the bill's title or in the regulatory framework sections.

underreported.section: Section 7 — Federal Reserve Override Authority for State-Qualified Issuers
underreported.summary: Grants the Federal Reserve authority to issue enforceable cease and desist directives limiting redemptions and affiliate transactions of state-qualified stablecoin issuers in 'unusual and exigent circumstances,' after only 48 hours' notice to the state regulator.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill establishes a state regulatory pathway as an alternative to federal licensing for issuers under $10B. This provision allows federal override of state regulatory authority in circumstances defined by the Board through rulemaking, and includes authority to suspend redemptions — a power that, if exercised, would directly affect stablecoin holders' ability to redeem their tokens.

gaps: The act permits reserves to include tokenized versions of permitted reserve assets, provided they comply with applicable law, but does not specify what regulatory standard applies to tokenized reserves or which regulator oversees them.

The effective date is the earlier of 18 months after enactment or 120 days after the primary Federal regulators issue final implementing regulations — meaning the act can take effect at the 18-month mark even if those implementing regulations have not been finalized, with no provision addressing how it operates in that interim.

The act prohibits rehypothecation of reserves but permits exceptions for repo liquidity purposes with prior regulatory approval; the act does not specify the standard regulators must apply when granting or denying that approval.

The act covers payment stablecoins but does not address non-payment stablecoins (algorithmically collateralized or endogenously collateralized stablecoins) other than requiring Treasury to study them within one year.
