bills.title: Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To provide for a system of regulation of the offer and sale of digital commodities by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act creates a legal framework for digital commodities — digital assets whose value comes from blockchain use — by splitting oversight between the SEC and the CFTC. The CFTC gets exclusive authority over spot and cash markets for digital commodities traded on registered exchanges, while the SEC handles token offerings and regulates broker-dealers who trade digital assets on alternative trading systems.
bills.brief: Splits regulation of digital commodities between the CFTC (spot markets and exchanges) and the SEC (token offerings and broker-dealers), and creates a certification path for blockchains to move from SEC oversight to CFTC jurisdiction once they become decentralized.

top_lines.headline: CFTC Gets Exclusive Spot Market Jurisdiction
subs: CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over spot and cash market transactions in digital commodities on registered entities or by entities required to register with the CFTC

Any trading facility offering a cash or spot market in at least one digital commodity must register as a digital commodity exchange, unless it handles only de minimis trading or serves only a single state
Digital commodity brokers and dealers must also register with the CFTC; existing operators have 180 days after enactment to file provisional registration statements

top_lines.headline: Blockchain Maturity Determines Regulator
subs: Issuers may certify their blockchain as a mature blockchain system — not controlled by any person or group — to the SEC; certification takes effect 60 days after filing unless the SEC objects
The SEC may stay a certification for up to an additional 120 days for novel or complex issues; rebutted certifications cannot be refiled for 90 days

Token issuers with blockchains not yet mature may raise up to $75M in a 12-month period under an SEC exemption, provided the blockchain is on track to mature within four years of first sale and no single purchaser acquires more than 10% of outstanding units

top_lines.headline: Insider Resale Restrictions Before Maturity
subs: Related persons (1%+ holders, promoters, senior employees within prior 6 months) and affiliated persons (5%+ holders, founders, directors within prior 12 months) face resale limits before blockchain maturity
Insiders must hold units at least 12 months from delivery before selling; in any 12-month period sales may not exceed 15% of units acquired directly from the issuer
Total insider sales may not exceed 50% of units acquired directly from the issuer prior to maturity certification

top_lines.headline: DeFi Activities Exempt from Registration
subs: Operating a node, validating transactions, providing a read-only blockchain interface, developing or distributing open-source blockchain or DeFi protocol software, operating non-custodial wallets, and participating in liquidity pools are all exempt from SEC registration
A parallel CFTC exemption under Title IV covers the same six categories of decentralized finance activity
Anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority of both the SEC and CFTC still applies to exempt decentralized finance activities

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 294-134 in July 2025 with bipartisan support and the Senate Banking Committee ordered a favorable substitute amendment in May 2026, but 60 votes are still needed to overcome a Senate filibuster. Democrats have raised concerns about the SEC's reduced role over tokens that may still function as securities, and the bill's Republican sponsor and cosponsor mix means several Democratic senators would need to cross over.

sections.label: Title I — Definitions, Rulemaking, and Provisional Registration

items.main: Defines core terms across three statutes — blockchain, digital commodity, mature blockchain system, decentralized governance system, and permitted payment stablecoin — in the Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and Commodity Exchange Act.
items.detail: A digital commodity is defined as a digital asset intrinsically linked to a blockchain system whose value is derived from the use of that blockchain, and must not be a security, stablecoin, commodity derivative, banking deposit, or pooled investment vehicle. A mature blockchain system is one not controlled by any person or group of persons under common control. Permitted payment stablecoins are excluded from the definitions of both security and digital commodity.

items.main: Requires joint CFTC-SEC rulemaking to further define key terms within 360 days of enactment, to issue delisting rules and guidance within 180 days, and to issue joint portfolio margining rules within 360 days.
items.detail: The bill also codifies the right of U.S. individuals to maintain hardware or software wallets and to conduct direct peer-to-peer digital asset transactions for personal lawful purposes with non-financial-institution counterparties, provided the transactions do not involve sanctioned property.

items.main: Requires existing digital commodity exchanges, brokers, and dealers to file provisional registration with the CFTC within 180 days of enactment, disclosing management information, financial condition, customer order rules, risk management procedures, and Bank Secrecy Act compliance policies.
items.detail: Provisional registrants must join a registered futures association and comply with its customer protection rules. The CFTC collects filing fees from provisional registrants; fees may only be collected in amounts provided in advance by an appropriations act. Late payment incurs a 5% penalty of the fee due multiplied by the number of consecutive 30-day periods overdue. Excess fees collected in any fiscal year must be refunded pro-rata within 60 days after year end.

items.main: Extends Bank Secrecy Act anti-money laundering obligations to digital commodity brokers, digital commodity dealers, and digital commodity exchanges that permit direct customer access.
items.detail: The Comptroller General must issue a report to Congress within one year of enactment assessing risks from foreign-based centralized intermediaries serving U.S. persons without BSA-equivalent requirements, with regulatory or legislative recommendations.

sections.label: Title II — Offers and Sales of Digital Commodities

items.main: Removes investment contract assets from the definition of investment contract in the Securities Act, Securities Exchange Act, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, and Securities Investor Protection Act. An investment contract asset is a digital commodity transferable person-to-person without an intermediary.
items.detail: Secondary market sales of a digital commodity by persons other than the issuer or its agents are not treated as sales of the original investment contract. End user distributions — broad, equitable distributions not involving more than a nominal exchange of value, such as mining rewards or staking incentives — are not offers or sales of a security.

items.main: Creates a new SEC exemption for token issuers raising up to $75M in a 12-month period via investment contracts in digital commodities, provided the blockchain is on track to achieve maturity within four years of first sale and no purchaser acquires more than 10% of outstanding units.
items.detail: Issuers relying on the $75M exemption must file an offering statement with the SEC including financial information, source code location, transaction history access, unit supply and release schedule, consensus mechanism description, a blockchain maturity development plan, and ownership disclosures for insiders. The exemption is not available to shell companies, investment companies, or issuers subject to an SEC enforcement order in the prior five years.

items.main: Imposes resale restrictions on digital commodity related persons (1%+ holders or promoters/senior employees within the prior 6 months) and affiliated persons (5%+ holders, founders, or current or former directors within the prior 12 months).
items.detail: Insiders must hold units for at least 12 months from delivery before resale. In any 12-month period, sales may not exceed 15% of units acquired directly from the issuer. Total sales prior to maturity certification may not exceed 50% of units acquired directly from the issuer.

items.main: Establishes the blockchain maturity certification process: any issuer, related person, affiliated person, or decentralized governance system may file a certification with the SEC that its blockchain is not controlled by any person or group under common control.
items.detail: A certification takes effect 60 days after filing unless the SEC stays it. The SEC may stay a certification once for up to an additional 120 days for novel or complex issues; a public comment period of at least 30 days may be opened within the initial 60-day window. Rebutted certifications may not be refiled for 90 days. If the SEC rebuts a certification, the filer may appeal within 60 days to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit under de novo review.

sections.label: Title III — Registration for Intermediaries at the SEC

items.main: Removes digital commodities and permitted payment stablecoins from the definition of security across five federal statutes: Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, and SIPA.
items.detail: The SEC retains jurisdiction over digital commodity transactions only when a digital commodity is brokered, traded, or custodied by a registered broker-dealer, through a national securities exchange, or through an alternative trading system. Anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules under Securities Exchange Act Section 10(b) apply to digital commodity and stablecoin transactions in those circumstances to the same extent they apply to securities transactions.

items.main: Allows SEC-registered broker-dealers and national securities exchanges to trade digital commodities and stablecoins without separate CFTC registration; the SEC has rulemaking authority over such activities.
items.detail: The SEC must revise its rules governing national securities exchanges within 270 days of enactment to account for digital commodity trading. Trading platforms may not be precluded from operating under a covered SEC exchange exemption solely because they also trade digital commodities alongside securities.

items.main: Exempts six categories of decentralized finance activity from SEC registration: operating nodes or oracle services, providing read-only blockchain interfaces, developing or distributing blockchain software or DeFi protocols, developing non-custodial wallet software, participating in liquidity pools, and providing computational work or network bandwidth.
items.detail: The exemption does not limit SEC anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority. Banks, broker-dealers, and trust companies providing digital asset custody may not be required to record custodied assets as liabilities on their balance sheets or to hold regulatory capital against them beyond what is necessary to mitigate operational risk.

sections.label: Title IV — Registration for Digital Commodity Intermediaries at the CFTC

items.main: Grants the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over spot and cash market transactions in digital commodities on registered entities or by entities registered or required to register with the CFTC, amending Commodity Exchange Act Section 2.
items.detail: The CFTC's new jurisdiction does not extend to stablecoin issuer operations, SEC-regulated securities offerings involving digital assets, or custodial activities by entities regulated by a federal banking agency. Digital commodity brokers may, subject to CFTC requirements, offer margin financing agreements to customers for digital commodity purchases.

items.main: Requires trading facilities offering spot or cash markets in at least one digital commodity to register with the CFTC as digital commodity exchanges, subject to CFTC core principles covering trading rules, risk management, customer protection, recordkeeping, and anti-manipulation obligations.
items.detail: Registered digital commodity exchanges and their affiliates may not trade on the exchange for their own account except for customer-directed transactions, risk management, operational needs, or functional blockchain use, with prior CFTC notice. Exchanges accepting customer funds must join a registered futures association. Digital commodity listing requires a written certification to the CFTC that the asset meets applicable requirements, effective 20 business days after filing unless the CFTC disapproves.

items.main: Defines qualified digital asset custodians as entities supervised for digital asset custody by a federal banking agency, NCUA, CFTC, SEC, state bank supervisor, state credit union supervisor, or appropriate foreign governmental authority, meeting minimum capital, asset protection, recordkeeping, and BSA compliance standards.
items.detail: Before CFTC issues final custody rules, state-licensed trust companies expressly permitted by their state bank supervisor to hold digital assets and meeting the minimum standards are deemed qualified custodians. The CFTC must provide a transition period of at least 2 years for such trust companies after final rules take effect.

items.main: Establishes ongoing blockchain control person restrictions: persons with unilateral authority over a certified mature blockchain, or who direct 20% or more of voting rights on that blockchain, must file notice with the CFTC and comply with CFTC-set disclosure and sales restriction rules before selling digital commodity units.
items.detail: The same six categories of decentralized finance activity that are exempt from SEC registration under Title III are also exempt from CFTC registration under Title IV. CFTC anti-fraud, anti-manipulation, and false reporting enforcement authority still applies to exempt activities.

sections.label: Title V — Innovation and Technology Improvements

items.main: Adds "innovation" as an explicit consideration in the efficiency provisions of the Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and Investment Company Act of 1940.
items.detail: The SEC must establish the Strategic Hub for Innovation and Financial Technology (FinHub) within 180 days of enactment, drawing members from the Divisions of Trading and Markets, Corporate Finance, and Investment Management. FinHub must report annually to the Commission by October 31 of each year after 2025. A parallel provision codifies LabCFTC within the CFTC.

items.main: Directs the CFTC and SEC to conduct studies and report to Congress on decentralized finance, non-fungible tokens, financial literacy among digital commodity holders, financial market infrastructure improvements, and foreign adversary participation in U.S. digital commodity markets.
items.detail: The foreign adversary participation study must assess national security implications of persons domiciled in foreign adversary countries participating in U.S. digital commodity markets.

underreported.summary: The bill codifies the right of U.S. individuals to maintain hardware or software wallets and to engage in direct peer-to-peer digital asset transactions for their own lawful purposes with non-financial-institution counterparties, provided the transactions do not involve sanctioned property.
underreported.why_unreported: Coverage focuses on the exchange registration and SEC-CFTC jurisdiction split. This provision limits federal agencies' ability to restrict individual self-custody and peer-to-peer transactions — a direct response to concerns about non-custodial wallet software regulation — but is embedded in the rulemaking section of Title I.

underreported.summary: Prohibits the SEC, federal banking agencies, and the NCUA from requiring banks, broker-dealers, or trust companies providing digital asset custody to record custodied assets as liabilities on their balance sheets or to hold regulatory capital against them beyond what is needed for operational risk.
underreported.why_unreported: This changes bank accounting and capital treatment for digital asset custody arrangements — a banking regulatory question separate from the market-structure framework the bill is primarily described as creating.

underreported.section: Section 412 — Control Person Restrictions on Mature Blockchains
underreported.summary: Even after a blockchain achieves certified maturity, persons who retain unilateral authority over the blockchain or who direct 20% or more of its voting rights must file notice with the CFTC and comply with CFTC-set disclosure and sales restriction rules before selling digital commodity units.
underreported.why_unreported: The maturity certification is widely described as a clean transition from SEC to CFTC jurisdiction, but this section imposes ongoing CFTC-enforced obligations on control persons even after the SEC oversight period ends — a continuing restriction that persists past maturity.

gaps: The bill requires the CFTC to expand into spot digital commodity market regulation but Section 410 provides only a fee-collection mechanism; fees may be collected only in amounts provided in advance by a separate appropriations act, leaving the CFTC's new mandate unfunded until Congress appropriates separately.

The bill defines mature blockchain system as one not controlled by any person or group of persons under common control, but does not specify quantitative thresholds for what constitutes control; the SEC must rebut or accept self-certifications within 60 days using this qualitative standard.

The bill exempts decentralized finance activities from registration but does not define the point at which a protocol becomes sufficiently centralized to lose the exemption; this boundary must be established through joint CFTC-SEC rulemaking.

The bill's own stated purpose covers protection of investors in digital commodities but does not establish any compensation or insurance fund analogous to SIPC for customers of digital commodity exchanges that fail or are defrauded.

bills.title: HALT Fentanyl Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Controlled Substances Act with respect to the scheduling of fentanyl-related substances, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The HALT Fentanyl Act permanently places all fentanyl-related substances as a class into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act, subjecting them to the same quantity-based mandatory minimum penalties that apply to fentanyl analogues under existing law. The law also creates a faster registration process for researchers who want to study Schedule I substances, including fentanyl, by allowing some research to begin as soon as 30 days after notifying the Attorney General.
bills.brief: Permanently schedules all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I drugs and imposes the same mandatory minimum penalties as fentanyl, while creating an expedited process for researchers to study Schedule I substances.

top_lines.headline: Class Scheduling of Fentanyl Variants
subs: Any substance structurally related to fentanyl by one of five defined chemical modifications is permanently placed in Schedule I
Includes salts, isomers, and salts of isomers of any qualifying fentanyl-related substance
Attorney General may publish a Federal Register list of qualifying substances; unlisted substances still qualify if they meet the structural definition

top_lines.headline: Criminal Penalties for Fentanyl Variants
subs: Offenses involving fentanyl-related substances now trigger the same quantity-based mandatory minimums that apply to fentanyl analogues
The specific quantity thresholds for each mandatory minimum tier are set by cross-reference to the existing analogue provisions in Section 401(b)(1) and are not restated in the bill
Importation and exportation penalties under the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act also updated to include fentanyl-related substances

top_lines.headline: Research Registration Reforms
subs: Researchers already registered for Schedule I or II research may begin fentanyl-related research 30 days after notifying the Attorney General
New researchers without prior registration receive a registration decision within 45 days of submitting a notice
Single registration now permitted for related research sites in the same city or county under the same institution

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 16, 2025, as Public Law 119-26. The bill passed with bipartisan support in both chambers.

sections.label: Section 2 — Class Scheduling of Fentanyl-Related Substances

items.main: Permanently adds a new category (e) to Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act covering any substance structurally related to fentanyl by one of five defined chemical modifications.
items.detail: The five structural modification criteria are: replacement of the phenethyl group's phenyl portion with any monocycle; substitution on the phenethyl group; substitution on the piperidine ring; replacement of the aniline ring with an aromatic monocycle; or replacement of the N-propionyl group with another acyl group. A substance is excluded from the class if it is already controlled under another schedule or expressly listed elsewhere.

sections.label: Section 3 — Research Registration Reforms

items.main: Creates an alternative registration process for researchers conducting studies on Schedule I substances that are the subject of an investigational new drug exemption or funded by the Departments of Health and Human Services, Defense, or Veterans Affairs.
items.detail: Researchers already holding a Schedule I or II registration may proceed 30 days after sending notice to the Attorney General. New researchers without prior registration receive a decision — either a registration or an order to show cause — within 45 days. Researchers may continue studying a substance that is newly added to Schedule I while their registration application is pending, up to 90 days after the scheduling action.

items.main: Allows registered researchers to perform small-quantity manufacturing activities — including creating extracts, tinctures, oils, solutions, and dosage forms — without obtaining a separate manufacturing registration.
items.detail: The activities must be within the scope stated in the researcher's notification or research protocol. Multiple staff at a single institution may conduct research under one researcher's registration without each obtaining a separate registration, provided the lead registered researcher notifies the Attorney General of each staff member's name and position.

sections.label: Section 6 — Criminal Penalties

items.main: Amends the mandatory minimum penalty provisions of the Controlled Substances Act and the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act to include fentanyl-related substances alongside fentanyl analogues.
items.detail: Under Section 401(b)(1)(A)(vi) and (B)(vi), offenses involving fentanyl-related substances now trigger the same quantity-based mandatory minimums as offenses involving fentanyl analogues. The specific quantity thresholds for each tier are set by cross-reference to those existing analogue provisions and are not restated in the bill text. Parallel amendments apply to importation and exportation offenses.

underreported.summary: States that the bill's class scheduling amendment to penalty provisions may not be construed as evidence that, before enactment, a fentanyl-related substance was not already an analogue of fentanyl under existing law.
underreported.why_unreported: This provision preserves the government's ability to prosecute pre-enactment conduct involving fentanyl-related substances under prior analogue theory, meaning the bill's penalty framework extends backward in time through its rule of construction, not just forward. The bill title and stated purpose focus on prospective scheduling.

underreported.summary: Requires the Attorney General to publicly disclose on the Drug Enforcement Administration website when a particular Schedule I substance is subject to different research application criteria than other Schedule I substances, including the criteria and how they differ.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's primary research reform focuses on expediting approvals, but this transparency provision separately addresses situations where the Attorney General is applying non-standard criteria to specific substances, which may affect which substances researchers can practically access even with the new expedited process.

gaps: The bill permanently places fentanyl-related substances in Schedule I but does not establish any mechanism for de-scheduling a substance if it is later found to have accepted medical use, which is one of the criteria for Schedule I classification.

The expedited research registration process applies only to research funded by HHS, DOD, or VA, or involving an investigational new drug application — it does not apply to privately funded academic research outside those categories.

The bill imposes the same mandatory minimums on fentanyl-related substances as on fentanyl analogues but does not address the quantity thresholds used to distinguish between the two mandatory minimum tiers, which are set by cross-reference to existing analogue provisions and may not match the actual potency of all covered substances.

added: Schedule I class designation for all fentanyl-related substances meeting structural modification criteria
Expedited 30-day notice-based research registration for researchers already holding a Schedule I or II registration
45-day decision deadline for new researcher registration applications involving qualifying Schedule I research
Single-registration option for related research sites in the same city or county under the same institution
Authorization for registered researchers to perform small-quantity manufacturing without a separate manufacturing registration
Continuation authority for researchers studying substances newly added to Schedule I while applications are pending

Controlled Substances Import and Export Act Section 1010(b)(1)(F) and (2)(F): import/export penalties extended to fentanyl-related substances

bills.title: SAVE Act
bills.official_title: To amend the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 to require proof of United States citizenship to register an individual to vote in elections for Federal office, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The SAVE Act requires anyone registering to vote in a federal election to show documentary proof that they are a U.S. citizen. Acceptable documents include a REAL ID-compliant ID showing citizenship, a U.S. passport, or a government photo ID paired with a certified birth certificate or naturalization certificate. States must build programs to remove non-citizens from voter rolls and may be sued by private citizens if they register someone who did not provide required proof.
bills.brief: Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship — such as a passport or REAL ID plus birth certificate — to register to vote in any federal election.

top_lines.headline: Citizenship Proof Required to Register
subs: States may not accept or process a federal voter registration application unless the applicant presents documentary proof of U.S. citizenship

Acceptable documents: REAL ID-compliant ID indicating citizenship, valid U.S. passport, military ID with service record showing U.S. birth, or government photo ID paired with a certified birth certificate or naturalization certificate
Takes effect immediately upon enactment; applies to all applications submitted on or after enactment

top_lines.headline: Fallback Process for Applicants Without Documents
subs: States must create an alternative process where applicants who lack documents may submit other evidence and sign an attestation under penalty of perjury
A state or local official must sign a separate affidavit explaining why the applicant sufficiently established citizenship before registration may proceed
The Election Assistance Commission must develop a uniform affidavit form for state and local officials to use when registering such applicants

top_lines.headline: Voter Roll Maintenance and Enforcement
subs: States must remove non-citizens from voter rolls immediately upon receiving documentary proof or verified information that a registrant is not a citizen
States must establish programs using DHS, Social Security Administration, or state ID agency data to identify and remove non-citizen registrants within 30 days of enactment
Private right of action against election officials who register applicants who failed to provide citizenship proof; criminal penalties added for officials who knowingly register such applicants

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House in April 2025 with Republican support but has stalled in the Senate, where Democrats can filibuster and no bipartisan path has emerged. The SAVE Act addresses a voter registration requirement that opponents argue will disenfranchise millions of eligible citizens who lack easily accessible documents, making Democratic support unlikely. With 53 Republican senators and 60 votes needed to break a filibuster, passage requires substantial Democratic crossover that has not materialized.

sections.label: Section 2 — Requiring Proof of Citizenship for Voter Registration

items.main: Amends the National Voter Registration Act to prohibit states from accepting a federal voter registration application unless the applicant presents documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.
items.detail: The requirement applies to all registration methods: motor vehicle license applications, the national mail voter registration form, voter registration agencies (such as public assistance offices), and in-person registration. For mail registrations, applicants must subsequently present proof in person to the appropriate election official by the state's registration deadline, or at a polling place if the state allows same-day registration.

items.main: Creates an alternative process for applicants who cannot produce standard documentary proof, requiring a signed attestation under penalty of perjury and a separate affidavit from the registering official.
items.detail: If a state official determines the applicant has sufficiently established citizenship without standard documents, the official must file an affidavit developed by the Election Assistance Commission explaining the basis for that determination. States must establish a program within 30 days to identify non-citizen registrants using data from DHS's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, the Social Security Number Verification Service, or state driver's license agency records. Federal agencies must respond to state verification requests within 24 hours at no charge.

sections.label: Sections 5–8 — DHS Notification, Enforcement, and Construction Rules

items.main: Requires DHS to notify state chief election officials when an individual becomes a naturalized citizen, so states can update voter roll status.
items.detail: Section 12 of the National Voter Registration Act is amended to add criminal penalties for federal executive branch employees who provide material assistance to a non-citizen attempting to register or vote, and for election officials who register applicants who failed to present required documentation. The Paperwork Reduction Act is explicitly exempted from applying to new voter registration forms, allowing the Election Assistance Commission to update forms without the standard OMB review process.

underreported.section: Section 2(f)(4)(D) — Investigation for Purposes of Removal
underreported.summary: Requires DHS to initiate an investigation and consider removal proceedings under the Immigration and Nationality Act against any non-citizen found to be unlawfully registered to vote after a state election official's verification request.
underreported.why_unreported: This provision is located within the voter roll maintenance section but extends the bill's effect beyond election administration into immigration enforcement, requiring DHS to consider deportation for individuals identified through the voter verification process. The bill's stated purpose is voter registration integrity, not immigration removal.

underreported.section: Section 4 — Inapplicability of Paperwork Reduction Act
underreported.summary: Exempts all voter registration materials developed or modified under this Act from the standard Paperwork Reduction Act review process, bypassing Office of Management and Budget review requirements for the new forms.
underreported.why_unreported: The Paperwork Reduction Act waiver enables the Election Assistance Commission to redesign federal voter registration forms without the public comment and OMB approval process that typically applies to new federal information collection requirements. The bill's title and stated purpose do not reference this procedural exemption.

gaps: The bill requires states to establish a fallback process for applicants without documents but does not define a minimum standard for what constitutes sufficient alternative evidence of citizenship, leaving the standard to state and local official discretion.

The bill applies only to federal elections; it does not address registration for state and local elections, creating the possibility of separate registration tracks for federal and non-federal elections in states that do not adopt parallel requirements.

The bill requires DHS to respond to state verification requests within 24 hours but does not specify consequences if DHS fails to meet that deadline, leaving no enforcement mechanism for states when the federal agency is unresponsive.
The bill requires the Election Assistance Commission to issue implementation guidance within 10 days of enactment but does not specify consequences if the Commission fails to act within that window.

The bill adds citizenship proof requirements for voter registration but Section 6 explicitly preserves the right to cast a provisional ballot for applicants who are later verified as citizens — the analysis of the registration requirement does not discuss how this interacts with same-day registration states where verification may not be complete before the election.

added: Documentary proof of U.S. citizenship requirement for all federal voter registration applications
State fallback process for applicants who cannot provide standard documents, with official affidavit requirement
State obligation to establish non-citizen identification program using DHS, SSA, or state ID agency data within 30 days
Mandatory removal of non-citizens from voter rolls upon receipt of documentary proof or verified information
Federal agency 24-hour response requirement for state citizenship verification requests at no charge
DHS obligation to notify state election officials of new naturalizations
Private right of action against officials who register applicants lacking required citizenship proof
Criminal penalty for election officials who register applicants who failed to present documentation
Criminal penalty for federal executive branch employees who assist non-citizens in registering or voting
modified: National Voter Registration Act Section 4: voter registration methods now subject to citizenship proof requirement
NVRA Section 8: removal from voter rolls expanded to include non-citizenship as a removal basis
NVRA Section 12: criminal penalties expanded to cover election officials and federal employees

bills.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
bills.official_title: An act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.
bills.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill permanently extends the 2017 Trump-era tax cuts, adds new deductions for tips and overtime pay, tightens eligibility for SNAP food assistance and Medicaid, funds more than $109.7B in new border security and immigration enforcement, and rescinds most of the Inflation Reduction Act's climate and clean energy spending. It also raises the federal debt ceiling by $5 trillion to finance the combined cost.
bills.brief: Makes the 2017 Trump tax cuts permanent, creates tip and overtime deductions, funds a $109.7B border buildup, imposes Medicaid work requirements, and terminates most IRA clean energy programs.

top_lines.headline: Tax Cuts Made Permanent
subs: Individual tax rates of 10%–37% made permanent; estate tax exemption increased to $15M
Standard deduction raised to $15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint filers (inflation-adjusted)
Child tax credit increased to $2,200 per qualifying child; SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 through 2029, reverting to $10,000 in 2030

top_lines.headline: New Deductions for Workers
subs: Up to $25,000 deduction for qualified tip income (2025–2028)
Up to $12,500 deduction for overtime compensation (2025–2028)
Up to $10,000 deduction for passenger vehicle loan interest (2025–2028)
New "Trump accounts" — tax-advantaged IRAs for under-18s with a one-time $1,000 government deposit for births in 2025–2028

top_lines.headline: Border Security and Immigration Enforcement
subs: $46.55B to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for physical barriers, technology, and access roads through FY2029
$45B to ICE for expanded detention capacity through FY2029
$29.85B to ICE for hiring, transportation, and removal operations through FY2029
New immigration court fees: $100 for asylum applications, $1,000 for parolees, $5,000 for individuals apprehended between ports of entry

top_lines.headline: SNAP and Medicaid Changes
subs: SNAP work requirements extended to adults up to age 65 (from 55); parents of children 14 and older must also meet requirements
States required to share 5–15% of SNAP benefit costs starting FY2028 based on payment error rate; federal admin cost share cut from 50% to 25%
Medicaid expansion enrollees must complete 80 hours per month of work or community service beginning in FY2027
Medicaid eligibility redetermined every six months for expansion population (previously annual)

top_lines.headline: Defense and Security Investments
subs: $29.18B for the shipbuilding industrial base and naval shipbuilding (FY2025)
$24.41B for space-based missile intercept and ground-based missile defense (FY2025)
$25.38B for hypersonic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles (FY2025)
$14.69B for nuclear forces and production, including B-21 bomber expansion (FY2025)

top_lines.headline: Clean Energy Tax Credits Terminated
subs: Consumer EV tax credit (up to $7,500) and used EV credit (up to $4,000) terminated October 1, 2025
Home energy efficiency credit (up to $3,200) and residential clean energy credit terminated 2026
Wind and solar clean electricity production and investment credits terminated for new projects after 2027
Clean hydrogen production credit terminated for projects starting construction after 2027

top_lines.headline: Energy Production and IRA Rescissions
subs: Oil and gas royalty rates reduced on federal lands; onshore lease sales resumed in specified states
ANWR: at least 4 lease sales within 10 years; NPR-A: at least 5 lease sales within 10 years
$389M for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; repeals Biden-era drawdown requirement
Rescinds unobligated IRA funds for Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, school air quality, climate justice grants, and dozens of other EPA climate programs

top_lines.headline: Student Loans and Education
subs: Graduate PLUS loans eliminated for new loans on or after July 1, 2026
Aggregate student loan caps: $100,000 for graduate students, $200,000 for professional students, $257,500 lifetime limit
All current income-based repayment plans terminated for new loans; borrowers limited to standard plan or new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP)
$10.5B in additional Pell Grant funding for FY2026; new Workforce Pell Grants for 150–600 clock-hour programs

top_lines.headline: Debt Limit and Other Provisions
subs: Statutory debt limit increased by $5 trillion
$24.59B to the Coast Guard for vessels, aircraft, and shore infrastructure through FY2029
$12.52B for FAA facilities modernization including $4.75B for telecom infrastructure and $3B for radar replacement
$9.995B to NASA for Moon and Mars missions and International Space Station deorbit

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 4, 2025, as Public Law 119-21. The bill passed both chambers along party lines under the Senate's reconciliation procedure, which requires only a simple majority and cannot be filibustered. Republicans held the House and Senate majority and used reconciliation to bypass the Senate's 60-vote threshold.

sections.label: Title I — Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

items.main: Tightens SNAP eligibility and cost structure: work requirements extended to age 65, state cost-sharing of 5–15% beginning FY2028, and federal administrative cost share cut from 50% to 25%.
items.detail: SNAP state cost-sharing is calculated on a sliding scale based on the state's payment error rate — states below 6% pay nothing; states at 10% or above pay 15%. States may no longer request waivers of the three-month SNAP time limit based on insufficient job availability. SNAP-ED nutrition education grants are eliminated. SNAP eligibility is removed for certain legally present immigrants, including domestic violence and trafficking survivors.

items.main: Extends farm program authorities through crop year 2031, including ARC and PLC commodity support, Dairy Margin Coverage, and crop insurance enhancements.
items.detail: ARC and PLC payment limits increased to $155,000 per person (from $125,000), adjusted for inflation annually. The ARC program coverage guarantee increases from 86% to 90% of benchmark revenue; maximum payment amount increases from 10% to 12% of benchmark revenue. Crop insurance premium subsidies increase 3–5% depending on coverage level. The Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) premium subsidy increases from 65% to 80%.

sections.label: Title II — Armed Services

items.main: Provides $156.22B in FY2025 supplemental defense funding across shipbuilding, missile systems, space, nuclear forces, aircraft, and personnel.
items.detail: $29.18B for naval shipbuilding; $24.41B for missile defense and space-based sensors; $25.38B for hypersonic and other missiles; $16.05B for unmanned aerial systems and AI integration; $14.69B for nuclear forces including B-21 bomber expansion; $8.64B for aircraft modernization and prevention of F-22 retirement; $12.66B for Indo-Pacific military exercises and satellites; $7.48B for military quality of life including basic housing allowance and child care.

sections.label: Title VII — Individual and Business Tax Reforms

items.main: Permanently extends the individual income tax rates, standard deduction, and most deduction and credit provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
items.detail: Standard deduction set at $15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint filers (inflation-adjusted). Estate tax exemption increased to $15M. Child tax credit increased to $2,200 and indexed to inflation. SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 through 2029, then reverts to $10,000. Qualified Business Income deduction made permanent with expanded phase-in range. Alternative minimum tax exemptions permanently raised.

items.main: Creates new above-the-line deductions for tip income (up to $25,000), overtime compensation (up to $12,500), and passenger vehicle loan interest (up to $10,000), all available for tax years 2025–2028.
items.detail: All three deductions phase out for individuals with modified AGI above $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers) and require work-eligible Social Security numbers. A new "Trump account" IRA for individuals under 18 allows up to $5,000 annually; the federal government deposits a one-time $1,000 into accounts for children born in 2025–2028.

items.main: Extends 100% bonus depreciation permanently, allows immediate expensing of domestic R&D, and increases the Section 179 deduction limit to $2.5M.
items.detail: Section 179 phase-out begins at $4M in asset purchases. BEAT (base erosion minimum tax) rate set permanently at 10.5% (up from 10%), repealing the scheduled increase to 12.5% for tax years after 2025. GILTI and FDII renamed Net CFC Tested Income and Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income, with the foreign tax credit haircut reduced from 20% to 10%.

items.main: Terminates most IRA clean energy tax credits for consumers and businesses, including EV credits, home efficiency credits, and wind and solar electricity credits.
items.detail: New and used EV credits terminated for vehicles purchased on or after October 1, 2025. Home energy efficiency and residential clean energy credits terminated effective 2026. Wind and solar clean electricity production and investment credits terminated for new projects placed in service after December 31, 2027. Clean hydrogen production credit terminated for construction beginning after 2027.

sections.label: Title VII — Medicaid and Medicare

items.main: Requires Medicaid expansion enrollees to complete 80 hours per month of work, community service, or education beginning in FY2027; states must redetermine expansion enrollees' eligibility every six months.
items.detail: Exemptions apply to individuals with serious medical conditions or dependent children aged 13 or younger. States may not waive the requirement, though the CMS may grant a state an implementation delay through December 31, 2028. Cost-sharing of up to $35 per service required for expansion enrollees with income above the poverty line beginning FY2029. Federal Medicaid payment suspended for one year for essential community providers with more than $800,000 in Medicaid revenue that furnish abortions outside of rape, incest, or life-threatening circumstances.

items.main: Reduces the maximum provider tax states may impose to fund Medicaid matching funds, phasing down to 3.5% by FY2032 from the current 6%.
items.detail: States that have not expanded Medicaid are precluded from increasing their provider tax rate. New provider taxes may not be created by states without an existing one. Medicaid and Medicare eligibility restricted to U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, and specified immigrant categories — excluding DACA recipients, TPS holders, asylees, and refugees beginning in FY2027 (Medicaid) and within 18 months of enactment (Medicare).

items.main: $10B per fiscal year for FY2026–FY2030 for a Rural Health Transformation Program providing states with funds to improve rural health access.
items.detail: 50% of funds distributed equally among approved states; remaining 50% based on proportion of rural health facilities. States must submit rural health transformation plans; no matching funds required. $200M for FY2025 for CMS implementation.

sections.label: Title IX — Border Security and Homeland Security

items.main: Appropriates more than $109.7B through FY2029 for border barriers, CBP personnel, ICE detention, CBP surveillance equipment, and state border reimbursements.
items.detail: $46.55B to CBP for physical barriers, access roads, and detection technology; $45B to ICE for detention facility expansion; $12.01B for CBP personnel, bonuses, and fleet; $6.17B for CBP inspection and surveillance equipment; $10B to reimburse states and localities for border security actions taken on or after January 20, 2021.

items.main: $300M to FEMA to reimburse state and local law enforcement for costs of protecting a presidential residence; $625M for 2026 FIFA World Cup security and $1B for 2028 Olympics security.
items.detail: FEMA State Homeland Security Grant Program also receives $500M for drone detection technology and $450M for Operation Stonegarden border coordination through FY2029. The Federal Employees Health Benefits program receives $66M for a mandatory eligibility audit to verify family members.

sections.label: Title X — Immigration, Judiciary, and Radiation Compensation

items.main: Establishes new or increased fees across the immigration system: $100 for asylum applications, $1,000 for parolees, $550 for asylee employment authorization, and $5,000 for individuals apprehended between ports of entry or ordered removed in absentia.
items.detail: $29.85B to ICE for hiring, removal operations, and detention; $3B to DOJ for immigration courts and drug trafficking prosecution; $3.5B to reimburse states for incarcerating non-citizen criminals; $5B for the Bureau of Prisons; $1B for the Secret Service. $100 fee per calendar year that an asylum application remains pending.

items.main: Reestablishes and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program through 2028, increasing compensation amounts and expanding geographic coverage to include additional areas of Idaho, New Mexico, Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky.
items.detail: Extends the statute of limitations for filing claims through 2027. Expands eligible groups to include additional uranium miners and individuals near Manhattan Project waste sites who developed certain cancers.

sections.label: Title V — Energy and Natural Resources

items.main: Reduces oil and gas royalty rates on federal lands, reinstates noncompetitive leasing, and mandates at least 4 ANWR lease sales and 5 NPR-A lease sales within 10 years.
items.detail: Offshore royalty rates also reduced; Gulf state revenue-sharing cap raised from $500M to $650M per year for FY2025–FY2034. Methane royalties on vented or flared gas from federal lands eliminated. $389M for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; Biden-era mandatory drawdown repealed. Forest Service must sell 250 million board feet of additional timber per year through FY2034.

sections.label: Title VIII — Student Loans and Education

items.main: Eliminates Grad PLUS loans for new borrowers on or after July 1, 2026, and caps federal student borrowing at $100,000 aggregate for graduate students and $257,500 lifetime across all federal loan types.
items.detail: Parent PLUS loans capped at $20,000 annually and $65,000 lifetime per dependent undergraduate. All current income-based repayment plans (SAVE, PAYE, ICR) terminated for new loans; borrowers limited to a standard repayment plan or the new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP). Economic hardship and unemployment deferments eliminated for loans originated on or after July 1, 2027.

items.main: $10.5B in additional Pell Grant funding for FY2026; new Workforce Pell Grants created for programs of 150–600 clock hours in workforce training.
items.detail: Low-earning outcome programs — programs where graduates earn less than high school diploma holders — lose eligibility for federal funds beginning July 1, 2026. Institutions must notify enrolled students when a program loses eligibility. Borrower defense to repayment and closed school discharge regulations delayed until July 1, 2035.

sections.label: Title IV — Commerce, Transportation, and Infrastructure

items.main: $24.59B to the Coast Guard through FY2029 for new vessels, aircraft, and shore facilities; $12.52B to the FAA for facilities modernization including $4.75B for telecom infrastructure and $3B for radar replacement.
items.detail: FCC spectrum auction authority reauthorized through September 30, 2034; FCC must auction at least 300 MHz including 100 MHz in the Upper C-Band within two years; NTIA must identify 500 MHz of additional federal spectrum for reallocation within four years. CAFE standard civil penalty set to $0, eliminating enforcement.

items.main: $9.995B to NASA for Moon and Mars missions, ISS deorbit preparation, and Artemis IV and V spacecraft procurement; $9.995B includes a Mars telecommunications orbiter.
items.detail: NASA must identify a previously-flown crewed spacecraft to be relocated and placed on public display near a NASA field center within 18 months. Brand USA tourism promotion funding reduced from $100M to $20M per year through FY2027.

underreported.summary: Sets the civil penalty for a manufacturer's violation of CAFE fuel economy standards to $0, removing NHTSA's ability to enforce those standards through monetary penalties.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is titled and described as modifying the civil penalty amount, but the operative effect is to eliminate meaningful enforcement of federal fuel economy standards for automakers — a substantive change to federal vehicle emissions policy that is not referenced in the bill's title or stated purpose.

underreported.summary: Eliminates the $200 federal excise tax on the transfer of National Firearms Act items other than machine guns and destructive devices, effectively removing the tax on silencers, short-barreled rifles, and short-barreled shotguns.
underreported.why_unreported: The section appears in a tax chapter primarily focused on deductions and credits for families and businesses. The NFA excise tax removal is a standalone firearms regulatory change unrelated to the chapter's stated subject matter and is not mentioned in the bill's title.

underreported.summary: Prohibits federal Medicaid payment for one year to any nonprofit health care provider with more than $800,000 in annual Medicaid payments if the provider primarily furnishes family planning services and provides abortions outside of rape, incest, or life-threatening circumstances.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision is structured as a Medicaid payment restriction on a category of providers meeting specific criteria, but its operative effect — cutting off federal Medicaid funding to qualifying Planned Parenthood affiliates — is not stated in the section title or described in the bill's stated purposes.

underreported.summary: Eliminates the $800 de minimis customs exemption effective July 1, 2027, ending duty-free treatment for small-value imports that currently allows platforms like Shein and Temu to ship directly to U.S. consumers without tariffs.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision appears in a chapter captioned as enhancing deduction guardrails. It eliminates a longstanding customs exemption that has shaped the structure of direct-to-consumer international e-commerce, with broad implications for import pricing and retail competition not discussed in the bill's tax-focused framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Babin
featured_quotes.text: I rise today in very strong support of H.R. 1, President Trump's one big, beautiful bill. Here we are, despite months of our Democratic colleagues' best efforts to delay, fearmonger, and mislead the public about this bill, and we are ready to deliver for the American people. Here is the thing about fear-mongering. You can only say ``the sky is falling'' so many times before folks start waking up and seeing for themselves exactly what is going on. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act secures our border.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Brown
featured_quotes.text: For the first time in history, this bill would force States to pay for part of SNAP benefits, and it would require States to increase their share of administrative costs. This is an unfunded mandate, plain and simple. Let's be clear. The costs are staggering, the consequences are devastating, and the cruelty is deeply disturbing. This policy punishes those who can least afford it: seniors on a fixed income, veterans, and families already forced to choose between gas and groceries. States will be stuck in a corner.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Langworthy
featured_quotes.text: The stakes for the American people could not be higher. We are rapidly approaching a fiscal cliff. If we do nothing, the Trump tax cuts, the most progrowth tax reforms in generations, will expire. That means higher taxes on nearly every American. That means a gutted child tax credit. That means small businesses will lose the tools they need to survive and to thrive. That means less take-home pay for working families that have already been crushed by the Biden-era inflation. This isn't some hypothetical scenario.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, Republicans are openly bragging about how the bill kicks children and the elderly off Medicaid, nutritional assistance, and more, all to pay for another tax break for wealthy Republican donors. My Republican colleagues are not talking about the trillions and trillions of dollars their political giveaway is going to cost. In fact, Mr. Speaker, Vice President Vance has said historic levels of Homeland Security funding in the bill sweetens the deal for the devil.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Alford
featured_quotes.text: Today, Mr. Speaker, we face a watershed moment for the American people. This Republican majority was given a clear mandate by the American people, which is the America First agenda. This bill is our opportunity to deliver on that agenda. H.R. 1 stops the largest tax increase in U.S. history, while providing the largest tax cut for working-and middle-class families ever, with no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and tax breaks for seniors.

gaps: The bill increases the statutory debt limit by $5 trillion but includes no spending cap, enforcement trigger, or fiscal review mechanism tied to the increase.

The SNAP state cost-sharing provisions create financial liability for states beginning FY2028, but the bill provides no additional administrative resources to help states reduce payment error rates below the 6% threshold required to avoid cost-sharing.
The bill terminates consumer and commercial EV credits and most clean energy investment credits but does not include transition support for workers or businesses in those sectors.

Medicaid work requirements are established for the expansion population but the bill specifies no federal remedy or enrollment fallback for individuals who lose coverage due to reporting failures unrelated to actual eligibility.

bills.title: Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Bureau of Indian Affairs to process and complete all mortgage packages associated with residential and business mortgages on Indian land by certain deadlines, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) must now process mortgage applications on Indian trust land within strict deadlines — completing preliminary reviews within 10 days, and approving or disapproving leasehold mortgages within 20 days and land mortgages within 30 days. The law also creates a new Realty Ombudsman within the BIA to monitor compliance, serve as a liaison to federal mortgage agencies, and resolve complaints from tribes, tribal members, and lenders.
bills.brief: Sets mandatory processing deadlines for BIA mortgage packages on Indian trust land and creates a Realty Ombudsman to enforce compliance.

top_lines.headline: BIA Processing Deadlines
subs: Preliminary review of mortgage package within 10 calendar days of receipt
Leasehold mortgages approved or disapproved within 20 days; land mortgages and right-of-way documents within 30 days
First certified title status report completed within 14 days of request; subsequent reports within 10 days of approval

top_lines.headline: Delay Notification and System Access
subs: BIA must immediately notify affected parties upon missing any processing deadline
Must respond to all status inquiries within 2 calendar days
Relevant federal agencies and Indian Tribes receive read-only TAAMS portal access effective on enactment

top_lines.headline: Oversight and Reporting
subs: New Realty Ombudsman — a BIA official who monitors deadline compliance and resolves complaints from tribes and lenders — established within BIA Division of Real Estate Services
BIA Director must submit annual compliance report to Congress by March 1 each year
GAO must report on cost and feasibility of digitizing tribal mortgage records within 1 year

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 4, 2026 as Public Law 119-88. The bill passed both chambers with bipartisan support — it had 3 Senate cosponsors, a companion House bill (H.R. 2130) with a House Natural Resources Committee report, and cleared both the Senate Indian Affairs Committee and the House Natural Resources Committee before floor passage.

sections.label: Section 3 — Mortgage Review and Processing

items.main: BIA must complete preliminary review of any mortgage package within 10 calendar days of receipt, then approve or disapprove leasehold mortgages within 20 days and land mortgages or right-of-way documents within 30 days.
items.detail: Missing documents must be flagged to the lender within 2 calendar days of the preliminary review. Approval or disapproval decisions must be in writing; denials must state the basis. The 20-day leasehold approval deadline does not apply when the applicant is an Indian tribe approved for self-governance leasing under 25 U.S.C. § 415(h).

items.main: First certified title status reports must be completed within 14 calendar days of request; subsequent reports within 10 calendar days of mortgage approval — delivered directly to lenders, applicable bureau field offices, and relevant federal guarantor agencies.
items.detail: Notice of completion is provided electronically via secure encryption software and by U.S. mail; lenders may opt out of electronic delivery. If BIA misses any processing deadline, it must immediately notify all affected parties and respond to all subsequent status inquiries within 2 calendar days.

sections.label: Section 4 — Realty Ombudsman

items.main: The BIA Director must establish a Realty Ombudsman within the Division of Real Estate Services, reporting directly to the Secretary of the Interior.
items.detail: The Ombudsman monitors deadline compliance, ensures bureau offices comply with notification requirements, serves as a liaison to USDA, HUD, and VA on mortgage matters, and receives and resolves inquiries and complaints from Indian Tribes, tribal members, and lenders. The Comptroller General must submit to Congress a report on the cost and feasibility of digitizing tribal mortgage records within 1 year of enactment.

underreported.summary: The 20-day approval deadline for leasehold mortgages does not apply when the applicant is an Indian tribe approved for self-governance leasing under 25 U.S.C. § 415(h). Individual tribal members applying for mortgages on the same land remain subject to the full deadline regime.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around processing deadlines that apply uniformly to Indian land mortgages, but the operative exemption carves out tribal self-governance leasing activity from the 20-day approval requirement without any discussion in the bill title or stated purpose.

gaps: The bill requires annual reporting on deadline compliance by bureau office but specifies no penalties or corrective measures for offices that chronically miss the processing deadlines.
The bill title and purpose focus on homeownership, but the processing deadline framework applies equally to business leasehold mortgages and commercial right-of-way documents.
Read-only TAAMS portal access is granted to relevant federal agencies and Indian Tribes as institutional entities, but not to individual tribal members who are the direct mortgage applicants.

added: Mandatory BIA processing deadlines for mortgage packages (10-day preliminary review, 20-day leasehold approval, 30-day land mortgage and right-of-way approval)
Notification requirement: immediate notice to parties upon missed deadline, 2-day response window for status inquiries
Direct delivery requirement for certified title status reports to lenders, bureau offices, and federal guarantor agencies
Read-only TAAMS access for relevant federal agencies and Indian Tribes effective on enactment
Annual BIA Director report to Congress due March 1 each year
GAO study on digitization feasibility for tribal mortgage records, due within 1 year of enactment
Realty Ombudsman position within BIA Division of Real Estate Services, reporting to Secretary of Interior
