This is nuts. Is that ``America First''? That is ``America Last.''

Copper sulfide mining is the most toxic industry in America, and it is particularly ill-suited to water-rich environments because it acidifies the water. It leaches heavy metals like arsenic, lead, and mercury into that water, which is part of the reason it has never been done in Minnesota before.

allowing public land orders to be rescinded under the Congressional Review Act, which is what would be happening here tonight, is a dangerous precedent that would affect every State in our country. Public land orders have never been previously submitted by any administration, including the first Trump administration, as a rule under the CRA.
The type of mining that Twin Metals has proposed has a 100 percent track record of toxic pollution. There has never been a mine of this kind that did not leach toxic pollution.

gaps: The joint resolution nullifies Public Land Order 7917 but does not address the Congressional Review Act bar under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, which prevents the Bureau of Land Management from issuing a substantially similar rule in the future without explicit congressional authorization.

The resolution removes the 20-year withdrawal but does not address the status of any tribal consultation obligations associated with the original order regarding the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa.

bills.title: Ensuring Children Receive Support Act
bills.official_title: Ensuring Children Receive Support Act
bills.summary: When a parent owes more than $2,500 in unpaid child support, federal law already requires the State Department to deny them a new passport — but revoking an existing passport is currently optional. This bill makes revocation mandatory in those same circumstances, requires the government to notify the individual before acting, and gives the State Department explicit statutory authority to issue a short-term return-home passport for individuals abroad who need to come back to the United States.
bills.brief: Makes passport revocation mandatory — not optional — for individuals owing more than $2,500 in unpaid child support.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Revocation
subs: Removes State Department's option to merely restrict a passport — revocation required at $2,500+ arrearage
Individual must be notified of intent to revoke before action is taken

top_lines.headline: Emergency Exception
subs: Individuals abroad may receive a temporary, limited-duration passport solely for return travel to the United States

bills.likelihoodReason: Child support enforcement has broad bipartisan appeal, but the bill carries only 1 cosponsor and passed the House without significant floor debate coverage. The Senate calendar for narrowly supported House bills is uncertain, and mandatory revocation without a specified appeal window may draw procedural objections.

sections.label: Section 2 — Passport Revocation for Child Support Arrearage

items.main: Amends Section 452(k) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 652(k)) to make revocation of a previously issued passport mandatory when an individual owes more than $2,500 in child support.
items.detail: Current law gives the State Department discretion to "revoke, restrict, or limit" a passport in these circumstances. This bill removes restrict and limit as options, changing the authority to a mandatory revoke. The State Department must notify the individual of the intent to revoke before taking action. The $2,500 arrearage threshold set by the Office of Child Support Enforcement of the Department of Health and Human Services is unchanged.

items.main: Authorizes the State Department to issue a limited-duration temporary passport solely for return travel to the United States for affected individuals who are abroad in an emergency.
items.detail: Notwithstanding the mandatory revocation requirement, the State Department may issue a temporary passport to an individual with a $2,500+ arrearage who is abroad and needs to return to the United States on an emergency basis. The temporary passport is valid only for the return trip home and is limited in duration.

underreported.summary: The bill adds a requirement that the State Department notify the individual of the intent to revoke their passport before taking action, but specifies no minimum notice period, required content for the notification, or appeal process before revocation takes effect.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's operative change is the mandatory revocation requirement. The notification obligation is added as a subordinate clause with no procedural detail, leaving the timing, form, and any pre-revocation remedy entirely to agency implementation.

gaps: The bill makes revocation mandatory but does not specify a minimum notice period between notification and revocation, nor any right to contest the arrearage determination before the passport is revoked.
The bill does not address the process or timeline for passport restoration after an arrearage is resolved or a payment plan is established.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: This legislation has a simple premise: Parents must meet their obligations to care for their kids, period. It is pretty simple. To ensure that is happening, State-level child support agencies rely in part on the Passport Denial Program, which is run out of the State Department and, as its name suggests, is used to deny the ability of delinquent parents to obtain a passport to leave the country when they owe back child support.

added: Requirement for the State Department to notify the individual of intent to revoke before acting
Statutory authority for the State Department to issue a limited-duration emergency return-home passport for individuals abroad with a $2,500+ arrearage
modified: Section 452(k)(2) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 652(k)) — State Department authority to act on existing passports changed from discretionary ("may revoke, restrict, or limit") to mandatory ("revoke")

bills.title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
bills.official_title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
bills.summary: Under current tax law, settlement and judgment damages are only tax-free if they stem from a personal physical injury or physical sickness, which has generally been read to require observable physical harm. This bill creates a separate tax exemption for sexual assault and abuse damages that requires no proof of physical injury and no medical records. If a judgment or settlement states that damages result from sexual acts or contact, the IRS must prove otherwise in court rather than the survivor having to prove it.
bills.brief: Creates a tax exemption for sexual assault damages requiring no physical injury proof or medical records, and shifts the burden of proof to the IRS.

top_lines.headline: New Tax Exemption
subs: Sexual assault and abuse damages excluded from gross income — no visible injury or medical records required
Applies to non-punitive damages from judgments and settlements entered after enactment

top_lines.headline: Burden of Proof Shift
subs: IRS must prove damages are not on account of sexual acts if the judgment or agreement says they are
Medical records alone cannot be required to deny the exemption

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill addresses a sympathetic population with bipartisan appeal — sexual assault survivors facing unexpected tax liability — and passed the House. However, only 3 cosponsors and no Senate companion bill has been identified. Tax exclusions for personal injury damages have historically attracted broad support, making Senate passage plausible but not certain without floor time being scheduled.

sections.label: Section 2 — Exclusion from Gross Income

items.main: Amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income damages received on account of any sexual act (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(2)) or sexual contact (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(3)), other than punitive damages.
items.detail: Current law limits the exclusion to damages "on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness." The IRS has interpreted this to require observable bodily harm. The amendment adds sexual acts and sexual contact as an independent basis for the exclusion, removing the physical injury requirement for these claims. The amendment applies to amounts received pursuant to judgments made, and agreements entered into, after the date of enactment.

items.main: New Section 104(d) establishes that damages are substantiated as on account of sexual act or contact if the judgment or agreement so states, and prohibits denying the exclusion solely for lack of medical records.
items.detail: The IRS bears the burden of proving that damages characterized as on account of sexual act or contact in a judgment or agreement are not so characterized, in any related court proceeding. A judgment is treated as made after enactment if the first payment pursuant to it is received after enactment. An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises an agreement entered into before enactment does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of the Treasury to conduct a public awareness program about the new exclusion in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women.
items.detail: The Secretary must work with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women and other relevant federal agencies to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income provided by the new Section 104(a)(2)(B). No timeline, funding level, or required outreach methods are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises a pre-enactment agreement does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement, even if the replacement is reached after enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to extend the tax exemption to sexual assault survivors. This provision specifically bars survivors who renegotiate or revise a pre-existing settlement after enactment from accessing the new exemption, a limitation not apparent from the bill's title or the headline exemption provision.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

gaps: The bill applies to amounts received under judgments made and agreements entered after enactment but does not address the tax treatment of damages already received under pre-enactment judgments that are still paying out.
The bill requires a public awareness program but specifies no timeline, appropriated funding, or minimum required outreach activities.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Survivors of sexual assault face a long road to recovery without having to battle with the IRS over keeping the compensatory damages or settlements that they receive. Unfortunately, right now, the burden of proof that a sexual assault survivor would have to provide to the IRS, including medical records to prove that they deserve to have their settlement funds excluded from gross income for tax purposes, ignores the fact that such victims often do not have the same observable physical injuries that other victims of assault might have.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smucker
featured_quotes.text: I think the chairman and Ms. Moore both have described it really well. The core problem here, first of all, we believe our current law already says that any victim of physical abuse and any victim of sexual abuse who receives a settlement does not owe tax on that settlement, which makes complete sense.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Moore
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

added: Section 104(a)(2)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 — tax exclusion for non-punitive damages on account of sexual acts or sexual contact, with no physical injury or medical records requirement
Section 104(d) — burden of proof rule placing the obligation on the IRS to disprove the characterization in any judgment or agreement stating damages are on account of sexual acts or contact
Requirement for the Secretary of the Treasury to conduct a public awareness program in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women

bills.title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.official_title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act lets the NSA collect the communications of foreign targets without a warrant — and when those targets contact Americans, those conversations are swept up too. The FBI can then search that database for information about U.S. persons without getting a separate warrant. This bill extends that authority through April 30, 2026 with no new limits, oversight requirements, or reforms added.
bills.brief: Extends the NSA's authority to collect foreign targets' communications without a warrant — including Americans' conversations when they contact those targets — through April 30, 2026, with no reforms attached.

top_lines.headline: What Section 702 Does
subs: Allows the NSA to compel U.S. tech companies to hand over communications of designated foreign targets without a warrant
When those targets communicate with Americans, those conversations are collected — the FBI can then search that database for U.S. person data without a separate warrant

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extended through April 30, 2026 — no new limits or reforms
Introduced and signed into law in 48 hours

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 18, 2026 as Public Law 119-84.

sections.label: Section 1 — Extension of Title VII Authorities

items.main: Title VII of FISA (Section 702) authorizes the NSA to surveil foreign targets abroad without a warrant. This bill extends that authority through April 30, 2026 with no new conditions attached.
items.detail: Amends Section 403(b)(1) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261) to set a fixed April 30, 2026 repeal date for Title VII, replacing a rolling deadline tied to the enactment of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act. The amendment takes effect on the earlier of the date of enactment or April 19, 2026. No new minimization requirements, no new oversight mechanisms, and no restrictions on FBI queries of the collected data are included.

gaps: The bill extends Title VII surveillance authorities through April 30, 2026 but sets no reporting requirement on how those authorities are used during the extension period.
The bill sets a fixed April 30, 2026 expiration date but does not establish any conditions or framework governing further reauthorization after that date.

modified: Section 403(b)(1) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261) — Title VII repeal date changed from two years after enactment of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act to April 30, 2026

bills.title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
bills.official_title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
bills.summary: Directs the President to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)). Forces required to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack may remain, provided the President fully complies with the 60-day withdrawal requirement in section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution. Continued operations against Iran require either a declaration of war or a specific congressional authorization for use of military force.
bills.brief: Invokes the War Powers Resolution to direct the President to end U.S. military operations against Iran without a declaration of war or specific congressional authorization.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive
subs: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c))
Carve-out for forces defending the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, conditioned on the President complying with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(b))

top_lines.headline: Authorization Threshold
subs: Military operations against Iran may continue only if authorized by a declaration of war or a specific congressional authorization for use of military force against Iran
90 cosponsors in the House; failed 213-214 in the House on April 16, 2026

bills.likelihoodReason: The concurrent resolution failed in the House on April 16, 2026 by a vote of 213-214. Because it did not pass the House, it cannot proceed to the Senate, and the matter is effectively closed for this measure.

sections.label: Resolving Clause — Withdrawal from Iran Hostilities

items.main: Congress directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)).
items.detail: The directive exempts forces necessary to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, provided the President fully complies with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(b)). Section 5(b) generally requires removal of forces within 60 days of their introduction into hostilities unless Congress authorizes continued engagement. Continued operations require explicit authorization through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force against Iran.

comments.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY): One person does not have the power to take this Nation to war alone.
Rep. Keith Self (R-TX): We have neutered Iran, which has been at war with us for 47 years.

underreported.summary: The resolution permits forces to remain if needed to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, conditioned on the President complying with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution.
underreported.why_unreported: The term imminent attack is not defined in the resolution. The resolution does not specify who determines when a threat qualifies as imminent or what evidence is required, leaving that threshold determination entirely to the executive branch.

criticisms.why: Opposed the withdrawal directive on grounds that U.S. military operations had achieved a strategic objective against Iran.

gaps: The resolution directs withdrawal from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran but does not define what operations constitute hostilities, a term whose scope the resolution does not address.
The resolution invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution but does not specify a timeline by which the President must comply after the directive is transmitted.

The resolution's imminent attack exception covers forces defending an ally or partner of the United States but does not specify which allies or partners qualify or how eligibility for the exception is determined.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Himes
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I have been listening carefully to my Republican colleagues, and they will get no argument from me on the notion that we have been at war with Iran for decades. They will get no argument at all. As Mr. Mast keeps saying, this is a bad and evil regime. Yes, we have been at war, but at no point in those decades have we been so obviously losing that war in any strategic sense. The Iranian Navy is at the bottom of the ocean.

bills.title: Main Street Capital Access Act
bills.likelihoodReason: Rep. Hill (R-AR), Chair of the House Financial Services Committee, sponsored this bill with 33 Republican cosponsors and zero Democratic support — a strictly partisan track. House passage is plausible given the Republican majority, but Senate passage requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, and the complete absence of Democratic cosponsors signals no crossover appeal. The CBLR capital floor reduction and the one-way GDP ratchet will draw organized opposition from consumer protection and banking reform groups, making Senate passage unlikely without significant amendment.

sections.label: Title I — New Bank Formation and Local Community Access

items.main: Creates a 3-year phase-in for new depository institutions to meet federal capital requirements and requires regulators to act on a new bank's business-plan-change request within 30 days, with non-response deemed approval.
items.detail: During a new bank's first 3 years, a rural depository institution (under $10B in assets and located in a rural area) receives a Community Bank Leverage Ratio set at the lesser of the standard ratio or 7.5%, phased in at lower percentages during the first 2 years. The bill also adds agricultural-loan authority for Federal savings associations and requires the federal banking agencies to study the causes of the low number of new (de novo) banks and report within 1 year.

items.main: Requires the OCC, NCUA, Federal Reserve, and FDIC to each publish annual reports on charter and deposit-insurance application volumes, mean and median approval times, and common reasons for denial.
items.detail: Section 104 separately directs the federal banking agencies to jointly study how to improve the growth, capital adequacy, and profitability of rural-serving depository institutions and to identify statutes and regulations that limit them, with a report to Congress within 1 year.

sections.label: Title II — Tailoring Bank Regulation

items.main: Requires federal financial regulators to tailor each regulation to the risk profile and business model of affected institutions, document that tailoring, and review regulations issued over the prior 15 years.
items.detail: Section 202 directs the Federal Reserve to raise the Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement's consolidated asset threshold to $25B within 180 days. Banks eligible for the Community Bank Leverage Ratio get short-form call reports for the first and third reports of each year.

items.main: Raises the Community Bank Leverage Ratio eligibility ceiling from $10B to $15B and lowers the qualifying ratio range from 8%-10% to 6%-8% (Section 203), and raises a series of enhanced-regulation asset thresholds — most from $250B to $370B (Section 204).
items.detail: Section 204 raises thresholds across the Financial Stability Act (sections 116, 121, 163, 164, 165), the Federal Reserve Act, the Bank Holding Company Act, and the EGRRCPA — including $250B to $370B, $100B to $150B, $50B to $75B, and $10B to $15B. New Financial Stability Act Sections 177-178 require the Federal Reserve and other agencies to raise these and rule-based thresholds every 5 years (beginning April 1, 2031, and June 30, 2026, respectively) by the ratio of GDP growth, but only when that ratio is greater than 1.

sections.label: Title III — Fair and Transparent Bank Supervision

items.main: Directs the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council to overhaul the CAMELS rating system with objective criteria and to either eliminate or narrow the subjective 'management' component, and sets timeliness rules for examinations.
items.detail: New examination rules require exams to be completed within 270 days, final reports within 90 days of the exit interview, and exit interviews within 30 days. A new Office of Independent Examination Review — a 3-member board appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate — gives banks a de novo appeal of material supervisory determinations, with judicial review in the D.C. Circuit or the bank's local circuit and a prohibition on agency retaliation.

items.main: Gives well-managed, well-capitalized institutions with $6B or less in assets examination relief (alternating limited-scope exams and, on request, combined exams), prohibits regulators from using 'reputational risk' in supervision, and bars climate-related stress tests.
items.detail: Section 304 raises an FDI Act examination-cycle asset threshold from $3B to $6B. Section 305 requires the Federal Reserve to set stress-test methodologies by rule, disclose scenarios at least 60 days in advance, and bars climate-related stress tests. Section 307 requires agencies to purge 'reputational risk' from guidance, manuals, and exams and prohibits basing any rating or enforcement action on it, with findings citing the 2018 'Operation Choke Point.' Section 306 creates a Federal Reserve Board community-bank policy role covering banks under $17B.

sections.label: Title IV — Regulatory Accountability and Transparency

items.main: Restructures the FDIC Board, requires a non-binding 'guidance clarity statement' on agency guidance, shortens the regulatory-review cycle, and adds reporting on regulators' participation in global standard-setting bodies.
items.detail: Section 401 requires one FDIC board appointee with state bank supervisory experience and one with experience at institutions under $17B, makes the CFPB Director a non-voting observer, and caps service at two terms / 12 years. Section 402 requires guidance from nine named agencies (including the CFPB, Fed, OCC, FDIC, and SEC) to carry a statement that it is not binding. Section 403 shortens the EGRPRA regulatory-review cycle from every 10 years to every 7. Section 404 requires the Fed, OCC, and FDIC to report annually on interactions with global forums such as the Basel Committee, Financial Stability Board, and the Network for Greening the Financial System.

sections.label: Title V — Strengthening Local Bank Funding

items.main: Directs a Federal Reserve review of the discount window and expands the amounts of reciprocal and custodial deposits that are not treated as brokered deposits.
items.detail: Section 502 amends the reciprocal-deposit brokered-deposit exception into tiers — 50% of an agent institution's liabilities up to $1B, 40% of the portion from $1B to $10B, and 30% of the portion from $10B to $250B — and ties eligibility to a CAMELS rating of 1, 2, or 3. Section 503 adds a custodial-deposit exception of up to 20% of total liabilities for eligible institutions under $10B that are well capitalized with a composite rating of 1, 2, or 3.

sections.label: Title VI — Promoting Bank Competition and Merger Clarity

items.main: Bars regulators from considering monopoly or competition effects when a merger or acquisition would result in an institution with less than $10B in assets, with the threshold indexed to GDP.
items.detail: The antitrust/competition carve-out applies under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, the Bank Holding Company Act, and the Home Owners' Loan Act. Sections 602 and 603 require a GAO study of merger conditions and commitments (report within 1 year) and recurring Inspector General reviews of merger-review timeliness (within 1 year and every 3 years thereafter).

sections.label: Title VII — Strengthening Transparency and Involvement in Bank Resolutions

items.main: Creates a 'least cost resolution' exception letting the FDIC choose a costlier resolution of a failed bank to avoid further concentrating the banking system in global systemically important banks.
items.detail: The FDIC and Federal Reserve, after consulting Treasury, may select an alternative that is not least-cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund if the added risk is outweighed by the benefit of limiting G-SIB concentration, subject to a rule-set maximum cost and a report to Congress within 30 days. Section 702 requires a joint study of shelf charters and the FDIC's modified bidder-qualification process, including their potential use in the 2023 bank failures, with a report within 1 year.

sections.label: Title VIII — Facilitating Innovation and Bank Partnerships

items.main: Sets a minimum 15-year holding period for merchant banking investments and directs studies of bank-fintech and credit union-fintech partnerships.
items.detail: Section 801 amends the Bank Holding Company Act so that the permitted holding period for merchant banking investments is not less than 15 years (and not less than 15 years from the initial investment date for existing holdings). Section 802 requires the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC (and separately the NCUA) to study the effects of bank- and credit-union-fintech partnerships and recommend legal changes, with reports within 1 year.

underreported.section: Section 203 — Community Bank Leverage Ratio Qualifying Range
underreported.summary: Beyond raising the eligibility ceiling to $15B, the bill lowers the qualifying Community Bank Leverage Ratio range from 8%-10% to 6%-8%, allowing banks to hold less capital and still use the simplified capital regime that exempts them from risk-based capital rules.
underreported.why_unreported: The section's headline change is the $10B-to-$15B eligibility increase. The reduction of the capital-ratio floor from 8% to 6% is a separate loosening of how much loss-absorbing capital a qualifying community bank must hold, embedded in the same subsection.

underreported.summary: The new GDP-indexing mechanism increases enhanced-regulation thresholds by the ratio of GDP growth only when that ratio is greater than 1, with no provision to lower thresholds if GDP contracts.
underreported.why_unreported: The indexing is framed as keeping thresholds current with the economy. Because the adjustment applies only when GDP has grown, the thresholds ratchet upward permanently — fewer banks face enhanced regulation over time, and a recession cannot pull more banks back into scope.

underreported.summary: The bill lets the FDIC choose a more expensive resolution of a failed bank — one not least-cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund — when doing so avoids selling the failed bank to a global systemically important bank.
underreported.why_unreported: The 'least cost' requirement is a core discipline on FDIC resolutions under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. This exception permits a higher charge against the Deposit Insurance Fund, subject to a rule-set cap, specifically to limit further concentration among the largest banks — a trade-off not evident from the bill's title.

criticisms.why: We strongly support community banks and credit unions and stand ready to work with Republicans to advance sensible reforms to do just that. However, this package of overwhelmingly Republican and partisan bills represents the greatest amount of bank deregulation since before the 2008 global financial crisis. Instead of focusing on sensible improvements to support community banks and credit unions on Main Street, this bill will help megabanks on Wall Street and harm consumers.

gaps: The GDP-indexing in Sections 177-178 adjusts enhanced-regulation thresholds upward when GDP grows but contains no mechanism to lower them if GDP contracts, so the share of banks subject to the toughest rules can only shrink over time.

Multiple provisions impose 90-day or 30-day 'deemed approved' deadlines on regulators but do not address how agencies are to complete adequate review of complex applications within those windows without defaulting to approval.

The bill waives antitrust and competition review for any merger resulting in an institution under $10B in assets but does not address the cumulative competitive effect of a series of such sub-threshold mergers in the same market.

Section 307 requires agencies to stop using 'reputational risk' and any 'substantially similar' term but does not define what counts as substantially similar, leaving the boundary of the prohibition to agency interpretation.

bills.brief: Raises the asset thresholds for the toughest bank regulations ($250B to $370B, among others) and indexes them to GDP, eases capital and exam rules for community and new banks, waives antitrust review for sub-$10B mergers, and restricts supervisory practices including reputational-risk reviews and climate stress tests.

top_lines.headline: Enhanced Regulation Thresholds Raised and GDP-Indexed
subs: The Financial Stability Act asset threshold for enhanced prudential standards is raised from $250B to $370B, and the $100B trigger for certain requirements is raised to $150B
Going forward, the Federal Reserve must raise these thresholds every 5 years (beginning April 1, 2031) by the growth in nominal GDP — and only when GDP has grown, never downward
Matching thresholds in the Federal Reserve Act, Bank Holding Company Act, and Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act are also raised

top_lines.headline: Community Bank Leverage Ratio Loosened
subs: The asset ceiling to qualify for the simplified Community Bank Leverage Ratio framework is raised from $10B to $15B
The qualifying leverage ratio range is lowered from 8%-10% to 6%-8%, letting banks hold less capital and still use the simplified regime

top_lines.headline: New Bank Formation Relief
subs: New depository institutions get a 3-year phase-in to meet federal capital requirements
Regulators must approve or deny a new bank's request to change its business plan within 30 days — non-response is deemed approval
New rural depository institutions (under $10B in assets) get a Community Bank Leverage Ratio set at the lesser of the standard ratio or 7.5%

top_lines.headline: Faster Application and Merger Deadlines
subs: Holding-company and bank-merger applications must be granted or denied within 90 days of initial submission — an application is deemed granted if the agency misses the deadline
Agencies have 30 days to tell an applicant whether its record is complete, extendable by 30 days for complex applications

top_lines.headline: Antitrust Review Waived for Small-Bank Mergers
subs: For mergers and acquisitions resulting in an institution with less than $10B in assets, regulators may not consider monopoly or competition effects
The $10B threshold is itself indexed to nominal GDP growth

top_lines.headline: Limits on Bank Supervision Practices
subs: Federal banking agencies must remove "reputational risk" from all guidance, manuals, and exams and may not base supervisory actions on it — the findings cite the 2018 "Operation Choke Point"
The Federal Reserve is prohibited from subjecting banks to climate-related stress tests and must disclose stress-test scenarios at least 60 days in advance
A new Office of Independent Examination Review gives banks a de novo appeal of material supervisory determinations, with further review available in federal appeals court

The CFPB Director's voting seat on the FDIC Board — converted to a non-voting observer (Sec. 401)

bills.summary: The Main Street Capital Access Act (Main Street Act) is a broad banking deregulation bill. It raises the asset thresholds that trigger the toughest federal bank regulations — including lifting the Financial Stability Act's enhanced-prudential-standards threshold from $250B to $370B — and requires those thresholds to be ratcheted up with GDP growth going forward. It eases capital and examination rules for new and community banks, waives antitrust review for bank mergers that produce institutions under $10B, bars regulators from using "reputational risk" in supervision, and prohibits climate-related stress tests.

bills.title: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act — Further Extension Through June 12, 2026
bills.official_title: A bill to amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Section 702 of FISA lets the NSA collect the communications of foreign targets without a warrant — including conversations involving Americans. This bill is the second short-term extension in as many weeks, stretching that authority from its April 30, 2026 expiration to June 12, 2026 with no new limits or reforms added.
bills.brief: Extends NSA warrantless surveillance authority under FISA Section 702 by six more weeks, to June 12, 2026, with no changes to oversight or limitations.

top_lines.headline: What Section 702 Allows
subs: NSA can compel U.S. tech companies to hand over communications of designated foreign targets without an individual warrant
When foreign targets communicate with Americans, those conversations are collected — FBI can then query that data for U.S. persons without a separate warrant

top_lines.headline: What This Extension Changes
subs: Repeal date moved from April 30, 2026 to June 12, 2026 — no new oversight requirements or limits added
Second short-term extension in two weeks; Congress has not passed a long-term reauthorization

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 30, 2026 as Public Law 119-87.

sections.label: Section 1 — Extension of Title VII Authorities

items.main: Amends Section 403(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to change the repeal date of Title VII authorities from April 30, 2026 to June 12, 2026.
items.detail: The bill amends both the main repeal date and a cross-reference in the sunset clause, ensuring the extension applies to all Title VII provisions including Section 702.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, it is nice to have the gentleman from Maryland on the pro-warrant side of this conversation this go-round. I will note that there was a significant amount of abuses by the previous President with respect to the amount of focus on the American people using FISA and the abuses therein. I hope we can achieve a bipartisan consensus here on how we reform this regardless of who is in the White House and regardless of who controls Congress. We need to do that in defense of the Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act is a fine tool for foreign intelligence. Unfortunately, it has been abused and corrupted. I am encouraged to hear Mr. Raskin reclaim his opposition to warrantless surveillance, and I am encouraged that there is a bipartisan effort to reform it. In fact, I think the will of this body is that we defend the Constitution and we defend this Nation. We can do both. We are presented this false dilemma that somehow if you just abandon your freedom, you can be more secure. That is a false tradeoff.

Mr. Speaker, everyone here wants 702 reauthorized. The case has been made that it is a national security issue, that our troops on the ground need it. They need the intelligence that it provides. We want the CIA and the NSA to run as fast and as far as they can to identify the bad guys. I have deployed on three continents, and believe you me, we want our military to know who to deal with when they get on foreign soil. The FBI has abused 702, and that is why we are here today.

gaps: The bill sets a June 12, 2026 expiration date but establishes no conditions, reporting requirements, or reform benchmarks governing what happens at that expiration.
The bill title references additional purposes beyond the extension, but the text contains only the extension — no other changes to FISA are made.

bills.title: Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026
bills.official_title: Making further consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: After a 75-day partial DHS shutdown triggered by lapsed appropriations, this bill provided the Department of Homeland Security with its full-year FY2026 budget — the first dedicated annual appropriations act for DHS in this cycle. Division A is the complete DHS Appropriations Act, funding all major department components through September 30, 2026. Division B extends the existing governmentwide continuing resolution (Public Law 119-37) for other unfunded federal agencies and retroactively covers the appropriations lapse that began on or about February 14, 2026. The law also authorizes back pay for furloughed federal employees and retroactively ratifies obligations made during the shutdown to maintain essential operations.
bills.brief: Ended a 75-day partial DHS shutdown with the department's first full-year FY2026 appropriations — $11.08B for CBP, $10.64B for TSA, $11.27B for the Coast Guard, and $26.4B in the FEMA disaster relief fund — plus a short-term CR for remaining unfunded agencies through May 22.

top_lines.headline: DHS Shutdown Ends — Back Pay Authorized
subs: The partial DHS shutdown, which began February 14, 2026, is ended — 75 days after the previous continuing resolution expired
Furloughed federal employees are authorized to receive back pay; obligations incurred during the shutdown are retroactively ratified

top_lines.headline: Border and Enforcement Agencies Fully Funded
subs: CBP receives $11.08B for operations and support plus $222.9M for construction and improvements
TSA receives $10.64B for operations; Coast Guard receives $11.27B including $530M for defense-related activities
Secret Service receives $3.13B with up to $40M for premium pay above standard caps

top_lines.headline: FEMA Disaster Relief Fund — $26.37B
subs: $26.4B appropriated to the FEMA Disaster Relief Fund for major disaster declarations
$494M for State Homeland Security grants; $300M for Nonprofit Security grants split between high-risk urban and non-urban areas
$684M for firefighter grants under the SAFER and Assistance to Firefighter programs

top_lines.headline: Coast Guard MQ-9 Drone Program
subs: $98M for Coast Guard procurement of MQ-9 unmanned aircraft and base stations
Explicitly prohibits equipping any long-range unmanned aircraft with kinetic capabilities — no weapons on government drones

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 30, 2026 as Public Law 119-86.

sections.label: Title II — Security, Enforcement, and Investigations

items.main: Provides full-year FY2026 appropriations for CBP, TSA, Coast Guard, and Secret Service through September 30, 2026.
items.detail: CBP operations and support: $11.08B (includes unaccompanied minor transportation, air/marine law enforcement support, and up to 7,500 police vehicles). CBP construction: $222.9M with border security infrastructure funded through September 2030. TSA operations: $10.64B (offsetting aviation security fee collections reduce the general fund share to approximately $7.61B). Coast Guard operations: $11.27B including $530M for defense-related activities and $24.5M from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund. Coast Guard construction: $991.9M available through September 2030. USSS operations: $3.13B with up to $40M in premium pay above standard limits and a $2M grant for Missing and Exploited Children investigations.

sections.label: Title III — Protection, Preparedness, Response, and Recovery

items.main: Funds CISA and FEMA including a $26.37B Disaster Relief Fund appropriation and $3.84B in Federal Assistance grants.
items.detail: CISA operations and support: $2.22B plus $386.5M for construction. FEMA operations: $1.67B. FEMA federal assistance grants: $3.84B, allocated across State Homeland Security ($494M), Urban Area Security Initiative ($584M), Nonprofit Security ($300M, split evenly between high-risk urban and non-urban areas), firefighter grants ($684M across SAFER and AFG), Port Security ($95M), emergency management performance ($337M), and flood hazard mapping ($297M). Disaster Relief Fund: $26.4B for major disaster declarations under the Stafford Act.

sections.label: Title V — General Provisions

items.main: Includes $20M for body-worn cameras for ICE and CBP agents, $98M for Coast Guard MQ-9 drones, and bans new land border crossing fees.
items.detail: Sec. 109 appropriates $20M for body-worn cameras for agents performing immigration enforcement, with a 30-day spend plan requirement. Sec. 204 prohibits the Secretary from establishing, collecting, or studying any new border crossing fee at land ports of entry on the Southern or Northern border. Sec. 207 limits border surveillance procurement to autonomous systems as defined in Pub. L. 119-21. Sec. 208 requires CBP to maintain its November 2021 policy protecting pregnant women in custody. Sec. 219 provides $98M for Coast Guard MQ-9 aircraft and prohibits equipping any long-range unmanned aircraft with kinetic capabilities. Sec. 222 restricts Secret Service protection of federal agency heads to DHS Secretary only; all other agency-head protection must be on a reimbursable basis.

sections.label: Division B — Further Additional Continuing Appropriations

items.main: Extends FY2025 appropriations rates for agencies not covered by a full-year bill through the earlier of May 22, 2026, or enactment of applicable full-year appropriations.
items.detail: Retroactively ratifies obligations incurred during the partial DHS shutdown that were necessary to maintain essential operations to protect life and property. Authorizes back pay, in accordance with current law, for federal employees who were furloughed or required to work without pay during the partial shutdown.

underreported.section: Section 209 — No TSA Exemptions for Officials
underreported.summary: Members of Congress, Cabinet secretaries, agency heads, and senior White House staff are explicitly barred from exemptions from federal passenger and baggage screening. A separate provision bars future legislation from overriding this requirement using funds from this act.
underreported.why_unreported: Appropriations bills frequently include policy riders that never surface in coverage of the headline funding numbers. This provision directly names elected officials and executive appointees as subject to the same screening requirements as the public.

underreported.section: Section 227 — Canadian Prescription Drug Imports Protected
underreported.summary: CBP is barred from preventing individuals from importing up to a 90-day personal-use supply of prescription drugs from Canada that comply with FDA standards. Controlled substances and biological products are excluded.
underreported.why_unreported: This carve-out for Canadian drug imports sits quietly inside a DHS spending bill and has significant implications for border enforcement priorities around pharmaceutical imports.

underreported.section: Section 204 — No New Border Crossing Fees
underreported.summary: The Secretary of Homeland Security is prohibited from establishing, collecting, or studying any new fee charged to pedestrians, cyclists, or vehicle occupants crossing the Southern or Northern border at a land port of entry.
underreported.why_unreported: Border crossing fees have been discussed as a potential revenue mechanism. This provision explicitly blocks even a feasibility study, making it a quiet but firm policy prohibition embedded in the appropriations text.

bills.title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
bills.summary: Under current law, gasoline blended with 15% ethanol (E15) cannot be sold at gas stations during summer months because E15 evaporates more readily than E10, contributing to ground-level ozone. This bill removes that summer ban by extending the existing E10 vapor pressure waiver to cover E15 year-round, allowing gas stations in all states to sell E15 from June 1 through September 15.
bills.brief: Allows E15 ethanol-blended gasoline to be sold year-round by extending the E10 Reid Vapor Pressure waiver to E15, removing the current summer ozone-season prohibition.

top_lines.headline: Ethanol Blend Waiver
subs: Applies the existing Clean Air Act Reid Vapor Pressure waiver for E10 to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol
Removes the current June 1–September 15 prohibition on E15 sales that applies in most of the country

top_lines.headline: Who It Affects
subs: Fuel retailers who currently stock separate summer and year-round fuel blends would be able to carry E15 year-round
Consumers in corn-belt states where E15 is already common would no longer face seasonal supply interruptions

bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House with 54 bipartisan cosponsors, signaling strong rural-state support. The Senate has passed similar measures before. However, opposition from oil refiners and some environmental groups over ozone concerns remains, and no Senate companion bill has advanced. Senate leadership is currently focused on the budget reconciliation process, limiting floor time for standalone bills.

sections.label: Section 1 — Ethanol Waiver Extension

items.main: Amends Section 211(h) of the Clean Air Act to extend the Reid Vapor Pressure waiver that currently applies to gasoline with 10% ethanol to gasoline blended with any percentage of ethanol up to 15%.
items.detail: Reid Vapor Pressure measures how readily gasoline evaporates; higher RVP fuel contributes to ground-level ozone formation in warm weather. The Clean Air Act currently caps summer RVP at 9.0 psi in most areas but waives that limit for E10. This bill extends the waiver to E15, allowing it to be sold at the same locations that carry E10 without requiring separate summer and winter fuel inventories.

underreported.summary: The RVP waiver extension applies to all ethanol blend percentages from 10% up to 15%, not just to E15 specifically. A retailer blending at 12% or 13% ethanol would also fall under the waiver.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and sponsor statements focus on E15, but the statutory amendment covers any blend up to 15%, meaning mid-range blends sold during the summer ozone season would also be exempt from the 9.0 psi RVP cap.

gaps: The bill removes the summer RVP restriction on E15 but does not address the separate infrastructure requirements — many fuel pumps and storage tanks require upgrades to handle E15 — that limit its availability regardless of the waiver.
The bill extends the waiver nationally but does not address California, which operates under a separate state waiver system and would require additional EPA approval to participate.

modified: Clean Air Act Section 211(h) — Reid Vapor Pressure waiver extended from gasoline blended with 10% ethanol to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol
removed: Seasonal prohibition on selling E15 during the summer ozone season (June 1–September 15) in non-waiver areas

bills.official_title: Making further consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 funds five of the twelve regular FY2026 appropriations packages — Defense, Labor/HHS/Education, Transportation/Housing, Financial Services/Treasury, and National Security/State — while extending DHS funding at FY2025 rates through February 13, 2026, and extending over a dozen expiring programs including the National Flood Insurance Program, TANF, E-Verify, and trade preferences for Africa and Haiti. It also contains a health care extenders division adding Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection tests and extending telehealth flexibilities, hospital payment adjustments, and community health center funding.
bills.brief: Funds defense, health care entitlements, education, housing, and foreign assistance for FY2026 while extending DHS under a short-term CR and adding Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection screening.

sections.label: Title I — Military Personnel

items.main: Appropriates pay, allowances, clothing, subsistence, travel, and retirement fund contributions for all active-duty, reserve, and National Guard components of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, Space Force, and ROTC.
items.detail: Active component: Army $54.54B, Navy $40.54B, Air Force $38.77B, Marine Corps $16.99B, Space Force $1.49B. National Guard: Army $10.48B, Air Force $5.47B. Reserve components: Army $5.73B, Navy $2.71B, Marine Corps $1.00B, Air Force $2.70B.

sections.label: Title II — Operation and Maintenance

items.main: Appropriates funds for day-to-day operations including facilities, training, and intelligence, with legislated reductions totaling $2.8B for efficiency, excess working capital, and bulk fuel savings.
items.detail: Navy and Marine Corps combined: $74.72B; Army: $58.25B; Air Force: $61.54B; Defense-Wide: $56.09B; Space Force: $5.69B. Three separate reductions: $1.2B for efficiency measures, $1.05B for excess working capital cash, and $550M for bulk fuel savings.

sections.label: Title III — Procurement

items.main: Appropriates funds for shipbuilding, aircraft, missiles, and other weapons systems including Columbia Class and Virginia Class submarines, CVN carriers, DDG destroyers, and the first procurement for the FF(X)-Frigate.
items.detail: Columbia Class: $3.93B + $5.35B advance. Virginia Class: $2.74B + $3.13B advance. CVN-81: $1.62B. CVN Refueling Overhauls: $1.58B. DDG-51 advance: $1.75B. FF(X)-Frigate: $242M. Medium Landing Ship: $800M. Professional technical services capped at $2.886B.

sections.label: Title VI — Other Department of Defense Programs

items.main: Appropriates $41.77B for the Defense Health Program, plus counter-narcotics, drug demand reduction, chemical weapons destruction, and overseas security cooperation funds.
items.detail: Defense Health Program: $41.77B total ($38.94B O&M; $1.27B minimum research). Counter-narcotics: $678.7M; National Guard counter-drug: $305M; drug demand reduction: $134.9M. Chemical agents/munitions destruction: $213.3M. ISIS Train and Equip Fund: $342.5M. Cooperative Threat Reduction: $282.8M.

sections.label: Title VIII — General Provisions

items.main: Sets transfer authorities, designates $500M for Israeli cooperative missile defense programs, limits professional technical services to $2.886B, and authorizes $650M for contingency contracts.
items.detail: Sec. 8021: $500M for Israeli Cooperative Programs — Arrow 3 ($173M), SRBMD ($127M), Arrow upper-tier co-production ($100M). $150M minimum for Jordan. Defense Security Cooperation Agency: $1.5B and $1.0B in separate security assistance tranches. Sec. 8001 prohibits use of funds for propaganda within the United States.

sections.label: Title I — Department of Labor

items.main: Appropriates $3.98B for WIOA workforce training grants, $4.00B for unemployment insurance administration, and related employment programs.
items.detail: WIOA grants: $875.6M adult employment, $948.1M youth activities, $1.10B dislocated workers. National programs: $1.06B including $300.9M dislocated workers national reserve. Unemployment Insurance: $4.00B from Employment Security Administration trust fund.

sections.label: Title II — Department of Health and Human Services

items.main: Appropriates $593.82B for Medicare, $508.15B for Medicaid (plus $316.51B Q1 FY2027 advance), $8.83B for Child Care Block Grant, $7.35B for NCI, $6.59B for NIAID, and $14.92B for Social Services Block Grant.
items.detail: SSI advance: $23.5B for Q1 FY2027. Foster care/adoption: $6.84B Title IV-E. SAMHSA: $4.09B. CMS administrative expenses: $14.67B not to exceed. Global health/HIV-AIDS: $5.16B. Child support and self-sufficiency programs also funded.

sections.label: Title III — Department of Education

items.main: Appropriates $24.62B for Pell Grants, $19.13B for Title I education grants, $15.49B for IDEA special education, and includes a $11.66B rescission of unobligated Inflation Reduction Act education funds (Sec. 529).
items.detail: Title I: $6.46B basic grants, $5.30B targeted grants, $5.30B finance incentive grants, $862M concentration grants. Pell: $22.48B basic grants. Vocational Rehabilitation: $4.65B. Sec. 529 rescinds $11.66B from Public Law 117-169 unobligated balances.

sections.label: Title I — Department of Transportation

items.main: Appropriates $63.4B from the Highway Trust Fund for federal-aid highways, $13.71B for the FAA, $14.64B for transit from the Mass Transit Account, $850M and $1.577B for Amtrak, and funds for FHWA, FRA, and other modal agencies.
items.detail: FAA: $13.71B total, $13.04B from Airport/Airway Trust Fund; air traffic $10.34B, safety $1.84B. FAA research: $74.5M including $9M for the new ARPA-I office. Amtrak national network: $1.577B available until expended. Transit: $14.64B from Mass Transit Account.

sections.label: Title II — Department of Housing and Urban Development

items.main: Appropriates $34.44B for housing choice vouchers, $8.32B for public housing operations, $6.995B for CDBG, $4.42B for homeless assistance, and $1.25B for HOME; sets loan guarantee ceilings of $400B (single-family) and $550B (Ginnie Mae).
items.detail: Section 8 renewals: $34.96B. Public Housing Capital Fund: $3.30B. HOME: $1.25B, available until September 30, 2029. Continuum of Care: $4.01B. Loan guarantee ceilings are contingent liability caps, not direct appropriations.

sections.label: Title I — Department of the Treasury

items.main: Appropriates $3.04B for IRS taxpayer services, $5.00B for IRS enforcement, $3.16B for operations support, $271.2M for business systems modernization, $237.7M for terrorism and financial intelligence, and $21M for CFIUS (offset by fees).
items.detail: IRS taxpayer services: $3.04B; up to $186M remains available until September 30, 2027. IRS enforcement covers tax collection, legal support, and criminal investigation. CFIUS: $21M general fund reduced to $0 as filing fee collections are received. Treasury Office of Intelligence: $185.2M.

sections.label: Title III — The Judiciary

items.main: Appropriates $6.13B for courts, probation, and pretrial services; $1.77B for defender services; and $892M for court operations.
items.detail: The $6.13B judiciary account includes firearms for Probation and Pretrial Services staff. Defender services cover federal public defenders under the Criminal Justice Act. Operations funded across district courts, circuit courts, Supreme Court, and Court of International Trade.

sections.label: Title V — Independent Agencies

items.main: Funds the SBA's loan guarantee programs ($35.5B 7(a), $15B disaster, $6B SBIC debentures), the General Services Administration, OPM, SEC, and other independent agencies.
items.detail: GSA Federal Buildings Fund: $9.69B installment purchases, $5.57B rental, $3.01B building operations. SBA administrative expenses within Title V. SEC operations primarily offset by transaction fees under the Securities Exchange Act.

sections.label: Title I — Department of State and Related Programs

items.main: Appropriates $9.36B for Administration of Foreign Affairs including Worldwide Security Protection ($3.03B), embassy operations, the Truman Building renovation ($812.8M), and international broadcasting ($3.99B).
items.detail: Diplomatic policy: $1.44B. Embassy security construction: $1.2B. Educational and cultural exchange: $983.3M from consular fees. Permanent rescission of $900M in prior-year State/Foreign Ops funds in Sec. 7006. Public diplomacy and international media: $3.99B.

sections.label: Title III — Bilateral Economic Assistance

items.main: Appropriates $6.77B for SEED Act East European democracy programs, $5.88B for PEPFAR HIV/AIDS, $3.53B for global health, $1.65B minimum for Jordan, and $1.43B minimum for Egypt.
items.detail: SEED Act: 15% minimum for Ukraine. Global health: $3.53B in addition to PEPFAR. Jordan: $1.65B minimum, $845.1M minimum budget support. Egypt: $1.43B minimum. Democracy programs: $2.175B recommended across multiple accounts.

sections.label: Title IV — International Security Assistance

items.main: Appropriates $6.16B for Foreign Military Financing; $3.3B designated as grants-only for Israel; $1.4B for International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement.
items.detail: FMF: $6.16B total, $3.3B of which must be grants for Israel. International Narcotics Control: $1.4B for counter-narcotics and rule-of-law programs. IMET and other security assistance within Title IV.

sections.label: Title VII — General Provisions

items.main: Establishes the America First Opportunity Fund (up to $850M transfer authority), permanently rescinds $900M from prior-year funds, and sets conditions on aid to specific countries.
items.detail: Sec. 7045: up to $850M from Peacekeeping Operations, ESF, and FMF may be redirected for 'America First' purposes. Sec. 7006: $900M permanent rescission. Country-specific conditions and certifications in Secs. 7029-7071.

sections.label: Section 101 — Funding Limitation

items.main: Prohibits use of any Division F funds or other State/Foreign Ops appropriations for any contribution, grant, or payment to UNRWA for prior fiscal year, FY2026, or FY2027 amounts prior to March 25, 2027.
items.detail: The prohibition covers funds from Division F and any other Acts making appropriations for State, foreign operations, and related programs, including supplemental appropriations. It applies retroactively to prior-year funds not yet transferred to UNRWA.

sections.label: Sections 101–105 — CR Extension and Ratification

items.main: Amends Public Law 119-37 CR expiration to February 13, 2026, ratifies all lapse-period obligations as valid, authorizes employee back pay, and repeals Section 213 of the prior CR.
items.detail: Sec. 101: amends date in Sec. 106(3) of Public Law 119-37 to February 13, 2026. Sec. 102: lapse period treated as covered by the CR. Sec. 103: personnel pay authorized under 31 U.S.C. § 1341(c). Sec. 104: obligations for essential activity and orderly termination ratified. Sec. 105: repeals Section 213 of the prior CR affecting legislative branch operations.

sections.label: Sections 5001–5003 — Agriculture and Commodity Extenders

items.main: Extends U.S. Grain Standards Act through September 30, 2026, CFTC Whistleblower Program through September 30, 2026, and Forest Service ACES Program through October 1, 2026.
items.detail: Grain Standards: Secs. 7(j)(5), 7A(l)(4), 21(e) amended. CFTC Whistleblower: Public Law 117-25 paragraphs (3) and (4) amended. Forest Service ACES: Agricultural Act of 2014 Sec. 8302(b) amended to October 1, 2026.

sections.label: Sections 5004–5009 — Homeland Security and Cybersecurity Extenders

items.main: Extends NFIP through September 30, 2026 (retroactive to January 30, 2026), TSA Reimbursable Screening through 2026, Motor Carrier Safety Advisory Committee through September 30, 2026, and three cybersecurity authorities.
items.detail: NFIP: 42 U.S.C. 4016(a) and 42 U.S.C. 4026 both amended; retroactive effective date applies if Act enacted after January 30, 2026. Cybersecurity: NCPS (6 U.S.C. 1525(a)), CISA Act (6 U.S.C. 1510(a)), State/Local Grant (6 U.S.C. 665g(s)(1)) each extended one year.

sections.label: Sections 5010–5018 — Government Operations and Justice Extenders

items.main: Extends Technology Modernization Fund through September 30, 2026, Parole Commission to January 30, 2031, makes sex offense special assessment permanent, and modifies bankruptcy fee provisions.
items.detail: Technology Modernization Fund: 40 U.S.C. 11301 note amended. Parole Commission: 18 U.S.C. 3551 note extended to January 30, 2031. Sex offense assessment: 18 U.S.C. 3014(a) expiration date removed — now permanent. Sentencing Commission: drone guidelines due December 31, 2026.

sections.label: Sections 5019–5021 — Trade Extenders and PAYGO Exemption

items.main: Extends AGOA and Haiti HELP Act to December 31, 2026 with retroactive application, and exempts all Division I and J budgetary costs from both PAYGO scorecards.
items.detail: AGOA: Trade Act Sec. 506B and AGOA Sec. 112(g) each amended to December 31, 2026; retroactive liquidation of entries after September 30, 2025 allowed within 180 days. Haiti HELP: extended to December 31, 2026. Sec. 5021: excludes I and J effects from statutory PAYGO, Senate PAYGO, and CBO allocation scoring.

sections.label: Title I — Medicaid

items.main: Streamlines multi-state provider enrollment (Sec. 6101), removes age restrictions for working disabled adults (Sec. 6102), standardizes military family Medicaid coverage (Sec. 6103), and modifies DSH allotments (Secs. 6105-6106).
items.detail: Sec. 6101: out-of-state providers use streamlined enrollment without duplicating in-state requirements. Sec. 6102: removes age cap for working adults with disabilities. Sec. 6103: military relocation cannot cause Medicaid coverage loss. DSH modifications in Secs. 6105-6106 adjust hospital payment calculations.

sections.label: Title II — Medicare

items.main: Extends low-volume hospital payments, Medicare-Dependent Hospital program, ambulance add-ons, APM incentives, telehealth, and hospital-at-home; adds MCED screening and infusion pump coverage; and increases the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.403B to $2.062B.
items.detail: Telehealth (Sec. 6209) continues COVID-19 era flexibilities. Acute Hospital Care at Home (Sec. 6210) extends CMS waiver for hospital-level home care. MCED (Sec. 6221) amends Section 1861 of the Social Security Act. PBM accountability (Sec. 6224): fiduciary requirements and spread pricing restrictions for Part D PBMs.

sections.label: Title III — Human Services

items.main: Extends TANF through December 31, 2026 (Sec. 6304), sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education programs (Secs. 6301-6302), and family-to-family health information centers (Sec. 6303).
items.detail: TANF extension: 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriation language; continues FY2025 program terms. Sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education extended under the same mechanism — no new conditions added.

sections.label: Title IV — Public Health and Other Extenders

items.main: Extends community health centers, NHSC, and teaching health center GME programs (Sec. 6401); Special Diabetes Programs at $350M for FY2026 (Sec. 6402); and appropriates $188M for No Surprises Act implementation (Sec. 6404).
items.detail: Community health centers: continued funding through extension period. Special Diabetes Programs: $350M for type 1 and type 2 programs. No Surprises Act (Sec. 6404): $188M to CMS Program Management Account, available until expended, for independent dispute resolution and consumer protection administration.

sections.label: Title VI — Food and Drug Administration

items.main: Extends rare pediatric disease priority review vouchers (Sec. 6604), modifies orphan drug exclusivity (Sec. 6605), and establishes an Abraham Accords Office within the FDA (Sec. 6611).
items.detail: Sec. 6604: rare pediatric disease voucher program extended. Sec. 6605: limits 30-month orphan drug exclusivity to prevent dual-use abuse. Sec. 6611: new FDA office for Abraham Accords implementation including regulatory cooperation with Israel and signatory states on pharmaceutical approvals.

sections.label: Title VII — Lowering Prescription Drug Costs

items.main: Adds PBM oversight requirements (Sec. 6701), remittance transparency rules (Sec. 6702), and generic drug application transparency (Sec. 6703).
items.detail: Sec. 6701: PBMs providing Medicare Part D services must comply with new reporting and oversight requirements. Sec. 6702: PBM remittance and pass-through structures in drug pricing made transparent. Sec. 6703: generic drug application transparency reduces barriers to market entry.

underreported.section: Sec. 6 — Payment to Widows and Heirs of Deceased Members of Congress
underreported.summary: Appropriates $174,000 to Jill Marie LaMalfa, widow of the late Representative Douglas L. LaMalfa of California, from the general fund of the Treasury.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 6 appears before Division A, outside any division or subject-matter title. The bill title identifies this as a government appropriations act; Sec. 6 directly appropriates a named payment to a private individual.

underreported.summary: Rescinds $11.66B in unobligated balances from section 10301(1)(A)(iii) of Public Law 117-169 (the Inflation Reduction Act), eliminating previously enacted education spending authority without modifying program eligibility rules.
underreported.why_unreported: Located in Division B Title V General Provisions, labeled as a rescission provision. Reduces previously enacted education spending by $11.66B without modifying the program's eligibility rules or structure.

underreported.section: Sec. 5021 — PAYGO Exemption for Health Extenders
underreported.summary: Excludes all budgetary effects of Divisions I and J from both statutory PAYGO scorecards and the Senate PAYGO scorecard, removing the requirement for spending offsets for all new or extended Medicare, Medicaid, and TANF spending in those divisions.
underreported.why_unreported: Placed in Division I, Sec. 5021 determines the fiscal treatment of all Division J health spending. The exemption covers the Medicare Improvement Fund increase, new MCED coverage, and all health extender costs — but this is not disclosed in any Division J provision.

underreported.summary: Bars all U.S. funds, including from prior fiscal years, from being contributed to UNRWA through March 25, 2027 — a retroactive restriction on already-enacted spending authority for prior years.
underreported.why_unreported: Division G is a single provision with no appropriations amounts. The retroactive application to prior-year funds makes it a clawback on previously enacted spending authority, not merely a prospective restriction — an effect not indicated by the division label 'Other Matters.'

criticisms.why: This amendment would completely eliminate funding for an office that helps some of the most vulnerable in our country. This office helps shelter and care for children who are seeking safety. It makes sure that these children aren't being trafficked. It makes sure these children aren't stuck in cages in Border Patrol facilities for extended periods of time.

This amendment would eliminate HHS funding provided in the bill — which the Trump administration actually requested in their budget — that will allow the Agency to drastically improve sponsor vetting for unaccompanied children, ensuring that they are no longer released to human traffickers.

gaps: The bill funds five of twelve FY2026 appropriations packages but does not include Agriculture, Commerce/Justice/Science, Energy/Water, Interior/Environment, full-year Homeland Security, or the Legislative Branch.
The DHS continuing resolution runs only through February 13, 2026, leaving border security and immigration enforcement funding unresolved within days of enactment.
Division G bars UNRWA contributions but does not specify alternative humanitarian delivery mechanisms for Palestinian refugees who rely on UNRWA for food, education, and health services.

items.detail: SSI advance: $23.5B for Q1 FY2027. Foster care/adoption: $6.84B Title IV-E. SAMHSA: $4.09B. CMS administrative expenses: $14.67B not to exceed. Global health/HIV-AIDS: $5.16B. Child support and self-sufficiency programs also funded.

sections.label: Title III — Department of Education

items.main: Appropriates $24.62B for Pell Grants, $19.13B for Title I education grants, $15.49B for IDEA special education, and includes a $11.66B rescission of unobligated Inflation Reduction Act education funds (Sec. 529).
items.detail: Title I: $6.46B basic grants, $5.30B targeted grants, $5.30B finance incentive grants, $862M concentration grants. Pell: $22.48B basic grants. Vocational Rehabilitation: $4.65B. Sec. 529 rescinds $11.66B from Public Law 117-169 unobligated balances.

underreported.section: Sec. 529 — Rescission of IRA Education Funds
underreported.summary: Rescinds the unobligated balance of $11.66B from section 10301(1)(A)(iii) of Public Law 117-169, eliminating previously enacted education spending authority without modifying program eligibility rules.
underreported.why_unreported: Located in Title V General Provisions, the provision permanently eliminates $11.66B in previously enacted spending authority. It is a rescission section rather than a programmatic education change.

underreported.section: Title II — CHIP Advance Unavailability Designation
underreported.summary: $12.34B in CHIP state matching payments is appropriated but simultaneously designated as unavailable for obligation — functioning as a spending ceiling rather than an immediate outlay.
underreported.why_unreported: The appropriation and simultaneous unavailability designation appear in the same paragraph. The $12.34B appears in appropriation totals but cannot be obligated until a future triggering event.

gaps: Medicare and Medicaid are funded at open-ended levels based on program formulas; the division does not set caps, block grant amounts, or per-capita limits on either program.
The $11.66B IRA education rescission eliminates spending authority without identifying which specific activities or grantees are affected by the removed unobligated balances.

modified: FY2026 levels set for Medicare ($593.82B), Medicaid ($508.15B), NIH institutes, WIOA, Pell Grants, and other programs
Title I and IDEA availability dates structured with July 1, 2026 release schedules

divisions.brief: Section 8 housing vouchers ($34.44B) and highway trust fund authorizations ($63.4B) dominate this division, alongside $13.71B for FAA operations and $4.42B for homeless assistance.

subs: $34.44B for housing choice vouchers; $34.96B available for contract renewals
$8.32B for Public Housing Operating Fund

subs: $63.4B from the Highway Trust Fund for federal-aid highway and safety construction
Obligation ceiling capped at $62.66B for FY2026

sections.label: Title I — Department of Transportation

items.main: Appropriates $63.4B from the Highway Trust Fund for federal-aid highways, $13.71B for the FAA, $14.64B for transit from the Mass Transit Account, $850M and $1.577B for Amtrak, and funds for FHWA, FRA, and other modal agencies.
items.detail: FAA: $13.71B total, $13.04B from Airport/Airway Trust Fund; air traffic $10.34B, safety $1.84B. FAA research: $74.5M including $9M for the new ARPA-I office. Amtrak national network: $1.577B available until expended. Transit: $14.64B from Mass Transit Account.

sections.label: Title II — Department of Housing and Urban Development

items.main: Appropriates $34.44B for housing choice vouchers, $8.32B for public housing operations, $6.995B for CDBG, $4.42B for homeless assistance, and $1.25B for HOME; sets loan guarantee ceilings of $400B (single-family) and $550B (Ginnie Mae).
items.detail: Section 8 renewals: $34.96B. Public Housing Capital Fund: $3.30B. HOME: $1.25B, available until September 30, 2029. Continuum of Care: $4.01B. Loan guarantee ceilings are contingent liability caps, not direct appropriations.

underreported.summary: Sets the single-family mortgage insurance ceiling at $400B, the Ginnie Mae MBS ceiling at $550B, and the HECM reverse mortgage ceiling at $35B — authorizing up to $985B in combined contingent federal liabilities.
underreported.why_unreported: These ceilings authorize contingent liabilities far exceeding any direct appropriation in the division. They are statutory borrowing authorizations that only convert to actual obligations when defaults occur and do not appear in budget authority totals.

underreported.summary: $9M of FAA Research and Technology funds is earmarked for the Advanced Research Projects Agency-Infrastructure (ARPA-I), established by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 as a new transportation research agency.
underreported.why_unreported: ARPA-I funding appears as a sub-allocation within the FAA Research and Technology account, not as a separate appropriations heading, despite funding an entirely new federal agency.

gaps: Housing voucher funding is set at $34.44B but the division does not include emergency voucher funding for tenants at risk of displacement from expiring pandemic-era tenant protections.
Federal highway programs are funded through trust fund obligation ceilings but no additional appropriation is provided for emergency road and bridge repair outside the ceiling.

added: ARPA-I receives $9M from FAA Research and Technology — first appropriation for this new infrastructure research agency
modified: Ginnie Mae MBS guarantee ceiling: $550B; single-family mortgage insurance ceiling: $400B; HECM ceiling: $35B
Highway obligation ceiling set at $62.66B for FY2026
Amtrak National Network grants: $1.577B

divisions.brief: The IRS receives approximately $11.2B across three accounts, the SBA is authorized for $35.5B in business loan guarantees and $15B in disaster loans, and the federal judiciary receives $6.13B.
