bills.title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
bills.summary: This bill requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs, to conduct an interagency review of the status of research on lung cancer in women and underserved populations — assessing existing research, identifying knowledge gaps, and recommending strategies to accelerate research, expand access to preventive services and screening, and improve public awareness. Findings must be reported to Congress within two years.
bills.brief: Directs HHS to conduct an interagency review of lung cancer research gaps for women and underserved populations and submit findings and recommendations to Congress.

top_lines.headline: HHS Interagency Review
subs: Requires the Secretary of HHS to conduct an interagency review of lung cancer research, prevention, and awareness with respect to women and underserved populations
Review must assess current knowledge gaps, collaborative research opportunities, and barriers to participation in lung cancer studies

top_lines.headline: Congressional Report
subs: Findings must be submitted to Congress, including the status of existing research, causes of lung cancer disparities in women, and recommended strategies to improve screening, diagnosis, and prevention

bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House with bipartisan support and has been placed directly on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 380), bypassing committee referral — a strong procedural signal that Senate leadership may bring it to the floor via unanimous consent. The bill is narrowly scoped as a study directive with no spending mandate, has no meaningful opposition, and its health equity framing attracts members across party lines.

sections.label: Section 2 — Interagency Review on Lung Cancer in Women

items.main: Directs the Secretary of HHS to conduct a review, in coordination with relevant federal agencies, to evaluate the status of research on lung cancer in women and underserved populations.
items.detail: The review must assess existing research and current knowledge gaps; identify new opportunities for collaborative research on the causes of lung cancer and to advance prevention, screening, and diagnosis; assess barriers to participation of women and underserved populations in lung cancer research; and recommend strategies to improve that participation. A report on findings and recommendations must be submitted to Congress.

gaps: The bill requires a review and report but does not appropriate any funding for the review, for new research programs, or for implementation of the recommendations.
The bill directs HHS to conduct an interagency review but does not specify which agencies must participate, leaving the scope of the coordination to agency discretion.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: Lung cancer is the leading cancer death among women, and it disproportionately impacts women who have never even smoked. This bipartisan bill requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs, to conduct an interagency review of current research on women and lung cancer. Madam Speaker, this bill addresses the disparities women with lung cancer face, and it addresses it head-on, strengthening research, access to preventative services, and raising awareness.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Boyle
featured_quotes.text: This is a bipartisan, commonsense bill that takes on a serious and too often overlooked public health disparity. The legislation would require the Secretary of HHS, in consultation with the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs, to conduct an interagency review of research on women and lung cancer, including access to preventive services. It would also strengthen interagency coordination on public awareness efforts so more women have the information they need to understand their risk, seek early detection, and get care sooner.

added: Requirement that the Secretary of HHS conduct an interagency review of lung cancer research, prevention, and awareness for women and underserved populations and report findings to Congress

bills.title: Cape Fox Land Entitlement Finalization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to provide equitable treatment for the people of the Village Corporation established for the Native Village of Saxman, Alaska, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 (ANCSA) gave Alaska Native corporations the right to select federal land as compensation for aboriginal land claims. Cape Fox Corporation — the Native village corporation for Saxman, Alaska — still has acres remaining from that original entitlement. This bill lets Cape Fox satisfy that remaining entitlement by selecting approximately 180 acres in the Tongass National Forest rather than a previously required township parcel near Saxman. The subsurface estate of the selected land goes to Sealaska Corporation, and a public access easement is reserved.
bills.brief: Lets Cape Fox Corporation fulfill its remaining Alaska Native land entitlement under the 1971 ANCSA settlement by selecting 180 acres in Tongass National Forest instead of the originally required township parcel.

top_lines.headline: Land Selection Change
subs: Cape Fox may select approximately 180 acres in Tongass National Forest instead of ~185 acres in the Saxman township

top_lines.headline: Conveyance Deadlines
subs: Cape Fox has 90 days from enactment to submit written notice of selection to the Secretary of the Interior
Interior must convey surface estate to Cape Fox within 180 days of receiving the selection notice
Subsurface estate of the same land conveyed simultaneously to Sealaska Corporation

top_lines.headline: Public Access Preserved
subs: Easement reserved under ANCSA Section 17(b) to allow public access to National Forest land via George Inlet on Revillagigedo Island

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 19, 2026 as Public Law 119-93. Passed the House on December 15, 2025 and the Senate on February 26, 2026.

sections.label: Section 3 — Waiver of Core Township Requirement

items.main: Removes the obligation for Cape Fox to select or receive conveyance of approximately 185 acres located within the township containing the Native Village of Saxman.
items.detail: The waiver overrides the core township selection requirement in Section 16(b) of ANCSA (43 U.S.C. 1615(b)). The specific parcels waived are approximately 40 acres in T. 74 S., R.90 E., sec. 10, and approximately 144.57 acres in T. 75 S., R.91 E., sec. 1.

sections.label: Section 4 — Selection Outside Exterior Selection Boundary

items.main: Cape Fox may select approximately 180 acres of surface land in Tongass National Forest and receive conveyance upon submitting written notice within 90 days of enactment.
items.detail: Interior must convey the surface estate to Cape Fox and, simultaneously, convey the subsurface estate to Sealaska Corporation. Congress intends completion within 180 days of receiving the selection notice. The conveyance fulfills both Cape Fox's Section 16 ANCSA entitlement and Sealaska's subsurface entitlement under Section 14(f).

sections.label: Section 5 — Public Access Easement

items.main: The conveyance of federal land to Cape Fox is subject to a public easement under ANCSA Section 17(b) allowing access to inland National Forest land from George Inlet.
items.detail: The easement runs with the land and is reserved regardless of Cape Fox's ownership. It preserves public ingress and egress to National Forest System land further inland on Revillagigedo Island.

underreported.summary: The conveyance to both Cape Fox and Sealaska Corporation is deemed to fulfill their respective entitlements under ANCSA in full — Cape Fox under Section 16 and Sealaska under Section 14(f). No further land claims by either entity against the federal government remain after this transaction.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and summary focus on Cape Fox's selection flexibility, but the simultaneous full discharge of both corporations' outstanding ANCSA entitlements is a separate legal consequence not apparent from the bill's name.

gaps: The bill does not specify what happens to Cape Fox's entitlement if no written selection notice is submitted within the 90-day window.
The bill conveys the subsurface estate to Sealaska upon Cape Fox surface conveyance but does not address the disposition of existing mineral rights or subsurface claims at the time of conveyance.

added: Cape Fox authority to select approximately 180 acres of Tongass National Forest land outside its current exterior selection boundary
Obligation for Interior to convey the subsurface estate of the selected land to Sealaska Corporation upon surface conveyance to Cape Fox
modified: Cape Fox land entitlement fulfillment mechanism — from required core township selection (~185 acres) to Tongass National Forest parcel selection (~180 acres)
removed: Core township selection requirement for Cape Fox's remaining ANCSA land entitlement under Section 16(b) (43 U.S.C. 1615(b))

bills.title: Investing in All of America Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 to exclude from the limit on leverage certain amounts invested in smaller enterprises located in rural or low-income areas and small businesses in critical technology areas, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Reduces the maximum leverage a Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) can obtain from the SBA from 300% to 200% of its private capital, while adding a new exclusion from the leverage calculation for investments in rural areas, covered technology categories, or small manufacturers — up to the lesser of 50% of private capital or $125M. Also expands what counts as private capital to include college and university endowments and foundations.
bills.brief: Lowers the SBIC leverage ceiling from 300% to 200% of private capital and creates a new $125M exclusion for investments in rural areas, critical technologies, and small manufacturers.

top_lines.headline: Leverage Cap Reduced
subs: Individual SBIC leverage ceiling reduced from 300% to 200% of private capital
Dollar cap for quarterly/semiannual interest-paying SBICs: $250M; all other SBICs: $175M

top_lines.headline: Common Control Limits
subs: Commonly controlled SBICs making quarterly/semiannual payments: $475M aggregate cap
All other commonly controlled SBICs: $350M aggregate cap

top_lines.headline: Rural and Technology Investment Exclusion
subs: Investments in rural areas, covered technology categories (10 U.S.C. 149(e)), or small manufacturers excluded from leverage calculation
Exclusion capped at lesser of 50% of the SBIC's private capital or $125M
Only investments made after the date of enactment qualify for the exclusion

top_lines.headline: Private Capital Definition Expanded
subs: Funds from college or university foundations, endowments, and trusts now qualify as private capital
New explicit exclusion for funds obtained directly or indirectly from government sources (with exceptions for pension plans and college/university trusts)

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 19, 2026 as Public Law 119-92. Passed the House on December 1, 2025 and the Senate on April 15, 2026.

sections.label: Section 2 — Small Business Investment Company Maximum Leverage Exclusion

items.main: Reduces individual SBIC leverage ceilings and restructures dollar caps by company type.
items.detail: Individual caps become 200% of private capital, not to exceed $250M for quarterly/semiannual interest payers or $175M for other companies. Commonly controlled caps become $475M or $350M respectively. A new subparagraph (C) explicitly excludes government-sourced funds from the private capital definition.

items.main: Creates a new exclusion from the outstanding leverage calculation for investments in rural areas, covered technology categories, or small manufacturers.
items.detail: The exclusion is capped at the lesser of 50% of the SBIC's private capital or $125M. Only investments made after enactment qualify. Rural areas are defined under 7 U.S.C. 1991(a)(13); covered technology categories under 10 U.S.C. 149(e); small manufacturers under Section 501(e)(6) of the Small Business Investment Act.

underreported.summary: A new subparagraph (C) added to the private capital definition explicitly excludes any funds obtained directly or indirectly from any federal, state, or local government or government agency, with limited exceptions for pension plan funds and college/university trust/endowment funds.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as expanding private capital to include university endowments, but Section 2(a)(3) simultaneously adds a government-funds exclusion that could disqualify capital sources previously counted under the prior definition's silence on the issue.

gaps: The bill expands the exclusion to cover investments in "covered technology categories" as defined in 10 U.S.C. 149(e) but does not reproduce that definition, requiring SBICs and SBA to cross-reference a separate statute.

The bill caps the combined exclusion at the lesser of 50% of private capital or $125M but does not specify how to allocate the cap if an SBIC invests across multiple qualifying categories simultaneously.
The bill reduces the individual leverage ceiling from 300% to 200% but does not address transition treatment for SBICs currently leveraged between 200% and 300% of private capital.

added: New investment exclusion from leverage calculation for SBIC investments in rural areas, covered technology categories, or small manufacturers — up to lesser of 50% of private capital or $125M
New government-funds exclusion from private capital definition (new subparagraph C to Section 103(9))
modified: Individual SBIC leverage ceiling — from 300% to 200% of private capital
Commonly controlled SBIC aggregate cap — restructured from a single $350M limit to two tiers: $475M for quarterly/semiannual interest payers and $350M for all others
Private capital definition — expanded to include college/university foundation, endowment, or trust

bills.title: Sloan Canyon Conservation and Lateral Pipeline Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area Act to adjust the boundary of the Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Expands the Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area in Clark County, Nevada from 48,438 to 57,728 acres and grants the Southern Nevada Water Authority mandatory rights-of-way through BLM land at no charge to construct and operate a water transmission pipeline, with BLM required to complete the rights-of-way grant within one year of enactment.
bills.brief: Adds 9,290 acres to Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area and requires BLM to grant the Southern Nevada Water Authority free pipeline rights-of-way within one year.

top_lines.headline: Conservation Area Expansion
subs: Boundary increases from 48,438 to 57,728 acres, adding approximately 9,290 acres
Expansion subject to valid existing rights and does not restrict authorized activities within existing utility corridors

top_lines.headline: Pipeline Rights-of-Way
subs: BLM must grant SNWA temporary and permanent water pipeline, powerline, facility, and access road rights-of-way within 1 year at no charge
Pipeline may not be routed through or under any designated wilderness area
Construction may not permanently adversely affect conservation area surface resources

top_lines.headline: Excavation and Disposal
subs: SNWA may excavate and dispose of sand, gravel, minerals, and other materials from pipeline tunneling without payment
BLM must identify federal disposal sites via MOU with SNWA within 30 days of granting rights-of-way

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 19, 2026 as Public Law 119-91. Passed the House on December 15, 2025 and the Senate on February 26, 2026.

sections.label: Section 3 — Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area Boundary Adjustment

items.main: Expands the conservation area boundary from 48,438 to 57,728 acres by updating the reference map to one dated May 20, 2024.
items.detail: The expansion is subject to valid existing rights, including utility transmission corridor designations and right-of-way grants approved before enactment. The expansion does not modify the existing management framework of the conservation area.

items.main: Requires BLM to grant SNWA mandatory rights-of-way for the Horizon Lateral Pipeline through the conservation area and adjacent BLM land within 1 year at no charge.
items.detail: Rights-of-way cover temporary and permanent water pipeline, powerline, facility, and access road routes. SNWA may excavate and dispose of tunneling materials without consideration. BLM must enter a disposal MOU with SNWA within 30 days of granting rights-of-way. The Secretary may impose conditions necessary to protect conservation area resources under FLPMA Section 505.

underreported.summary: The boundary expansion does not prevent the Secretary from authorizing new utility facility rights-of-way within existing designated transportation and utility corridors inside the newly protected land, subject to NEPA review.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill expands the conservation area boundary, which typically restricts new development, but Section 3(c)(2)(B) explicitly preserves the Secretary's authority to authorize new utility infrastructure within existing corridors inside the expanded boundary.

gaps: The bill requires rights-of-way 'not subject to the payment of rents or other charges' but does not address long-term maintenance obligations or liability allocation between BLM and SNWA once the pipeline is operational.
The bill defines the expansion using a map dated May 20, 2024 but does not specify which document controls if the map and the stated acreage figure of 57,728 acres are inconsistent.
The bill requires BLM to grant rights-of-way within 1 year but does not specify a remedy if BLM fails to meet the deadline.

added: Horizon Lateral Pipeline rights-of-way for SNWA through and adjacent to the conservation area, including temporary and permanent water pipeline, powerline, facility, and access road routes
SNWA authority to excavate and dispose of tunneling materials from federal land without payment
BLM obligation to enter into a disposal MOU with SNWA within 30 days of granting rights-of-way
modified: Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area boundary — from 48,438 to 57,728 acres, updated to the May 20, 2024 reference map

bills.title: A bill to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to extend the time period during which licensees are required to commence construction of certain hydropower projects.
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to extend the time period during which licensees are required to commence construction of certain hydropower projects.
bills.summary: Gives FERC authority to grant hydropower project licensees up to 6 additional years to begin construction, beyond the existing 8-year extension allowed under the Federal Power Act, for projects that received their license before March 13, 2020. FERC may also retroactively reinstate licenses that expired after December 31, 2023 and before enactment.
bills.brief: Extends available FERC hydropower construction deadlines by up to 6 additional years for projects licensed before March 13, 2020, and allows reinstatement of licenses that expired after December 31, 2023.

top_lines.headline: Construction Deadline Extension
subs: Up to 6 additional years beyond the existing 8-year Federal Power Act extension for projects licensed before March 13, 2020
Extension structured as no more than 3 consecutive 2-year periods, beginning after the existing maximum extension expires
FERC must provide reasonable notice and good cause must be shown before granting an extension

top_lines.headline: License Reinstatement
subs: FERC may reinstate licenses for covered projects that expired after December 31, 2023 and before enactment, effective retroactively as of the expiration date
Reinstated licenses become eligible for the 6-year extension under this bill

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 11, 2026 as Public Law 119-90. Passed the Senate on July 29, 2025 and the House on April 21, 2026.

sections.label: Section 1 — Extension of Time to Commence Construction of Certain Hydropower Projects

items.main: FERC may extend the construction commencement deadline for covered projects (licensed before March 13, 2020) by up to 6 additional years, in no more than 3 consecutive 2-year increments, upon licensee request and for good cause.
items.detail: The extension supplements — not replaces — the existing 8-year authority under Section 13 of the Federal Power Act (16 U.S.C. 806). The 6-year period begins only after the current maximum extension is exhausted. FERC must provide reasonable notice before granting an extension.

items.main: FERC may reinstate licenses for covered projects whose construction deadlines expired after December 31, 2023 and before enactment, effective as of the expiration date.
items.detail: Reinstatement is retroactive to the license expiration date, and the new 6-year extension authority under this bill attaches from that date. This applies to licenses that already lapsed under the prior 8-year deadline framework.

underreported.summary: FERC may reinstate expired licenses retroactively and grant the new 6-year extension starting from the expiration date. A project whose license lapsed in early 2024 could receive full retroactive reinstatement plus up to 6 years of new construction time.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title describes a forward-looking deadline extension, but Section 1(d) creates a retroactive reinstatement mechanism that restores federal authorization to projects that had already lost it before enactment.

gaps: The bill requires "good cause shown" for an extension but does not define good cause or establish criteria, leaving the standard entirely to FERC discretion.
The bill applies only to projects licensed before March 13, 2020 but does not explain the significance of that date or address treatment of projects licensed on that date.
The bill does not address whether environmental review requirements attached to the original license must be updated before construction may begin under the extended deadline.

added: FERC authority to grant up to 6 additional years of construction deadline extensions for hydropower projects licensed before March 13, 2020, in no more than 3 consecutive 2-year periods
FERC authority to reinstate expired licenses for covered projects whose deadlines lapsed after December 31, 2023, effective retroactively as of the expiration date
modified: Maximum extension authority for covered project construction deadlines — from up to 8 years to up to 14 years total extension time

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Federal Communications Commission to establish a vetting process for prospective applicants for high-cost universal service program funding.
bills.summary: Requires the FCC to establish within 180 days a formal vetting process for applicants seeking high-cost universal service fund grants to deploy rural broadband networks. Applicants must document technical, financial, and operational capabilities and submit a business plan; the FCC must evaluate compliance history with other government broadband programs and set a minimum $9,000 per-violation penalty for pre-authorization defaults.
bills.brief: Mandates FCC applicant vetting for rural broadband funding within 180 days and sets a minimum $9,000 penalty for pre-authorization defaults.

top_lines.headline: FCC Vetting Rulemaking
subs: FCC must initiate rulemaking within 180 days to establish a vetting process for high-cost universal service fund applicants
Funds may only be awarded to applicants that satisfy standards established in the final rules

top_lines.headline: Application Requirements
subs: Applicants must document technical, financial, and operational capabilities and submit a reasonable business plan
FCC must evaluate proposals against well-established technical and financial standards, including standards from its Digital Opportunity Data Collection orders
FCC must consider each applicant's compliance history with FCC and other government broadband deployment programs

top_lines.headline: Default Penalties
subs: Minimum $9,000 per violation for pre-authorization defaults
Base forfeiture may not fall below 30% of the applicant's total support unless FCC demonstrates the need for lower penalties in a particular instance

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 11, 2026 as Public Law 119-89. Passed the Senate on June 26, 2025 and the House on April 20, 2026.

sections.label: Section 2 — Vetting Process for Prospective High-Cost Universal Service Fund Applicants

items.main: Amends Section 254 of the Communications Act of 1934 to require FCC to initiate rulemaking within 180 days establishing a vetting process for high-cost USF applicants.
items.detail: Applies to any new high-cost USF funding for broadband deployment, including reverse competitive bidding. Applications submitted after rules are promulgated must meet the new standards. The FCC must evaluate applicants against its Digital Opportunity Data Collection technical standards and against each applicant's history of compliance with FCC and other government broadband funding programs.

items.main: Sets a minimum pre-authorization default penalty of $9,000 per violation, with a base forfeiture floor of 30% of the applicant's total support.
items.detail: The FCC may set the base forfeiture below 30% only by demonstrating in writing that lower penalties are warranted in a particular instance. The penalty applies during the evaluation and pre-award phase, before an applicant begins receiving support.

underreported.summary: The FCC must evaluate applicants against their history of compliance with not only FCC programs but also other government broadband deployment funding programs administered by other federal agencies.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as FCC vetting, but the compliance history requirement extends to programs run by other federal agencies. An applicant with unresolved compliance issues in another federal broadband program could be disqualified from FCC funding under this provision.

gaps: The bill requires FCC to initiate rulemaking within 180 days but sets no deadline for completing or finalizing the rulemaking, leaving the vetting process potentially pending indefinitely.
The vetting requirements apply only to applications submitted after rules are promulgated, leaving all pending applications and existing funding commitments outside the new standards.
The bill does not define what constitutes a pre-authorization default or how the $9,000 minimum penalty interacts with existing FCC forfeiture guidelines and statutory caps.

added: FCC obligation to initiate rulemaking within 180 days to establish applicant vetting for high-cost USF broadband funding
Applicant documentation requirements: technical, financial, and operational capability evidence plus a reasonable business plan
Compliance history review requirement covering FCC and other government broadband funding programs
Minimum $9,000 per-violation penalty for pre-authorization defaults with a 30% of total support base forfeiture floor
modified: High-cost USF award process — funds may only be awarded after applicants satisfy FCC-established vetting standards (applies to new applications after rules are finalized)

bills.title: Lulu’s Law
bills.official_title: Lulu’s Law
bills.summary: This bill orders the Federal Communications Commission to formally allow shark attacks to be sent out as wireless emergency alerts — the alert system defined in the FCC's existing rules (47 CFR 10.10(a)). The FCC has 180 days after the bill becomes law to issue the order.
bills.brief: Requires the FCC to issue an order making a shark attack an event for which a wireless emergency alert may be transmitted.

top_lines.headline: Shark Attack Alerts
subs: FCC must allow shark attacks to qualify for wireless emergency alerts
Uses the existing 'Alert Message' system defined in FCC rules (47 CFR 10.10(a))

top_lines.headline: FCC Deadline
subs: FCC has 180 days after enactment to issue the order

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill is sponsored by Sen. Britt (R-AL) with 9 bipartisan cosponsors spanning both parties (Schatz, Warnock, and Kaine among the Democrats; Fischer, Ricketts, Capito, Tuberville, and Cassidy among the Republicans). It has already reached Passed House status, and a narrow, low-cost directive simply adding a hazard category to an existing alert system attracts little opposition.

sections.label: Section 2 — Wireless Emergency Alerts

items.main: Directs the FCC to issue an order providing that a shark attack is an event for which an Alert Message may be transmitted, no later than 180 days after enactment.
items.detail: The bill ties the term 'Alert Message' to the definition in section 10.10(a) of title 47 of the Code of Federal Regulations (or any successor regulation), so it works within the FCC's existing Wireless Emergency Alerts framework rather than creating a new alert type. The bill specifies only that the order be issued within the 180-day window; it sets no further conditions on how the alerts are triggered or administered.

gaps: The bill makes shark attacks eligible for wireless emergency alerts but does not specify which authorities may originate such an alert or what criteria define a qualifying shark attack.
The bill sets a 180-day deadline for the FCC order but specifies no consequence or backstop if the order is not issued on time.
The bill addresses only that an alert may be transmitted, but does not address the geographic area, duration, or content standards for a shark-attack alert.

added: An FCC order designating a shark attack as an event eligible for a wireless emergency Alert Message, to be issued within 180 days of enactment

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.title: License to Drill Act
bills.official_title: License to Drill Act
bills.summary: Federal law requires the Bureau of Land Management to charge a fee on every new application to drill for oil and gas on federal land, with the money going into a fund used to speed up permit processing. That fee requirement was set to wind down in 2026. This bill extends it through 2037 and directs that all of the fees collected each year from 2027 through 2037 go into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund.
bills.brief: Extends the BLM oil and gas drilling-permit application fee through 2037 and routes all collected fees into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund.

top_lines.headline: What the Drilling Permit Fee Does
subs: BLM charges a fee on each new application for a permit to drill on federal land
Fees feed the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, used to process permits

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extends the fee-collection requirement from 2026 to 2037
Directs all fees collected for fiscal years 2027-2037 to the Improvement Fund

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Kennedy (R-UT) with 3 cosponsors in a Republican-majority House, the bill extends an existing energy-permitting fee rather than creating a new program, which limits cost objections. It passed the House by voice vote, but its narrow fee-extension scope leaves Senate scheduling uncertain.

sections.label: Section 2 — BLM Oil and Gas Permit Processing Fee

items.main: Amends Section 35(d) of the Mineral Leasing Act to extend the drilling-permit application fee collection period and redirect the proceeds.
items.detail: Paragraphs (1) and (4) are amended by striking '2026' and inserting '2037', extending the fee requirement by eleven years. Paragraph (3) is rewritten so that, for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2037, all of the fees collected under the subsection are transferred to the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, replacing the prior partial-transfer formula. The bill does not state the dollar amount of the fee.

gaps: The bill extends and fully redirects the application fee to the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund but does not set or adjust the dollar amount of the fee itself.
The bill routes all collected fees into the permit-processing fund through 2037 but does not specify any performance target, such as a permit-processing time the additional funding must achieve.
The bill extends the fee through 2037 but does not address what happens to fee collection after that date.

modified: Mineral Leasing Act Section 35(d) drilling-permit fee collection period: 2026 -> 2037
Distribution of collected fees: prior partial-transfer formula -> all fees for fiscal years 2027-2037 transferred to the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund

bills.title: CLEAN Act
bills.official_title: CLEAN Act
bills.summary: This bill amends the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 to make the federal government hold geothermal energy lease sales more often and on a tighter schedule. It requires lease sales every year instead of every two years, requires a replacement sale in the same year if a scheduled sale is canceled or delayed, and sets 30-day deadlines for the Interior Department to act on geothermal drilling permit applications.
bills.brief: Requires annual federal geothermal lease sales (up from every two years), mandates replacement sales for canceled ones, and imposes 30-day permit-review deadlines.

top_lines.headline: More Frequent Lease Sales
subs: Geothermal lease sales required every year instead of every 2 years
Canceled or delayed sales must be replaced with another sale the same year
Interior must offer all nominated parcels eligible under the state resource management plan

top_lines.headline: Permit Decision Deadlines
subs: Interior must confirm an application is complete (or list missing items) within 30 days
Final decision on a complete drilling-permit application due within 30 days of completeness notice

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Fulcher (R-ID) with cosponsors Maloy (R-UT) and Boebert (R-CO) in a Republican-majority House, the bill advances energy-permitting priorities likely to draw Republican support. It passed the House by voice vote, but its mandatory annual-sale and strict deadline requirements may attract opposition over agency workload and environmental-review timelines, leaving its Senate path uncertain.

sections.label: Section 2 — Geothermal Leasing

items.main: Changes the minimum frequency of geothermal lease sales under Section 4(b) of the Geothermal Steam Act from once every two years to annually, and adds a same-year replacement-sale requirement.
items.detail: Paragraph (2) is amended by striking '2 years' and inserting 'year'. A new replacement-sales provision requires the Secretary of the Interior to hold a replacement sale during the same year if a scheduled sale is canceled or delayed. A new requirement directs the Secretary to offer all nominated parcels eligible for geothermal development under the resource management plan in effect for the state.

items.main: Adds new 30-day deadlines for the Interior Department to process geothermal drilling permit applications.
items.detail: Within 30 days of receiving an application, the Secretary must either notify the applicant that it is complete or specify what information is missing. Once an application is deemed complete, the Secretary must issue a final decision within 30 days of that completeness notice.

gaps: The bill sets 30-day deadlines for completeness review and final decisions but does not state what happens to an application if the Secretary misses either deadline.
The bill requires offering all eligible nominated parcels under the state resource management plan but does not address parcels in states without a current geothermal resource management plan.
The bill mandates a same-year replacement sale for canceled or delayed sales but does not address sales that cannot be rescheduled within the same year.

added: Replacement-sale requirement: a canceled or delayed geothermal lease sale must be replaced with another sale in the same year
Requirement to offer all nominated parcels eligible under the state resource management plan
30-day deadline for completeness notice and 30-day deadline for a final decision on geothermal drilling permit applications
modified: Minimum frequency of geothermal lease sales under Geothermal Steam Act Section 4(b): every 2 years -> every year

bills.title: Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act
bills.official_title: Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act
bills.summary: This bill orders the Government Accountability Office to study how federal programs and rules help or get in the way of fighting wildfires across property lines — where federal land, state land, private land, and tribal land all meet. The GAO must report its findings and recommendations to Congress within two years. The bill itself makes no change to wildfire programs; it only commissions the study.
bills.brief: Directs the Comptroller General (GAO) to study and report within two years on federal programs and rules that enable or inhibit wildfire mitigation across land-ownership boundaries.

top_lines.headline: GAO Wildfire Study
subs: GAO studies federal programs and rules affecting cross-boundary wildfire mitigation
Examines whether changes would give agencies, states, local, and Tribal governments more funding or capacity
Reviews activities under the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003

top_lines.headline: Report to Congress
subs: GAO report due within 2 years of enactment
Must include recommendations to simplify cross-boundary wildfire mitigation

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Neguse (D-CO) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (Kim, Harder, Obernolte), the bill orders only a GAO study with no spending or regulatory mandate, which lowers opposition. Its bipartisan backing and low cost favor House passage, though as a study-only bill referred to two committees its Senate scheduling is uncertain.

sections.label: Section 2 — Study on Wildfire Mitigation Across Land Ownership Boundaries

items.main: Requires the Comptroller General to study existing federal programs, rules, and authorities that enable or inhibit wildfire mitigation across land-ownership boundaries on federal and non-federal land.
items.detail: The study must examine whether changes would give federal land management agencies, the Natural Resources Conservation Service, FEMA, the U.S. Fire Administration, states, and local and Tribal governments increased capacity or access to funding for wildfire mitigation. It must also review the activities carried out under subsection (e) of Section 103 of the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003, including how to improve their efficacy and whether that subsection increased agencies' and states' access to mitigation funding.

items.main: Requires a report to Congress within two years of enactment containing the study results and recommendations.
items.detail: The report goes to the House Committee on Natural Resources and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. It must include recommendations to simplify cross-boundary wildfire mitigation between federal land management agencies and state, local, and Tribal governments.

gaps: The bill commissions a study and recommendations on cross-boundary wildfire mitigation but does not direct any agency to act on the recommendations.
The bill requires the report within two years but specifies no funding for conducting the study.
The bill examines access to wildfire-mitigation funding but does not itself authorize or appropriate any mitigation funds.

added: A Comptroller General study on cross-boundary wildfire mitigation programs, rules, and authorities, with a report to Congress due within two years of enactment

bills.title: Florida Safe Seas Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act to prohibit feeding sharks in the exclusive economic zone off the State of Florida.
bills.summary: Federal law already makes it illegal to put food or other substances in the water to attract sharks in the ocean zone off Hawaii and U.S. Pacific territories, unless it is for harvesting sharks or covered by an exception. This bill extends that same ban to the federal waters off Florida.
bills.brief: Extends the existing federal shark-feeding prohibition to the exclusive economic zone off Florida.

top_lines.headline: What the Shark-Feeding Ban Does
subs: Bans putting food in the water to attract sharks, except to harvest them
Currently applies to federal waters off Hawaii and U.S. Pacific territories

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Adds Florida's exclusive economic zone to the prohibition

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Webster (R-FL) with cosponsor Soto (D-FL), the bill is a narrow bipartisan amendment extending an existing prohibition to one additional state, which limits opposition. It passed the House by voice vote, but with few cosponsors its Senate timing is uncertain.

sections.label: Section 2 — Prohibition on Feeding Sharks in Exclusive Economic Zone off State of Florida

items.main: Amends Section 317 of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act to add Florida to the existing shark-feeding prohibition.
items.detail: The amendment strikes 'the State' and inserts 'the States', and inserts 'and Florida' after 'Hawaii'. The underlying prohibition makes it unlawful to introduce food or other substances into the water to attract sharks for any purpose other than to harvest them, within the exclusive economic zone covered by the section. The statute's existing exceptions still apply: where the Secretary or state law finds no public health hazard or safety risk, or where the activity is part of a research program funded in whole or in part by appropriated funds.

gaps: The bill extends the shark-feeding prohibition to Florida's exclusive economic zone but does not state any penalty specific to violations off Florida, relying on the existing statute's enforcement.

The bill adds Florida to a prohibition originally written for the Pacific Ocean Area but does not address whether the section's Pacific-area exceptions translate to Atlantic and Gulf waters off Florida.
The bill bans attracting sharks by feeding but does not address other shark-attraction practices that do not involve introducing food or substances into the water.

modified: Magnuson-Stevens Act Section 317 shark-feeding prohibition coverage: exclusive economic zone off Hawaii and U.S. Pacific territories -> also includes the exclusive economic zone off Florida

bills.title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025
bills.summary: The FCC's high-cost universal service program pays companies to build broadband networks in rural and hard-to-serve areas. This bill requires the FCC to set up a vetting process so that money only goes to applicants who can show they actually have the technical, financial, and operational ability and a real business plan to build the networks they promise. It also requires minimum penalties for applicants that win an award and then default before they are authorized to begin.
bills.brief: Requires the FCC to create a vetting process for high-cost universal service fund applicants and set minimum penalties for pre-authorization defaults.

top_lines.headline: Applicant Vetting Process
subs: FCC must start a rulemaking within 180 days to vet applicants
Applicants must document technical, financial, and operational capability and a business plan
Proposals judged against established standards and the applicant's past compliance history

top_lines.headline: Default Penalties
subs: Penalty for pre-authorization defaults set at no less than $9,000 per violation
Base forfeiture may not be capped below 30 percent of the applicant's total support

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Houchin (R-IN) with one cosponsor, the bill passed the House and was placed on the Senate calendar. A Senate companion on the same subject (the Rural Broadband Protection Act, S-98) has already been enacted, which reduces the need for separate enactment of this House version even though the underlying policy enjoys bipartisan support.

sections.label: Section 2 — Vetting Process for Prospective High-Cost Universal Service Fund Applicants

items.main: Adds a new subsection (m) to Section 254 of the Communications Act requiring the FCC to vet applicants for new high-cost universal service funding awards.
items.detail: Within 180 days of enactment, the FCC must begin a rulemaking to establish the vetting process. Applicants must include in their initial application a proposal with enough detail and documentation for the FCC to determine they have the technical, financial, and operational capabilities and a reasonable business plan to deploy the proposed network. The FCC must evaluate proposals against established technical, financial, and operational standards — including the standards in its Digital Opportunity Data Collection orders (WC Docket No. 19-195) — and against the applicant's history of complying with federal broadband-deployment funding programs.

items.main: Requires minimum penalties for applicants that default before authorization.
items.detail: In adopting rules for any new covered funding award, the FCC must set a penalty for pre-authorization defaults of at least $9,000 per violation and may not limit the base forfeiture to less than 30 percent of the applicant's total support, unless the Commission demonstrates the need for lower penalties in a particular instance.

gaps: The bill applies the vetting process to new covered funding awards made on or after the date the rules are promulgated but does not address existing awards or recipients already receiving high-cost support.
The bill sets a floor for pre-authorization default penalties but does not address penalties for defaults that occur after an applicant is authorized.
The bill requires the FCC to evaluate an applicant's compliance history but does not specify how far back that history must be reviewed or what level of past non-compliance disqualifies an applicant.

added: A new Section 254(m) of the Communications Act requiring an FCC vetting process for high-cost universal service fund applicants
A minimum penalty of at least $9,000 per violation for pre-authorization defaults, with base forfeiture not capped below 30 percent of total support

bills.title: To direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from Venezuela that have not been authorized by Congress.
bills.official_title: To direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from Venezuela that have not been authorized by Congress.
bills.summary: This is a concurrent resolution invoking the War Powers Resolution to direct the President to pull U.S. Armed Forces out of Venezuela unless Congress has explicitly authorized their use through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for military force. It expresses the will of both chambers and does not change any law.
bills.brief: Directs the President, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Venezuela absent congressional authorization.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive on Venezuela
subs: Invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution
Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Venezuela
Exception only if authorized by a declaration of war or specific military-force authorization

bills.likelihoodReason: The concurrent resolution failed in the House on January 22, 2026 on a 215-215 tie vote (a tie defeats the measure). Because it did not pass the House, it cannot proceed to the Senate, and the matter is effectively closed for this measure.

sections.label: Section 1 — Removal of the Use of United States Forces for Hostilities Within or Against Venezuela

items.main: Directs the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)), to remove United States Armed Forces from Venezuela.
items.detail: The directive applies unless the use of those forces is explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific statutory authorization for the use of military force. The resolution is a single operative section and contains no findings or additional provisions.

gaps: The resolution directs removal of forces not authorized by Congress but does not state a deadline by which the President must complete the removal.
The resolution invokes the War Powers Resolution mechanism but does not specify which current U.S. military activities in or around Venezuela it considers unauthorized.
The resolution directs removal absent authorization but does not address forces engaged in self-defense or other activities not amounting to hostilities.

bills.title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran.
bills.official_title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran.
bills.summary: This concurrent resolution invokes the War Powers Resolution to direct the President to end U.S. military hostilities against Iran within 30 days unless Congress explicitly authorizes them through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for the use of military force. It states that U.S. forces were introduced into hostilities against Iran on February 28, 2026, and includes carve-outs preserving self-defense, a defensive troop presence, and intelligence-sharing. It expresses the will of both chambers and does not change any law.
bills.brief: Directs the President, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against Iran within 30 days of February 28, 2026, absent congressional authorization.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive on Iran
subs: Directs the President to end hostilities against Iran within 30 days
Triggered by U.S. forces entering hostilities against Iran on February 28, 2026
Exception only if authorized by a declaration of war or specific military-force authorization

top_lines.headline: Carve-Outs Preserved
subs: Does not bar self-defense of U.S. forces, facilities, or allies from imminent attack
Does not bar a defensive troop presence in the region
Does not disrupt intelligence collection, analysis, or coalition intelligence-sharing

bills.likelihoodReason: The concurrent resolution failed in the House on May 14, 2026 on a 212-212 tie vote (a tie defeats the measure). Because it did not pass the House, it cannot proceed to the Senate, and the matter is effectively closed for this measure.

sections.label: Section 1 — Findings

items.main: States congressional findings, including that U.S. Armed Forces were introduced into hostilities against Iran on February 28, 2026, and that Congress has not declared war or provided specific statutory authorization for those hostilities.
items.detail: The findings describe Iran as the leading state sponsor of terrorism and an adversary of the United States, cite its ballistic missile program, terrorist proxies, and pursuit of a nuclear weapon, and note Congress's sole constitutional power to declare war under Article I, Section 8. They also state the President is required to brief Congress on the deployment of forces, including the estimated scope and duration of their use, under the War Powers Resolution.

sections.label: Section 2 — Termination of Use of Force

items.main: Directs the President, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against Iran no later than 30 days after February 28, 2026, unless explicitly authorized by Congress.
items.detail: The termination covers hostilities against Iran or any part of its government or military, including potential ground forces in a combat role or used for occupation. A rule of construction states the section does not prevent the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, diplomatic facilities, or allied states from imminent attack; does not prevent maintaining a troop presence in the region for defensive purposes; and does not force removal of forces in the region not engaged in hostilities against Iran.

sections.label: Sections 3-4 — Rules of Construction

items.main: Adds rules of construction protecting intelligence activities and clarifying the resolution does not authorize force.
items.detail: Section 3 provides that nothing in the resolution may be construed to influence or disrupt intelligence, counterintelligence, or investigative activities relating to threats in or emanating from Iran or surrounding countries, including the collection, analysis, and coalition sharing of intelligence where the President determines sharing is appropriate. Section 4, consistent with section 8(a)(1) of the War Powers Resolution, states that nothing in the resolution may be construed as authorizing the use of military force.

gaps: The resolution directs removal from hostilities against Iran but does not define what constitutes the 'hostilities' that began on February 28, 2026.
The resolution preserves a defensive troop presence and self-defense but does not specify who determines whether a given action is offensive hostilities or permitted self-defense.
The resolution sets a 30-day removal deadline but does not address enforcement if the President does not comply.

bills.title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2025
bills.summary: This law gives veterans a cost-of-living raise. Effective December 1, 2025, it increases the dollar amounts paid for veterans' service-connected disability compensation and for dependency and indemnity compensation paid to survivors, raising them by the same percentage as the annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment.
bills.brief: Increases veterans' disability compensation and survivors' dependency and indemnity compensation rates, effective December 1, 2025, by the same percentage as the Social Security COLA.

top_lines.headline: Veterans' Compensation Raise
subs: Raises disability compensation and additional compensation for dependents
Raises the clothing allowance and dependency and indemnity compensation
Effective December 1, 2025

top_lines.headline: Tied to Social Security
subs: Increase equals the same percentage as the Social Security COLA effective December 1, 2025
VA must publish the adjusted rates in the Federal Register

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on November 25, 2025 as Public Law 119-42. It passed the Senate on November 9 and the House on November 17, 2025. Sponsored by Sen. Moran (R-KS) with 22 cosponsors, annual veterans' COLA legislation is routinely bipartisan.

sections.label: Section 2 — Increase in Rates of Disability Compensation and Dependency and Indemnity Compensation

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to increase, effective December 1, 2025, the dollar amounts in effect on November 30, 2025 for several veterans' benefit categories.
items.detail: The increased amounts are wartime disability compensation (38 U.S.C. 1114), additional compensation for dependents (1115(1)), the clothing allowance (1162), dependency and indemnity compensation to a surviving spouse (1311(a)-(d)), and dependency and indemnity compensation to children (1313(a) and 1314). Each amount is increased by the same percentage as the Social Security title II benefit increase effective December 1, 2025 under section 215(i) of the Social Security Act. The Secretary may administratively adjust certain other disability rates under Public Law 85-857 consistent with these increases.

sections.label: Section 3 — Publication of Adjusted Rates

items.main: Requires the Secretary to publish the adjusted rates in the Federal Register.
items.detail: Publication must occur no later than the date the corresponding Social Security amounts are required to be published under section 215(i)(2)(D) of the Social Security Act for fiscal year 2026.

gaps: The law ties the veterans' increase to the Social Security COLA percentage but does not state the numeric percentage of the increase in the bill text.
The law adjusts the listed compensation categories but does not address other VA benefits not enumerated in section 2(b).
The law sets the increase effective December 1, 2025 but does not provide for a separate raise if Social Security makes a later adjustment within the same period.

modified: Veterans' disability compensation, dependents' additional compensation, clothing allowance, and dependency and indemnity compensation rates: increased effective December 1, 2025 by the Social Security COLA percentage

bills.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
bills.official_title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
bills.summary: This law requires the Attorney General to publicly release all unclassified Justice Department records relating to Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days, in a searchable and downloadable format. It bars withholding anything to avoid embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity, while still allowing narrow redactions to protect victims, remove child sexual abuse material, and guard genuinely classified national-security information. The DOJ must justify every redaction in the Federal Register and report to Congress.
bills.brief: Requires the Attorney General to publicly release all unclassified DOJ records relating to Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days, in searchable form, with only narrowly defined redactions allowed.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Document Release
subs: AG must release all unclassified Epstein-related DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorney records within 30 days
Must be published in a searchable and downloadable format
Covers flight logs, immunity and plea deals, detention and death records, and internal DOJ communications

top_lines.headline: Limits on Withholding
subs: No record may be withheld for embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity
Redactions allowed only for victim privacy, CSAM, active investigations, images of death/abuse, or properly classified material
Every redaction needs written justification published in the Federal Register and sent to Congress

top_lines.headline: Reporting and Named Officials
subs: AG must report to the Judiciary Committees within 15 days of completing the release
Report must list all government officials and politically exposed persons named in the materials, with no redactions

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on November 19, 2025 as Public Law 119-38. The House passed it on November 18 and the Senate on November 19, 2025.

sections.label: Section 2 — Release of Documents Relating to Jeffrey Epstein

items.main: Requires the Attorney General, within 30 days of enactment, to make publicly available in searchable and downloadable format all unclassified DOJ records relating to Jeffrey Epstein.
items.detail: The mandate covers records held by the DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices across nine categories, including Epstein's investigations and prosecutions, Ghislaine Maxwell, flight logs and travel records, individuals and government officials named in connection with his activities, entities tied to his trafficking or financial networks, immunity and non-prosecution agreements and sealed settlements, internal DOJ communications about charging decisions, records concerning destruction or concealment of evidence, and documentation of his detention and death including autopsy and medical examiner files.

items.main: Bars withholding records to protect reputations or for political reasons, while permitting narrow, justified redactions.
items.detail: No record may be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity to any official, public figure, or foreign dignitary. The AG may redact only segregable portions that contain victim personally identifiable information, child sexual abuse material as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2256, material that would jeopardize an active investigation (narrowly tailored and temporary), images of death or abuse, or properly classified national-security information. Every redaction requires a written justification published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress, and classified covered information must be declassified to the maximum extent possible — with an unclassified summary required where it cannot be.

sections.label: Section 3 — Report to Congress

items.main: Requires the Attorney General to report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees within 15 days of completing the release.
items.detail: The report must list all categories of records released and withheld, summarize the redactions made and their legal basis, and list all government officials and politically exposed persons named or referenced in the released materials. No redactions are permitted on that list of named officials under the prohibited-grounds rule.

underreported.summary: Any decision to classify covered Epstein-related information after July 1, 2025 must be published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress, including the date of classification, the identity of the classifying authority, and an unclassified summary of the justification.
underreported.why_unreported: The headline obligation is releasing existing records, but this provision separately governs future classification actions, applying a retroactive cutoff date to constrain classifying covered information rather than disclosing already-held documents.

gaps: The law requires release within 30 days and reporting after completion but does not specify a consequence or enforcement mechanism if the Attorney General misses the deadline or withholds records improperly.
The law permits temporary withholding to protect active investigations but does not set an outer time limit on how long such material may remain withheld.
The law requires publishing a written justification for each redaction but does not provide a process for the public or Congress to challenge a redaction it considers unjustified.

added: A requirement that the Attorney General publicly release, within 30 days, all unclassified DOJ records relating to Jeffrey Epstein in searchable and downloadable format
A prohibition on withholding records for embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity
A requirement to publish a written justification in the Federal Register for every redaction and to report named officials and politically exposed persons to the Judiciary Committees
