bills.title: VA Home Loan Program Reform Act
bills.official_title: VA Home Loan Program Reform Act
bills.summary: This law overhauls how the VA helps veterans who fall behind on a VA-guaranteed home loan. It creates a new Partial Claim Program in which the VA buys part of a defaulted loan to bring it current, requires lenders to walk a veteran through a mandatory sequence of foreclosure-prevention options before the VA steps in, and raises funding authorization for homeless-veteran service programs.
bills.brief: Creates a VA Partial Claim Program to prevent foreclosures, mandates a loss-mitigation sequence before the VA purchases a defaulted loan, and raises homeless-veteran program funding.

top_lines.headline: Partial Claim Program
subs: VA may buy part of a defaulted VA-guaranteed loan to prevent foreclosure
Partial claim capped at 25% of unpaid principal (30% for borrowers who missed a payment between Mar 1, 2020 and May 1, 2025)
Program sunsets five years after enactment

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Loss Mitigation
subs: VA must prescribe a required sequence of loss-mitigation options lenders offer veterans
VA may not purchase an entire loan until the veteran completes the sequence
VA default decisions are final and not subject to judicial review

top_lines.headline: Homeless Veteran Funding
subs: $344M authorized for comprehensive homeless-veteran service programs for each of FY2025 and FY2026
$257.7M authorized for each fiscal year thereafter through FY2030

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 30, 2025 as Public Law 119-31. The House passed it on May 19 and the Senate on July 15, 2025, following a House Veterans' Affairs Committee report (No. 119-104).

sections.label: Section 2 — Authority of the Secretary in Case of Default

items.main: Amends Section 3732 of title 38 to expand the VA's authority to act on a defaulting guaranteed loan and adds a mandatory loss-mitigation sequence.
items.detail: The VA may pay the loan holder an amount necessary to avoid foreclosure, obtain a secured interest in the property, and require the holder to place the loan in forbearance and execute necessary documents. A new subsection (d) directs the Secretary to prescribe loss-mitigation procedures, including a mandatory sequence of options (such as a partial claim agreement) offered to the veteran, and bars the VA from purchasing an entire loan until the veteran completes that sequence. Decisions under this paragraph are final, not subject to judicial review, and not treated as benefit decisions under section 511. The VA may set processing standards based on lender certification and must conduct random-sampling post-payment audits.

sections.label: Section 3 — Partial Claim Program

items.main: Creates a new Partial Claim Program (38 U.S.C. 3737) under which the VA purchases a portion of a defaulted or at-risk guaranteed loan to prevent or resolve default.
items.detail: The VA pays the loan holder the amount needed to prevent default and takes a secured interest subordinate to the first-lien guaranteed loan. A partial claim may not exceed 25 percent of the unpaid principal balance, or 30 percent for borrowers who missed a payment during the period from March 1, 2020 to May 1, 2025. Only one partial claim is allowed per loan, except an additional claim is permitted for borrowers who missed payments during a presidentially declared major disaster or the 120 days after it. Funds are applied first to arrearages, decisions are final and not subject to judicial review, and the program terminates five years after enactment.

sections.label: Section 5 — Homeless Veteran Program Funding

items.main: Increases the authorization of appropriations for comprehensive service programs for homeless veterans under Section 2016 of title 38.
items.detail: The prior open-ended authorization is replaced with $344M for each of fiscal years 2025 and 2026, and $257.7M for each fiscal year thereafter through fiscal year 2030. The earlier 'fiscal year 2015 and each subsequent fiscal year' language is changed to cover fiscal years 2015 through 2024.

underreported.section: Section 4 — Real Estate Representation Strategy Report
underreported.summary: Within 90 days of enactment, the VA must report to the Veterans' Affairs Committees on its strategy to ensure veterans using a VA-guaranteed loan are not disadvantaged when seeking representation by a real estate agent or broker, possibly including amendments to 38 CFR 36.4313.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is captioned around default and foreclosure authority, but this section addresses an unrelated buyer-side problem — veterans' access to real estate agent representation — rather than loan default handling.

gaps: The law makes VA partial-claim and default decisions final and not subject to judicial review but does not provide an internal appeal process for a veteran who disputes a decision.
The law sets a five-year sunset on the Partial Claim Program but does not address loans that default after the program terminates.
The law caps a partial claim at a percentage of unpaid principal but does not state what happens to a veteran whose arrearages exceed that cap.

added: A new VA Partial Claim Program (38 U.S.C. 3737) allowing the VA to purchase part of a defaulted guaranteed loan, with a five-year sunset
A mandatory loss-mitigation sequence that lenders must offer veterans before the VA purchases a loan
A required VA report within 90 days on ensuring veterans are not disadvantaged in securing real estate agent representation
modified: Authorization for comprehensive homeless-veteran service programs (38 U.S.C. 2016): open-ended 'FY2015 and each subsequent year' -> $344M for each of FY2025-2026 and $257.7M per year through FY2030
VA default authority under 38 U.S.C. 3732: expanded to allow forbearance, secured interests, and payments to avoid foreclosure, subject to the new loss-mitigation sequence

bills.title: MEGOBARI Act
bills.official_title: MEGOBARI Act
bills.summary: This bill responds to democratic backsliding in the nation of Georgia and its government's deepening ties with Russia, China, and Iran. It directs reports and a five-year U.S. strategy on Georgia, and sets up sanctions — visa bans and asset freezes — against Georgian officials and others who engage in corruption or violence to block Georgia's integration with Europe and NATO or who undermine Georgia's sovereignty. It also offers a path to expanded U.S. cooperation if Georgia's government demonstrates democratic progress. The whole Act sunsets after five years.
bills.brief: Authorizes visa and financial sanctions on Georgian officials who block Euro-Atlantic integration or undermine Georgia's sovereignty, and orders reports and a five-year U.S. strategy on Georgia.

top_lines.headline: Sanctions on Georgian Officials
subs: President must determine within 90 days which Georgian officials blocked Euro-Atlantic integration through corruption or violence
Mandatory visa ineligibility and revocation for those affirmatively identified
Discretionary asset freezes plus mandatory visa sanctions for undermining Georgia's sovereignty

top_lines.headline: Reports and Strategy
subs: Classified report on Russian intelligence assets in Georgia within 180 days, with a China annex
Five-year U.S. bilateral strategy within 90 days, including whether Georgia stays the second-highest U.S. funding recipient in Europe and Eurasia

top_lines.headline: Conditional Re-engagement
subs: If the President certifies sustained democratic progress, the U.S. should expand exchanges and military cooperation
Sense of Congress to suspend the U.S.-Georgia Strategic Partnership Commission until reforms occur
Entire Act sunsets five years after enactment

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Wilson (R-SC) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (Cohen, Hudson, Veasey) and 18 cosponsors total, the bill passed the House and was placed on the Senate calendar. Georgia-focused, anti-Russia sanctions legislation generally draws bipartisan support, but mandatory sanctions on a partner government's officials and the discretionary waiver structure can slow Senate floor consideration.

sections.label: Section 5 — Reports and Briefings

items.main: Requires a classified report on Russian intelligence penetration in Georgia and a five-year U.S. strategy for bilateral relations.
items.detail: Within 180 days, the Secretary of State, with the Director of National Intelligence and Secretary of Defense, must submit a classified report on Russian intelligence elements and assets in Georgia, with an annex on Chinese influence and potential Russian-Chinese cooperation. Within 90 days, the Secretary and USAID Administrator must submit a five-year strategy outlining objectives for bilateral ties, the tools and funding to achieve them, an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest recipient of U.S. funding in the Europe and Eurasia region, and a plan to support civil society and independent media. The strategy is unclassified with a classified annex.

sections.label: Section 6 — Sanctions

items.main: Directs the President to determine within 90 days which Georgian officials and family members knowingly engaged in corruption or violence to block Euro-Atlantic integration, and to impose visa sanctions on them.
items.detail: Covered persons include anyone who served as a Member of Georgia's Parliament or senior party official on or after January 1, 2014, leadership officials of the Georgian government (law enforcement, intelligence, judicial, local), and benefiting immediate family. Those affirmatively identified face mandatory visa ineligibility and revocation under subsection (d)(2). A separate authority lets the President impose IEEPA asset-blocking (discretionary) and visa sanctions (mandatory) on foreign persons who undermine the peace, security, stability, sovereignty, or territorial integrity of Georgia.

items.main: Sets out the sanctions, waivers, exceptions, and a broader-corruption review.
items.detail: Sanctions consist of IEEPA property blocking and visa ineligibility/revocation. The President may waive sanctions for national-security reasons or changed circumstances (renewable 180-day waivers for the sovereignty-based sanctions). Implementing regulations are due within 120 days. Within 180 days the President must report on foreign persons engaged in significant corruption in Georgia. Exceptions cover authorized intelligence activities, U.N. headquarters obligations, humanitarian and agricultural/medical transactions, and the importation of goods. Sanctions terminate when the President certifies a person has stopped the triggering conduct or at the Act's sunset.

sections.label: Section 7 — Additional Assistance With Respect to Georgia

items.main: Provides for expanded U.S. cooperation with Georgia if the President certifies sustained democratic progress.
items.detail: Upon the President's certification that Georgia has shown significant and sustained progress reinvigorating its democracy and advancing Euro-Atlantic integration, the Secretary of State should enhance people-to-people contacts and academic exchanges, and the President, with the Secretary of Defense, should maintain and as appropriate expand military cooperation — including territorial-defense equipment and related training — to help deter Russian aggression.

underreported.summary: The mandatory inadmissibility review reaches any individual who served as a Member of Georgia's Parliament or as a senior official of a Georgian political party at any point on or after January 1, 2014, not only current officeholders.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around responding to recent backsliding, but this provision applies the corruption/violence screen to more than a decade of past and former parliamentarians and party officials, a far wider pool than sitting government officials.

underreported.summary: The required five-year strategy must include an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest recipient of U.S. funding in the Europe and Eurasia region.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond the sanctions headline, this directs an explicit review that could lead to reducing Georgia's U.S. assistance, a budgetary consequence not evident from the bill's title.

gaps: The bill mandates a determination of which officials blocked Euro-Atlantic integration but does not define the threshold of 'significant acts of corruption' that triggers mandatory sanctions.
The bill directs an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest U.S. funding recipient but does not itself change or condition any specific assistance program.
The bill provides broad national-security waivers for sanctions but does not set a limit on how many covered officials may be waived or for how long in aggregate.
The bill sets a five-year sunset for the entire Act but does not address what happens to sanctions still in effect on persons who continue the triggering conduct after sunset.

added: Mandatory visa sanctions on Georgian officials and family members determined to have engaged in corruption or violence blocking Euro-Atlantic integration
Discretionary IEEPA asset-blocking and mandatory visa sanctions for foreign persons undermining Georgia's sovereignty or territorial integrity
A classified report on Russian intelligence assets in Georgia and a five-year U.S. bilateral strategy
A five-year sunset on the entire Act

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.title: Making appropriations for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.official_title: Making appropriations for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: This is the annual spending bill that funds military base construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs for fiscal year 2027. It pays for new construction and family housing across the armed services, and funds veterans' disability and pension benefits, VA medical care, cemeteries, and related agencies. As is standard for the VA, most of its health care money is appropriated a year ahead, becoming available October 1, 2027 for fiscal year 2028.
bills.brief: Provides fiscal year 2027 appropriations for military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, including advance-funded VA medical care for fiscal year 2028.

top_lines.headline: Military Construction
subs: $5.51B for Navy and Marine Corps construction
$3.76B Defense-Wide and $3.71B Air Force construction
$2.13B for Army construction

top_lines.headline: VA Medical Care (Advance-Funded)
subs: $70.7B for medical services and $42B for community (non-VA) care, available Oct 1, 2027
$13.54B medical facilities and $12B medical support and compliance
$54.59B Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund

top_lines.headline: Veterans Benefits and Related Agencies
subs: $283.81B advance for compensation and pensions; $23.57B readjustment benefits
$3.74B for Veterans Benefits Administration operating expenses
$118M Arlington National Cemetery; $107.9M American Battle Monuments Commission

bills.likelihoodReason: Reported by Rep. Carter (R-TX) from the House Appropriations Committee, the bill passed the House and was received in the Senate. Military construction and VA appropriations are among the least controversial of the annual spending bills and typically advance with bipartisan support, though final enactment depends on the broader appropriations process and any continuing-resolution dynamics.

sections.label: Title I — Military Construction

items.main: Appropriates fiscal year 2027 military construction funds across the armed services, available until September 30, 2031.
items.detail: Accounts include $2.13B for Army construction, $5.51B for Navy and Marine Corps, $3.71B for Air Force, and $3.76B for Defense-Wide construction. Reserve and National Guard construction, family housing construction and operation, the NATO Security Investment Program ($481.8M), and the Department of Defense Base Closure Account ($465.2M) are also funded. Each service account reserves a capped amount for planning and design.

sections.label: Title II — Veterans Benefits Administration

items.main: Funds veterans' compensation, pension, and readjustment benefits, largely as advance appropriations for fiscal year 2028.
items.detail: Compensation and pensions receive $10.56B added for fiscal year 2027 plus a $283.81B advance becoming available October 1, 2027. Readjustment benefits receive a $23.57B advance, and veterans insurance and indemnities $90.9M. The Veterans Benefits Administration's general operating expenses are funded at $3.74B. Several loan-program accounts (housing, vocational rehabilitation, Native American veteran housing) receive administrative-expense appropriations.

sections.label: Title II — Veterans Health Administration

items.main: Provides VA medical care funding, with the health accounts appropriated a year in advance for fiscal year 2028.
items.detail: Medical services receive a $70.7B advance (plus $100M added for fiscal year 2027), medical community care $42B, medical support and compliance $12B, medical facilities $13.54B, and medical and prosthetic research $900M. The bill rescinds $1.65B from prior-year medical support and compliance funds and $754.3M from prior-year medical facilities funds. The Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund is funded at $54.59B.

sections.label: Title III — Related Agencies

items.main: Funds veterans- and military-cemetery-related agencies and the veterans courts.
items.detail: The American Battle Monuments Commission receives $107.9M, the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims $50M, Cemeterial Expenses (Arlington National Cemetery) $118M, and the Armed Forces Retirement Home $77M from its trust fund (with $27M paid from the general fund). The National Cemetery Administration is funded at $500M under Title II.

underreported.summary: The bill rescinds $1.65B from medical support and compliance funds and $754.3M from medical facilities funds that had become available October 1, 2026 under the Continuing Appropriations Act (division D of Public Law 119-37).
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is new VA appropriations, but these provisions claw back previously appropriated medical funds, reducing the net new money below the gross appropriation figures.

underreported.summary: 25 percent of the VA general administration appropriation may not be obligated until the Secretary of Veterans Affairs testifies before the Appropriations Committees on the President's fiscal year 2027 budget request.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond simply funding VA administration, this provision conditions release of a quarter of the money on a future congressional testimony appearance, a control mechanism not evident from the account heading.

gaps: The bill advance-funds VA medical care for fiscal year 2028 but does not itself set fiscal year 2028 funding for the rest of the VA or for military construction, which remain on the annual cycle.
The bill rescinds prior-year medical support and medical facilities funds but does not state which planned activities those rescinded amounts would have covered.
The bill funds military construction across the services but does not, in its text, specify the individual projects, which are left to the tables in the accompanying committee report.

added: Fiscal year 2027 appropriations for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies, with VA medical accounts advance-funded for fiscal year 2028
removed: $1.65B rescinded from prior-year VA medical support and compliance funds
$754.3M rescinded from prior-year VA medical facilities funds

bills.title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
bills.official_title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
bills.summary: This is a farm bill — the broad, multi-year law that reauthorizes most U.S. Department of Agriculture programs across twelve subject areas, from crop supports and conservation to food aid, farm credit, rural development, research, forestry, energy, and crop insurance. It also reauthorizes the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly food stamps) and makes administrative changes to how states run it. Many existing program authorizations that lapsed are extended through 2031.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes USDA farm, conservation, trade, rural, research, and crop-insurance programs and SNAP through 2031, with disaster-assistance, specialty-crop, dairy, and SNAP administrative changes.

top_lines.headline: Commodities and Disaster Aid
subs: Extends suspension of permanent price support authority from 2023 to 2031
Creates a Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework for disaster and market losses
Expands the Tree Assistance Program with initial payments and a Sept 30, 2035 sunset

top_lines.headline: SNAP and Nutrition
subs: Lets states hire contractors for SNAP processing when error rates hit 6 percent or backlogs occur
Requires EBT card security rulemaking within 6 months
Makes SNAP online purchasing authority permanent; reauthorizes anti-trafficking enforcement to 2031

top_lines.headline: Conservation, Credit, and Rural Programs
subs: Reauthorizes conservation programs (CRP, EQIP, CSP, easements, partnerships)
Updates farm ownership and operating loan eligibility and limits
Reauthorizes rural development, trade/food-aid, research, forestry, energy, and crop insurance programs

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Thompson (R-PA), the bill passed the House and was received in the Senate. Comprehensive farm bills typically have bipartisan agricultural-state support, but disagreements over the nutrition title and overall cost can stall reconciliation between the chambers, leaving final passage uncertain.

sections.label: Title I — Commodities

items.main: Extends commodity price-support authority and adds disaster and specialty-crop assistance.
items.detail: Section 1001 extends the suspension of permanent price support authority under the Agricultural Act of 2014 from 2023 to 2031. Section 1002 expands the Tree Assistance Program — covering biennial crops and pest losses, allowing replanting with alternative varieties, stand densities, or locations, adding a 120-day deadline for application decisions and an optional initial payment, with that payment authority sunsetting September 30, 2035. Section 1003 creates a new Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework for producers hit by adverse events, with payment limits tied to the Food Security Act and a floor of not less than $900,000 for entities deriving at least 75 percent of income from farming. The title also includes dairy reporting, storage facility loans, and supply-chain provisions.

sections.label: Title IV — Nutrition

items.main: Reauthorizes SNAP and makes administrative changes to how states operate the program.
items.detail: A new declaration of policy ties SNAP to preventing diet-related chronic disease. Section 4103 lets state agencies hire contractors to handle SNAP certification and other functions when they cannot process applications timely (for reasons such as pandemics, staffing shortages, or disasters), when their payment error rate is at or above 6 percent, or when applications surge — subject to safeguards against incentives to deny eligibility. Other sections extend prohibited-fee, anti-trafficking, and program authorization provisions from 2023 to 2031, require EBT card security rulemaking within 6 months, require reporting of all identified payment errors, and make SNAP online-purchasing authority permanent. Subtitles B and C reauthorize commodity distribution, the commodity supplemental food program, and nutrition-incentive programs.

sections.label: Title II — Conservation

items.main: Reauthorizes and adjusts USDA conservation programs.
items.detail: The title covers the Conservation Reserve Program and farmable wetland program, the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (including payment limits and conservation innovation grants), the Conservation Stewardship Program with state soil-health assistance, agricultural and forest conservation easement programs, the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, and other programs such as feral swine eradication and emergency conservation and watershed programs. Funding and administration provisions address the Commodity Credit Corporation and delivery of technical assistance.

sections.label: Titles III, V-XII — Trade, Credit, Rural, and Other Programs

items.main: Reauthorizes the remaining farm bill program areas, largely by amending existing USDA statutes.
items.detail: Title III reauthorizes food aid and agricultural trade programs (Food for Peace, McGovern-Dole, Food for Progress, market development). Title V updates farm ownership and operating loan eligibility, experience requirements, and limits. Title VI covers rural development, including rural health and broadband (Rural Electrification Act amendments). Title VII reauthorizes agricultural research, extension, and education. Title VIII addresses forestry, Title IX energy and biofuels, Title X horticulture and marketing, Title XI crop insurance (including a specialty crop advisory committee), and Title XII miscellaneous provisions on livestock and other matters.

underreported.summary: For a person or legal entity that derives at least 75 percent of average gross income from farming, ranching, or silviculture, the standard payment limitation does not apply and the Secretary sets the maximum specialty-crop emergency payment, which may not be set lower than $900,000.
underreported.why_unreported: The framework is presented as broad specialty-crop disaster assistance, but this provision exempts entities deriving at least 75 percent of income from farming from the standard payment limitation and guarantees them a payment ceiling of no less than $900,000, set by the Secretary.

underreported.section: Section 4103 — Contractor Trigger at 6 Percent Error Rate
underreported.summary: States may contract out SNAP certification and other functions whenever their payment error rate reaches 6 percent, in addition to during backlogs or application surges.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision is labeled staffing flexibility, but it also lets a state respond to a high error rate by adding contractors rather than by other corrective measures; the temporary-shortage authority expires only once the error rate falls below 6 percent.

gaps: The bill reauthorizes most programs through 2031 but, in the text reviewed, relies on existing statutory funding mechanisms rather than stating new multi-year funding totals for each title.
The bill creates a Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework but makes its payment factor subject to the availability of appropriations without guaranteeing a funding level.
The bill adds SNAP contractor authority tied to error rates and backlogs but does not set standards for contractor accuracy or accountability beyond barring incentives to deny eligibility.
The bill reauthorizes conservation and rural programs but, in the text reviewed, does not specify the enrollment acreage or funding caps for each program in this top-level pass.

added: A Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework (new section 196A) for producers affected by adverse events
SNAP staffing flexibility allowing states to hire contractors during backlogs, surges, or when error rates reach 6 percent
An optional initial-payment option under the Tree Assistance Program, sunsetting September 30, 2035
Permanent authority for SNAP online purchasing
modified: Suspension of permanent price support authority extended from 2023 to 2031
Multiple SNAP authorizations (prohibited fees, anti-trafficking, program appropriations) extended from 2023 to 2031

bills.title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
bills.official_title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
bills.summary: This is the annual defense authorization law, which sets policy and authorizes funding levels for the entire Department of Defense for fiscal year 2026, plus the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons work, military construction, and the armed forces' personnel and health programs. This year's version also carries full-year authorizations for the State Department, the intelligence agencies, and the Coast Guard, and a large 'Other Matters' division covering outbound-investment screening, development finance, and more. It does not itself spend money; it authorizes and directs how defense money may be used.
bills.brief: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 funding and policy for the Department of Defense, nuclear-weapons programs, military construction, and personnel, and carries State, intelligence, and Coast Guard authorizations plus other national-security measures.

top_lines.headline: Defense Authorizations
subs: Authorizes procurement, research and development, operations, and maintenance for the armed forces
Sets military personnel end strengths, pay, benefits, and health-care policy
Includes space, cyberspace, and strategic-programs authorizations

top_lines.headline: Nuclear, Construction, and Allied Programs
subs: Authorizes the Energy Department's national-security and nuclear-weapons programs
Authorizes military construction across the services, including specific projects
$1.58B authorized for construction at Naval Station Norfolk; $1.04B at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard

top_lines.headline: Beyond the Pentagon
subs: Carries the State Department and Intelligence authorization acts for 2026 and the Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2025
Enacts the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025
Reauthorizes the U.S. development-finance agency, raising its liability cap to $205B

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on December 18, 2025 as Public Law 119-60. The annual National Defense Authorization Act is considered must-pass legislation and is enacted every year with bipartisan support.

sections.label: Division A — Department of Defense Authorizations

items.main: Authorizes Department of Defense programs and sets defense policy across seventeen titles for fiscal year 2026.
items.detail: The division authorizes procurement (Title I); research, development, test, and evaluation (Title II); operation and maintenance (Title III); military personnel end strengths (Title IV) and personnel policy (Title V); compensation and benefits (Title VI); health care (Title VII); acquisition policy and reform (Titles VIII and XVIII); department organization (Title IX); general provisions (Title X); civilian personnel (Title XI); matters relating to foreign nations (Title XII); cyberspace matters (Title XV); and space, strategic programs, and intelligence (Title XVI). Specific funding levels are set in the Division D funding tables.

sections.label: Divisions B & C — Military Construction and Energy Department National Security

items.main: Authorizes military construction and the Energy Department's national-security and nuclear programs.
items.detail: Division B authorizes military construction for the Army, Navy, Air Force, and defense agencies, international programs, Guard and Reserve facilities, and base realignment and closure activities — including named projects such as $1.58B for Naval Station Norfolk and $1.04B for Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. Division C authorizes the Energy Department's national-security programs (nuclear weapons activities), the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board, the naval petroleum reserves, and the Maritime Administration.

sections.label: Divisions E, F & G — State, Intelligence, and Coast Guard Authorizations

items.main: Carries full-year authorization acts for the State Department, the intelligence community, and the Coast Guard.
items.detail: Division E is the Department of State Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, covering organization, workforce, information security and cyber diplomacy, public diplomacy, and diplomatic security. Division F is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, including a title on artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. Division G is the Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2025, addressing Coast Guard organization and personnel, shipping and navigation, oil-pollution response, and sexual assault and harassment response.

sections.label: Division H — Other Matters

items.main: Carries non-defense national-security measures, including outbound-investment screening and development-finance reauthorization.
items.detail: Division H enacts the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 (Title LXXXV), establishing screening of certain U.S. investments abroad. The DFC Modernization and Reauthorization Act of 2025 (Title LXXXVII) reauthorizes the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, raising its maximum contingent liability to $205B and authorizing $5B for its Equity Investment Account for fiscal years 2026 through 2031. The division also covers financial services, judiciary, foreign affairs, and oceanic and atmospheric matters.

underreported.section: Title LXXXV — Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025
underreported.summary: The defense authorization carries a standalone law establishing a federal regime to screen certain outbound U.S. investments for national-security risk.
underreported.why_unreported: Carried inside the defense authorization rather than as a freestanding bill, this title creates an investment-screening framework whose subject is economic and financial regulation rather than defense authorization.

underreported.section: Title LXXXVII — DFC Maximum Contingent Liability
underreported.summary: The bill raises the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation's maximum contingent liability outstanding at any one time to $205B in the aggregate, and authorizes $5B for its Equity Investment Account through fiscal year 2031.
underreported.why_unreported: This expansion of a development-finance agency's lending and equity-investment capacity sits within the defense authorization's 'Other Matters' division, separate from any defense program.

gaps: The bill authorizes defense programs and policy but does not itself appropriate the money, which depends on a separate defense appropriations bill.
The bill sets authorization levels through the Division D funding tables but, in this top-level pass, the overall dollar total is the sum of those tables rather than a single stated figure.
The bill carries State, intelligence, and Coast Guard authorizations but does not consolidate their separate authorization cycles into the defense schedule.
The bill enacts an outbound-investment screening regime but, in the portion reviewed, leaves the detailed covered-transaction definitions to implementing regulations.

added: A federal outbound-investment national-security screening regime (Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025)
Reauthorization of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation with a $205B maximum contingent liability and a $5B Equity Investment Account through fiscal year 2031
Full-year authorizations for the State Department, intelligence community, and Coast Guard carried within the defense authorization
modified: Department of Defense program authorizations and policy updated for fiscal year 2026 across procurement, research, operations, personnel, and space and cyber programs

votes.question: On the Motion (Motion to Concur in the House Amendment to S. 1071)
On the Motion to Proceed S. 1071

bills.title: Fiscal Year 2025 Veterans Affairs Major Medical Facility Authorization Act
bills.official_title: An Act to authorize a major medical facility project for the Department of Veterans Affairs for fiscal year 2026 in St. Louis, Missouri, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-97 on June 9, 2026. Passed the Senate on December 17, 2025 and the House on May 19-20, 2026.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.summary: Authorizes the Department of Veterans Affairs to build a new medical facility in St. Louis, Missouri, and approves up to $1.76B for the construction.
bills.brief: Authorizes a $1.76B VA medical facility construction project in St. Louis, Missouri, for fiscal year 2026.

top_lines.headline: St. Louis VA Medical Facility
subs: $1.76B authorized for VA construction in St. Louis, Missouri
New bed tower, clinical expansion, admin building, utility plant, garages
Authorized for fiscal year 2026

sections.label: Section 2 — Authorization of Major Medical Facility Project

items.main: Authorizes a new VA medical facility project in St. Louis, Missouri, at a cost not to exceed $1.76B.
items.detail: The project consists of a new bed tower, clinical building expansion, a consolidated administrative building and warehouse, a utility plant, and parking garages. The same $1.76B is authorized to be appropriated from the Construction, Major Projects account for fiscal year 2026 (or the year in which funds are appropriated).

gaps: The Act authorizes the $1.76B to be appropriated but does not itself appropriate the funds, which depend on a later appropriations act.
The bill authorizes the St. Louis project but sets no construction timeline or completion deadline beyond the fiscal year 2026 authorization.
Titled the 'Fiscal Year 2025' authorization act, the bill authorizes the project for fiscal year 2026 and addresses no other facility projects.

added: Authorizes a new VA major medical facility project in St. Louis, Missouri — a new bed tower, clinical building expansion, consolidated administrative building and warehouse, utility plant, and parking garages

bills.title: Disapproving the action of the District of Columbia Council in approving the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Disapproving the action of the District of Columbia Council in approving the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-78 on February 18, 2026. Passed the House on February 4, 2026 and the Senate on February 11-12, 2026.

votes.question: On the Motion to Proceed H.J.Res. 142

bills.summary: Uses Congress's authority over the District of Columbia to overturn a D.C. Council act that revised the District's income and franchise tax rules.
bills.brief: Disapproves the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025, blocking it from taking effect.

top_lines.headline: D.C. Tax Act Disapproval
subs: Overturns D.C. Act 26-217, a D.C. Council tax measure
Acts under section 602(c)(1) of the D.C. Home Rule Act
Enacted as Public Law 119-78

sections.label: Disapproval of D.C. Council Act

items.main: Disapproves the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025, blocking it from taking effect.
items.detail: Congress disapproves D.C. Act 26-217, enacted by the Council of the District of Columbia on December 20, 2025 and transmitted to Congress on December 30, 2025 under section 602(c)(1) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act. The disapproval prevents the D.C. act from taking effect.

gaps: The resolution disapproves the act by name but does not describe what tax changes the D.C. measure would have made.
It addresses the 'Temporary' amendment act as named and does not reference any related permanent or emergency D.C. measure.

removed: Blocks D.C. Act 26-217 (the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025) from taking effect

bills.title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from Lebanon
bills.official_title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from Lebanon.
bills.likelihoodReason: Failed in the House on June 4, 2026 by a 92-324 vote. As a concurrent resolution it carries no force of law and is not presented to the President; the House defeat ends its progress.
bills.summary: Directs the President to withdraw U.S. military forces from Lebanon within 7 days, using Congress's war powers authority.
bills.brief: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon no later than 7 days after the resolution is adopted.

top_lines.headline: Withdrawal of Forces from Lebanon
subs: Directs removal of U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon
Deadline: 7 days after the resolution is adopted
Invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution

sections.label: Section 1 — Removal of United States Armed Forces from Lebanon

items.main: Directs the President to remove all U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon no later than 7 days after the resolution is adopted.
items.detail: Acts under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)), which allows Congress to direct the removal of armed forces by concurrent resolution. The resolution sets the removal deadline at not later than 7 days after its adoption.

gaps: The resolution directs withdrawal from Lebanon but does not define which forces, units, or deployments it covers.
It sets a 7-day removal deadline but specifies no consequence or enforcement mechanism if forces are not withdrawn.

bills.title: Common-Sense Law Enforcement and Accountability Now in DC Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To repeal the Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 enacted by the District of Columbia Council.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Clyde (R-GA) with 29 cosponsors; passed the Republican-majority House. In the Senate it would need 60 votes, and repealing a D.C. policing-and-justice-reform law is likely to draw unified Democratic opposition, making passage uncertain.
bills.summary: Repeals a 2022 District of Columbia policing law, restoring the prior law as if that act had never been enacted.
bills.brief: Repeals the D.C. Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 and revives the law it had changed.

top_lines.headline: D.C. Policing Law Repeal
subs: Repeals the D.C. Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022
Restores any law that act had amended or repealed
Uses Congress's authority over the District of Columbia

sections.label: Section 2 — Repeal of Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022

items.main: Repeals the D.C. Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 (D.C. Law 24-345).
items.detail: Any provision of law that the 2022 D.C. act amended or repealed is restored or revived as if that act had never been enacted. The bill exercises Congress's constitutional authority over the District of Columbia.

gaps: The bill repeals the 2022 D.C. policing act but does not enumerate which underlying laws are restored beyond directing that they revive as if the act had never passed.
It repeals the act outright but does not establish any replacement policing or accountability standard for the District.

modified: Restores any law the 2022 D.C. act had amended or repealed, as if that act had never been enacted
removed: Repeals the D.C. Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 (D.C. Law 24-345)

bills.title: Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Energy Act of 2020 to include critical materials in the definition of critical mineral, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Ciscomani (R-AZ) with 13 cosponsors from both parties; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. The change is a technical, definitional alignment with bipartisan backing, which improves its odds of a Senate vote.
bills.summary: Changes federal law so materials the Energy Department designates as 'critical materials' are also treated as 'critical minerals,' and requires the official list to be updated quickly.
bills.brief: Amends the Energy Act of 2020 to fold 'critical materials' into the definition of 'critical mineral' and requires the list to be updated within 45 days of a new designation.

top_lines.headline: Critical Minerals Definition
subs: Adds 'critical materials' to the definition of 'critical mineral'
List must be updated within 45 days of a new designation
Amends Section 7002 of the Energy Act of 2020

sections.label: Section 2 — Critical Materials Included as Critical Minerals

items.main: Amends the Energy Act of 2020 so any material the Secretary of Energy designates as a 'critical material' also counts as a 'critical mineral.'
items.detail: Rewrites the definition of 'critical mineral' in Section 7002 of the Energy Act of 2020 (30 U.S.C. 1606) to include critical materials determined by the Secretary of Energy. When the Secretary determines a non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material is a critical material, the published critical minerals list must be updated to include it within 45 days.

gaps: The bill merges critical materials into the critical minerals list but does not change what benefits or requirements attach to that designation.
It sets a 45-day deadline to add new critical materials but specifies no process or deadline for removing materials no longer considered critical.

added: Requires the critical minerals list to be updated within 45 days of a new critical-material determination
modified: Definition of 'critical mineral' in the Energy Act of 2020 (30 U.S.C. 1606) now includes 'critical materials' determined by the Secretary of Energy

bills.title: Law-Enforcement Innovate to De-Escalate Act
bills.official_title: To modernize Federal firearms laws to account for advancements in technology and less-than-lethal weapons, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Fitzgerald (R-WI) with Rep. Correa (D-CA) and 95 cosponsors; passed the House. Broad bipartisan cosponsorship and a narrow, technical scope improve its chances in the Senate, though it has not yet received a Senate vote.
bills.summary: Carves 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' out of federal firearms restrictions and defines what qualifies, so they are not regulated as firearms.
bills.brief: Amends federal firearms law to exempt 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' from regulation and defines the term.

top_lines.headline: Less-Than-Lethal Device Exemption
subs: Exempts 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' from Title 18 firearms rules
Defines the term by velocity (under 500 fps) and design
Attorney General must rule on a device within 90 days

sections.label: Section 2 — Exemption of Certain Less-Than-Lethal Projectile Devices

items.main: Amends the firearms definitions in Section 921(a) of title 18 to exclude 'less-than-lethal projectile devices.'
items.detail: Defines a less-than-lethal projectile device as one not designed (and not readily convertible) to fire common handgun, rifle, or shotgun ammunition or any projectile faster than 500 feet per second, designed to be used in a way not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury, and unable to accept semiautomatic-style ammunition feeding devices. If a person asks the Attorney General to determine whether a device qualifies, the Attorney General must decide within 90 days of receiving the device.

gaps: The bill exempts qualifying devices from Title 18 firearms rules but does not address how state law treats the same devices.
It requires the Attorney General to rule within 90 days of receiving a device but specifies no consequence if that deadline is missed.

added: Creates a 90-day Attorney General determination process for whether a device qualifies as less-than-lethal
modified: Firearms definition in Section 921(a) of title 18 now excludes 'less-than-lethal projectile devices'

bills.title: Captain Accursio “Gus” Sanfilippo Young Fishermen's Development Act
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Young Fishermen's Development Act.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Moulton (D-MA) with 8 cosponsors from both parties; passed the House. As a straightforward reauthorization of an existing, modestly funded program, it faces little organized opposition, though it still needs Senate floor time.
bills.summary: Extends the funding authorization for the Young Fishermen's Development program — a Sea Grant marine program — for five more years, through fiscal year 2031.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Young Fishermen's Development program's funding through fiscal year 2031.

top_lines.headline: Young Fishermen's Development Program
subs: A Sea Grant marine program under federal law
$2M per year authorized through fiscal year 2026

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extends the funding authorization through fiscal year 2031
Strikes '2026' and inserts '2031' in the program's funding section

sections.label: Section 1 — Young Fishermen's Development Act Reauthorization

items.main: Extends the Young Fishermen's Development program's funding authorization from fiscal year 2026 through fiscal year 2031.
items.detail: Amends Section 5(a) of the Young Fishermen's Development Act (33 U.S.C. 1144(a)) by striking '2026' and inserting '2031.' Current law authorizes $2M per year for the program; the bill extends that authorization period by five years without changing the amount.

gaps: The bill extends the program's funding authorization but does not change the $2M annual amount or the program's activities.
It reauthorizes appropriations through fiscal year 2031 but does not itself appropriate any funds.

modified: Young Fishermen's Development Act funding authorization extended from fiscal year 2026 to fiscal year 2031

bills.title: A bill to amend chapters 83 and 84 of title 5, United States Code, to authorize an increase of the retirement age for members of the Capitol Police
bills.official_title: An Act to amend chapters 83 and 84 of title 5, United States Code, to authorize an increase of the retirement age for members of the Capitol Police.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-95 on May 29, 2026. Passed the Senate on May 14, 2026 and the House on May 19, 2026.
bills.summary: Lets the Capitol Police Board set the mandatory retirement age for Capitol Police officers anywhere from 57 to 62, instead of the fixed age of 60.
bills.brief: Replaces the fixed mandatory retirement age of 60 for the Capitol Police with a Board-set age between 57 and 62.

top_lines.headline: Capitol Police Retirement Age
subs: Mandatory retirement age changes from a fixed 60 to a Board-set 57-62
Applies under both the CSRS and FERS retirement systems

sections.label: Section 1 — Authorization To Increase Retirement Age for Member of the Capitol Police

items.main: Allows the Capitol Police Board to set the mandatory retirement age between 57 and 62, replacing the fixed age of 60.
items.detail: Amends Section 8335(c) (Civil Service Retirement System) and Section 8425(c) (Federal Employees' Retirement System) of title 5 by striking 'becomes 60 years of age' and inserting an age determined by the Board that is not less than 57 and not more than 62 years of age.

gaps: The bill authorizes a Board-set retirement age but does not state what age the Board will choose or when.
It changes the mandatory separation age going forward but does not address officers who already separated at 60.

modified: Capitol Police mandatory retirement age: fixed 60 -> Board-set, not less than 57 and not more than 62 (CSRS Section 8335(c) and FERS Section 8425(c) of title 5)

bills.title: SBA Fraud Enforcement Extension Act
bills.official_title: To extend the statute of limitations for fraud under certain pandemic programs, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Downing (R-MT) with 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. Extending fraud-enforcement deadlines for pandemic programs is a low-controversy measure, which favors Senate passage.
bills.summary: Sets a 10-year deadline for prosecuting or pursuing fraud in two pandemic relief programs: the Shuttered Venue Operators Grants and the Restaurant Revitalization Fund.
bills.brief: Establishes a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud in the Shuttered Venue Operators Grant and Restaurant Revitalization Fund programs.

top_lines.headline: Pandemic Grant Fraud Deadline
subs: 10-year statute of limitations for fraud in two pandemic grant programs
Covers Shuttered Venue Operators grants
Covers Restaurant Revitalization Fund grants

sections.label: Section 2 — Statute of Limitations for Certain Programs

items.main: Sets a 10-year statute of limitations for criminal prosecution or civil enforcement of fraud in two pandemic grant programs.
items.detail: Adds a 10-year filing deadline (from the date of the violation or conspiracy) for specified fraud offenses under sections 371, 641, 1001, 1028A, 1029, 1341, 1343, 1349, 1956, and 1957 of title 18 and sections 3729 and 3802 of title 31. It applies to the Shuttered Venue Operators Grants (15 U.S.C. 9009a) and the Restaurant Revitalization Fund (15 U.S.C. 9009c).

gaps: The title refers broadly to 'SBA' fraud and 'certain pandemic programs,' but the bill addresses only the Shuttered Venue Operators and Restaurant Revitalization programs.
It extends the deadline to file fraud cases but does not change the penalties or the underlying grant programs.

added: 10-year statute of limitations for fraud in the Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program (15 U.S.C. 9009a)
10-year statute of limitations for fraud in the Restaurant Revitalization Fund (15 U.S.C. 9009c)

bills.title: Flexibility for Workers Education Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to exclude certain activities from hours worked, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Failed in the House on January 13, 2026 by a 209-215 vote. A failed floor vote ends the bill’s progress in this Congress.
bills.summary: Says that time employees spend in voluntary, off-hours education or training does not count as paid 'hours worked' under federal wage law.
bills.brief: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so voluntary, off-the-clock education or training time is not counted as hours worked.

top_lines.headline: Off-Hours Training Not Paid Time
subs: Voluntary off-hours education or training excluded from 'hours worked'
Applies whether or not the employer offers the activity
Activity must be voluntary, with no productive work performed

sections.label: Section 2 — Treatment of Attendance or Participation in Certain Activities

items.main: Excludes voluntary, off-hours education or training time from 'hours worked' under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
items.detail: Rewrites FLSA Section 3(o) (29 U.S.C. 203(o)). For minimum-wage and overtime purposes, time spent attending lectures, education or training programs, and similar activities is excluded from hours worked if it occurs outside regular working hours, is voluntary (with no adverse effect on employment for not attending), and involves no productive work for the employer. The existing exclusion for clothes-changing and washing under a collective-bargaining agreement is retained. The change applies to hours worked on or after enactment.

gaps: The exclusion depends on attendance being 'voluntary' and not affecting employment, but the bill does not specify how a worker disputes an employer's claim that training was voluntary.
It excludes the time from 'hours worked' for federal wage purposes but does not address state wage-and-hour laws.

modified: FLSA 'hours worked' (Section 3(o), 29 U.S.C. 203(o)) now also excludes voluntary off-hours education and training time

bills.title: Save Local Business Act
bills.official_title: To clarify the treatment of 2 or more employers as joint employers under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Comer (R-KY) with 2 cosponsors. The House adopted a rule (H. Res. 988) to consider the bill, but no passage vote has been recorded. The joint-employer standard is among the most contested issues in labor law; a narrow direct-control test would draw unified opposition from labor and Democratic members, making the 60 votes needed in the Senate difficult.
bills.summary: Narrows when two companies are treated as 'joint employers' under federal labor and wage laws, requiring direct, hands-on control over the workers.
bills.brief: Sets a 'direct, actual, and immediate control' test for joint-employer status under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act.

top_lines.headline: Joint Employer Standard
subs: Joint-employer status requires direct, actual, immediate control
Control over hiring, firing, pay, supervision, scheduling, or discipline
Applies under both the NLRA and the FLSA

sections.label: Section 2 — Clarification of Joint Employment

items.main: Limits joint-employer status to employers that directly, actually, and immediately exercise significant control over another company's employees.
items.detail: Amends the National Labor Relations Act (Section 2(2), 29 U.S.C. 152(2)) and the Fair Labor Standards Act (Section 3(d), 29 U.S.C. 203(d)). An employer is a joint employer only if each employer directly, actually, and immediately exercises significant control over essential terms and conditions of employment — such as hiring, discharging, setting pay and benefits, day-to-day supervision, assigning schedules or tasks, or discipline. The FLSA applies the same test using that Act's own definitions of 'employee' and 'employer.'

gaps: The bill defines joint-employer status by direct control but does not name how franchise or staffing-agency relationships are treated.
It sets the standard for the NLRA and FLSA only and does not address joint-employer rules under other employment laws.

modified: Joint-employer test under the NLRA (Section 2(2)) and FLSA (Section 3(d)) limited to employers with direct, actual, and immediate control over essential terms and conditions of employment

bills.title: Hydropower Licensing Transparency Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Power Act to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to annually submit to Congress a report on the status of ongoing hydropower relicensing applications.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Schrier (D-WA) with Rep. Fulcher (R-ID) and 3 cosponsors; passed the House and was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. A bipartisan reporting-transparency measure with no spending or regulatory mandate tends to clear the Senate when floor time allows.
bills.summary: Requires federal energy regulators to send Congress an annual report on the status of hydropower dam relicensing applications that have been pending for years.
bills.brief: Requires FERC to submit an annual report to Congress on the status of long-pending hydropower relicensing applications.

top_lines.headline: Hydropower Relicensing Reports
subs: FERC must report annually on pending relicensing applications
Covers licenses where notice was given 3+ years earlier
First report due within 180 days of enactment

sections.label: Section 2 — Annual Relicensing Status Report

items.main: Requires FERC to report to Congress every year on hydropower relicensing applications that remain pending after early notice.
items.detail: Adds subsection (g) to Section 15 of the Federal Power Act (16 U.S.C. 808). Within 180 days of enactment and annually after, FERC must report on each new license where the existing licensee notified the Commission (under subsection (b)(1)) at least 3 years before the report that it intended to apply, but the new license has not yet been issued. Each report must include the notice date, any docket number, whether an application was filed, the status and anticipated issue date, upcoming proceedings, and any required actions by the licensee, FERC, and fish and wildlife agencies.

gaps: The bill requires annual status reports on delayed relicensing but sets no deadline for FERC to actually issue the licenses.
It requires reporting on applications pending 3+ years after notice but does not address applications where notice was given more recently.

added: Annual FERC report to Congress on the status of long-pending hydropower relicensing applications (new subsection (g) of Federal Power Act Section 15)
